summary: The Abhayapaddhati is an extensive commentary by the Indian Buddhist master Abhayākaragupta on the Buddhakapālamahātantra. Written at Vikramaśīla in the 25th regnal year of King Rāmapāla, it interprets esoteric ritual practices and yogic realization. This digital file comprises chapters 9 through 14, focusing on post-initiatory conduct (caryā) and related tantric practices.

summary: The Abhidharmakośakārikā consists of verses in eight chapters composed by Vasubandhu, synthesizing the doctrinal system of the Sarvāstivāda-Vaibhāṣika school of Abhidharma. The text classifies all conditioned and unconditioned phenomena across eight subjects: ultimate constituents (dhātu), sensory and psychological faculties (indriya), cosmological realms (loka), intentional action (karma), underlying afflictions (anuśaya), noble spiritual paths and attainers (mārgapudgala), transcendent cognitions (jñāna), and meditative absorptions (samāpatti). Designed for memorization, it served as the baseline verse manual upon which Vasubandhu constructed his famous auto-commentary (Abhidharmakośabhāṣya), and it remains a fundamental Abhidharma textbook.

summary: The Abhidharmasamuccaya is Asaṅga's synthesis of Abhidharma doctrine from a Mahāyāna perspective. The treatise is structured into two main parts: the Lakṣaṇasamuccaya, which categorizes dharmas across the skandhas, dhātus, āyatanas, and fifty-one mental factors (caittas), and the Viniścayasamuccaya, which analyzes the noble truths, doctrinal exposition, attainment of liberation, and rules of philosophical dialectic.

Adopting the structure of traditional Tibetan monastic textbooks (don bdun cu), it delineates the eight general subjects (aṣṭau padārthāḥ) and seventy specific topics (saptatiḥ padārthāḥ) of the Abhisamayālaṅkāra. Each topic is systematically analyzed by its formal definition (lakṣaṇa), taxonomic divisions (bheda), and spiritual stage boundary (avadhi / sīmā).

Expounded by Tathāgatas and Bodhisattvas led by Mahāvairocana and Vajrapāṇi, the sūtra teaches seventeen aphorisms on the innate purity of passion, sensory experience, and phenomenal reality (viśuddhi-pada) through the lens of emptiness. summary: The Anupalabdhirahasya ('The Secret of Non-Apprehension') is a treatise on Buddhist epistemology by Jñānaśrīmitra addressing the problem of negative cognition. Building on Dharmakīrti's framework, Jñānaśrīmitra defines non-perception (anupalabdhi) not as a mere absence of awareness (upalabdhivirahamātra), but as an implicative negation (paryudāsa) consisting in the apprehension of something incompatible or distinct. He defends the status of anupalabdhi as a valid inferential sign (liṅga) for proving absence (abhāva) against rival Buddhist formulations and non-Buddhist theories such as the Bhāṭṭa Mīmāṃsā doctrine of an independent means of knowledge (abhāvapramāṇa).

summary: The Aparimitāyurnāmamahāyānasūtra is a popular Mahāyāna dhāraṇī scripture wherein the Buddha instructs Mañjuśrī on the longevity dhāraṇī and boundless merits of the Buddha Aparimitāyurjñānasuviniścitatejorāja, who dwells in the pure land Aparimitaguṇasaṃcaya. summary: The Arthaviniścayasūtra ('Discourse on the Ascertainment of Meaning') is an early Buddhist doctrinal compendium that systematically presents twenty-seven core categories of Buddhist doctrine and meditation practice. It opens with a thematic list (uddeśa) followed by analytical definitions (vibhaṅga) of the five aggregates, eighteen elements, twelve sense fields, twelvefold dependent origination, four noble truths, twenty-two faculties, thirty-seven aids to awakening (bodhipakṣadharmāḥ), the absorptions (dhyānas), formless attainments, and the marks of a Buddha. Closely aligned with mainstream Abhidharma and Sautrāntika taxonomies, it served as the base text for Vīryaśrīdatta's *Nibandhana*.

Opening with homage to the Triratna and an epithet litany invoking Avalokiteśvara as the dispeller of fear and worldly suffering, the text proclaims the supreme heart incantation of Hayagrīva (hayagrīvabrahmaparamahṛdayam) to eliminate poisons, banish spirits, and destroy malevolent sorcery (kākhorda) and planetary afflictions (graha).

summary: The Avayavinirākaraṇa ('Refutation of the Composite Whole') is a short polemical treatise by the late Buddhist logician Aśoka. Defending the Dignāga–Dharmakīrti pramāṇa tradition against Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika realists, Aśoka refutes the objective reality of the avayavin (a single composite whole posited as distinct from its parts). Applying the core Buddhist criterion that assigning contradictory properties (such as motion and rest, or visibility and obscuration) to an entity necessitates numerical multiplicity, he demonstrates that gross objects are mental superimpositions upon aggregates of partless atomic particulars.

summary: The Avikalpapraveśadhāraṇī is a short Mahāyāna dhāraṇī-sūtra setting forth the doctrinal method for entering the nonconceptual realm (avikalpa-/nirvikalpadhātu). It outlines the sequential abandonment of four categories of conceptual signs—fundamental defiled phenomena (the five aggregates), remedies (the perfections), reality/suchness, and fruition/attainment—effected through non-mental engagement (amanasikāra). The sūtra was cited and commented upon by Indian masters including Kamalaśīla and Maitrīpa.

summary: The Aṣṭamātṛkāstotra is an 11-verse Sanskrit Buddhist hymn venerating the Eight Mothers (Aṣṭamātṛkā). Following an opening salutation to Vighneśvara (Gaṇeśa), each stanza addresses one of the eight protective mother goddesses assigned to a compass direction (Brahmāṇī in the East, Vārāhī in the South, Indrāṇī in the West, Māheśvarī in the North, Kaumārī in the Southeast, Vaiṣṇavī in the Southwest, Cāmuṇḍā in the Northwest, and Caṇḍikā/Mahālakṣmī in the Northeast), identifying her vehicle, complexion, and emblems. The final verses invoke the goddesses collectively in connection with the eight pilgrimage seats (aṣṭapīṭha), sacred trees, and the eight Bhairavas, concluding with reverence to the planetary deities (navagraha) and Yama.

summary: The Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā ('Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines') is the foundational and earliest extensive scripture in the Prajñāpāramitā corpus. Centered on dialogues between the Buddha and disciples including Subhūti, Śāriputra, and Ānanda at Vulture Peak, it expounds the core Mahāyāna doctrine of emptiness (śūnyatā), the non-apprehension (anupalambha) of independent dharmas, and the altruistic path of the bodhisattva aiming at omniscience (sarvākārajñatā). Across 32 chapters, it promotes the veneration, recitation, and copying of Prajñāpāramitā manuscripts, culminating in the pilgrimage and self-sacrifice of Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita under the teacher Dharmodgata.

summary: The Balimālikā by Ācārya Sumatisiṃha is a tantric Buddhist ritual manual setting forth verses, mantras, and procedures for presenting bali offerings. Beginning with verses derived from the Subāhuparipṛcchātantra, the manual prescribes 63 distinct offerings addressed to diverse Vajrayāna deities, protectors, and spirits, including Vajrayoginī, Mahākāla, Kurukullā, and Cakrasaṃvara. The text was preserved in Nepalese manuscript witnesses and transmitted to Tibet, where it was translated by Dharmadīpaṃkara and Dharmapālabhadra.

summary: A modern Sanskrit essay on Buddhist epistemology (pramāṇamīmāṃsā). It argues that Buddhist discussion of the means of knowledge cannot be shown to be later than the Nyāyasūtra, as Vidyabhusana and Dasgupta held, pointing to the Buddhist positions criticised in the Nyāyasūtra's pūrvapakṣas and to the Vigrahavyāvartanī, and to the canonical emphasis on refuting other doctrines (Udāna, Aṣṭasāhasrikā). It then discusses Dignāga's and Dharmakīrti's doctrine of the twofold form (dvairūpya) of cognition, defended both on the externalist and on the Vijñānavāda view.

summary: A modern comparative scholarly treatise composed in Sanskrit examining the concept and practice of compassion (karuṇā) in Buddhism and the Hindu Purāṇas. The author analyzes the early Buddhist canonical understanding of compassion, the Bodhisattva ideal, and the cultivation of the brahmavihāras, comparing them with depictions of empathy, grace, and forgiveness in Purāṇic narratives (including the Matsya, Viṣṇu, and Kūrma Purāṇas). The work concludes by emphasizing the fundamental ethical affinity between Buddhist and Purāṇic philosophical thought, as exemplified by the Purāṇic assimilation of the Buddha into the daśāvatāra.

summary: The Bhadracaryāpraṇidhāna (or Bhadracarīpraṇidhāna) consists of 62 verses formulating the bodhisattva Samantabhadra's supreme vows and aspiration prayer. It forms the climactic conclusion of the Gaṇḍavyūhasūtra (the final chapter of the Buddhāvataṃsakasūtra) and circulated widely throughout Mahāyāna Asia as an independent liturgical text and devotional hymn. It articulates the canonical sevenfold worship (saptavidhānapūjā: homage, offerings, confession of sins, rejoicing in merit, entreating buddhas to turn the Dharma wheel, requesting them to remain in the world, and dedication of merit) before concluding with aspirations for rebirth in Sukhāvatī.

summary: The Bhikṣuṇīvinaya of the Mahāsāṃghika-Lokottaravādin school is the sole Vinaya text governing Buddhist nuns preserved substantially in Sanskrit. It recounts the origin narrative of the nuns' order with Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī and the formulation of the eight 'weighty rules' (gurudharma), followed by an extensive vibhaṅga (rule-by-rule casuistry and commentary) on the nuns' Prātimokṣa, miscellaneous disciplinary matters (Bhikṣuṇīprakīrṇaka), and a concluding uddāna summary of the monks' miscellaneous section (Bhikṣuprakīrṇaka). summary: The Bhāvanākrama ('Stages of Meditation') by Kamalaśīla (c. 740–795 CE) is an influential triad of treatises formulating the graduated Mahāyāna path according to the Yogācāra-Madhyamaka synthesis. Composed in Tibet in connection with the Samyé (bSam yas) debate, it defends the classical Indian gradualist method of spiritual development against the sudden, non-conceptualizing quietism attributed to the Chinese Chan master Heshang Moheyan. Across the three works, Kamalaśīla systematizes the cultivation of compassion (karuṇā), the awakening mind (bodhicitta), and the balanced union (yuganaddha) of calm abiding (śamatha) and analytical discernment (vipaśyanā) leading to the non-conceptual realization of emptiness.

summary: The Bodhicaryāvatāra ('Entering the Way of Awakening') is an influential Mahāyāna verse manual and classic of Buddhist devotional-philosophical literature composed in ten chapters by Śāntideva. It outlines the spiritual cultivation of the bodhisattva, tracing the generation and stabilization of the awakening mind (bodhicitta), ritual confession, vigilance (apramāda), guard over awareness (saṃprajanya), and the perfections of patience (kṣānti), vigor (vīrya), meditative absorption (dhyāna), and dedication of merit (pariṇāmanā). The ninth chapter develops a Madhyamaka dialectical critique of intrinsic nature (svabhāva), refuting rival Buddhist and non-Buddhist philosophical systems.

summary: Śāntideva's Bodhicaryāvatāra is a foundational Mahāyāna Buddhist poetic treatise detailing the development and practice of the mind of awakening (bodhicitta) through the perfections (pāramitā). Prajñākaramati's Bodhicaryāvatārapañjikā is the principal surviving Sanskrit commentary, offering running grammatical glosses, extensive canonical citations, and detailed Madhyamaka exegesis across chapters 1 through 9. Its extensive commentary on chapter 9 (Prajñāpariccheda) forms a crucial monument of late Indian Prāsaṅgika-Madhyamaka philosophy, critiquing both non-Mahāyāna Buddhist and non-Buddhist systems.

summary: The Bodhisattvabhūmi constitutes the fifteenth section of the encyclopedic Yogācārabhūmi, composed in approximately the 4th century CE. It serves as an exhaustive manual of the Mahāyāna bodhisattva path, systematically treating spiritual lineage (gotra), the generation of the aspiration for awakening (bodhicitta), the perfections (pāramitās), ethics (śīla), and the stages of spiritual maturation (vihāras and bhūmis). Its fourth chapter, the Tattvārthapaṭala, forms a cornerstone of early Yogācāra philosophy, presenting a foundational analysis of the inexpressible nature of reality (nirabhilāpyasvabhāva) underlying linguistic and conceptual designations (prajñapti).

summary: Short excerpts of modern Sanskrit prose. The first paragraph defines nāṭya as the triad of dance, song and instrumental music and names Bharata's Nāṭyaveda and Abhinavagupta's Abhinavabhāratī. The 'Buddhamata' section describes Buddhism as a reaction against rigid caste rules and animal sacrifice, lists its ethical values, cites the Sigālovāda and Mahārāhula suttas, and outlines its spread to China, Japan and Lanka. The 'Buddhamuni' section summarises the Buddha's life from his birth at Kapilavastu to his nirvāṇa, dating events in the Kali era and ending with the Purāṇic view of the Buddha as an avatāra of Viṣṇu.

summary: An 18-verse Vajrayāna stotra celebrating the tutelary deity Cakrasaṃvara (Heruka) and his maṇḍala retinue. Following salutations to Heruka and Vajravārāhī, the hymn maps the twenty-four ḍākinīs to their traditional sacred pilgrimage sites (pīṭhas such as Pullīramalaya, Jālandhara, and Oḍḍiyāna) and the internal channels of the human body across the body, speech, and mind wheels (kāyavākcittacakra). The stotra concludes with praises to the four animal-faced peripheral goddesses (Kākāsyā, Ulūkāsyā, etc.) and four gatekeeping deities, ending with a dedication of merit wishing that all beings attain the status of Vajraḍāka.

summary: The Catuḥṣaṣṭisaṃvarastotra is an anonymous Buddhist tantric hymn of the Cakrasaṃvara/Heruka cycle preserved in Nepalese manuscript collections. In 75 anuṣṭubh stanzas, it invokes Śrī Heruka Cakrasaṃvara and an elaborate retinue of sixty-four theriomorphic aspects or emanations (such as Meṣasaṃvara, Aśvasaṃvara, Vyāghrasaṃvara, and Kūrmasaṃvara) conjoined with their consorts. The final portion consists of an extensive phalaśruti detailing worldly protection, pacification of epidemics and famines, and the attainment of classical tantric accomplishments (siddhis).

summary: The Chandoratnākara ('Ocean of Metres') along with its autocommentary (Chandoratnākaravṛtti) by the 11th-century Vikramaśīla master Ratnākaraśānti is a foundational Buddhist manual of Indian metrics (chandaḥśāstra). Spanning six chapters, it systematically expounds syllabic metres (varṇavṛtta), moraic metres (mātravṛtta/jāti), and combinatorial algorithms (pratyaya) for calculating and generating metrical variations. A hallmark pedagogical feature of the treatise is that each definition is composed in the exact metre that it defines; the text played an influential role in the study of metrics in medieval Nepal and in Tibetan monastic universities.

summary: The Ekādaśamukha (also known as Ekādaśamukhahṛdaya) is an early esoteric Buddhist dhāraṇī-sūtra in which the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara reveals his eleven-faced heart-spell (hṛdaya) before the Buddha in the Jetavana monastery at Śrāvastī. The text details ten mundane benefits (including freedom from illness, weapons, poison, fire, and untimely death) and four transcendental fruits (including beholding the Tathāgatas at death and rebirth in Sukhāvatī) promised to practitioners who recite the spell, followed by prescriptive ritual instructions for bali offerings, lustrations, and homa rites. Surviving in Sanskrit in a birch-bark manuscript unearthed at Gilgit, the scripture formed a foundational text for the cult of the Eleven-Faced Avalokiteśvara throughout Central and East Asia.

summary: The Gaṇḍavyūhasūtra is a major Mahāyāna scripture that circulated both independently and as the climactic final section of the Buddhāvataṃsakasūtra. It recounts the spiritual pilgrimage of the youth Sudhana, who is instructed by Mañjuśrī to seek out fifty-three spiritual mentors (kalyāṇamitra)—representing varied genders, occupations, and stations—to learn the practice of a bodhisattva. The narrative culminates in visions of Maitreya's kūṭāgāra and Samantabhadra, depicting the cosmos (dharmadhātu) as an interconnected web of mutual interpenetration and closing with the famous Samantabhadracaryāpraṇidhāna aspiration.

Preserved as text no. 10 (GSS 10) in the Nepalese codex of the Guhyasamayasādhanamālā, it is distinctive among works in that collection in that the practitioner visualizes himself as the male deity Padmanarteśvara while evoking the goddess.

summary: The Guhyeśvarīstotra is a seven-verse Newar Buddhist devotional hymn in Mālinī metre dedicated to the goddess Guhyeśvarī, venerated at her sacred shrine in the Kathmandu Valley as the root (mūla) of the lotus supporting the Svayambhū caitya and identified with Prajñāpāramitā or Nairātmyā. Extracted from the Svayambhūpurāṇa, the hymn is attributed in the narrative to the Bodhisattva Mañjunātha (Mañjuśrī), who praises the cosmic form (viśvarūpa) and transcendent nature of the goddess. The first six verses close with the uniform refrain praising her lotus feet ('caraṇakamalayugmaṃ naumi devi tvadīyam'), followed by a seventh verse detailing the spiritual accomplishments (siddhi) granted by devout recitation.

summary: The Guhyāvalī is an esoteric Buddhist tantric treatise of 25 Sanskrit stanzas attributed to the siddhācārya Dauḍīpāda. Opening with an invocation to Vajrayoginī, it expounds Anuttarayoga tantric praxis, focusing on consort meditation (vajrābjayoga), immutable bliss (akṣarasukha), the four blisses, and the non-dual realization imparted directly through the spiritual guru's empowerment (adhiṣṭhāna). The text survives in Nepalese palm-leaf manuscripts (e.g. Cambridge University Library MS Add. 1699.2), where it is preserved with a Sanskrit commentary (Guhyāvalīvivṛti) by Paṇḍitasthavira Śrīghanadeva.

summary: The Gururatnatrayastotra is a seven-verse Newar Buddhist liturgical stotra praising the Three Jewels (Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha) and venerating the Guru. The text contains three distinct two-verse subsections praising the Buddha as the conqueror of mental afflictions, the Dharma (incorporating the opening mangala stanza of Haribhadra's Abhisamayālaṅkārāloka in praise of Prajñāpāramitā), and the Saṅgha (honoring both the eight classes of noble disciples and the great Bodhisattvas). It concludes with a popular devotional verse equating the Guru directly with the Buddha, Dharma, Saṅgha, and Vajradhara.

summary: The Guṇakāraṇḍavyūhasūtra is an all-verse Mahāyāna sūtra composed in Nepal as an extensive poetical reworking and expansion of the earlier prose Kāraṇḍavyūhasūtra. Framed as a dialogue between Jinaśrīrāja and Jayaśrī recounting the spiritual instructions given to King Aśoka by Upagupta, it glorifies the cosmic deeds and salvific emanations of Avalokiteśvara (Karuṇāmaya), promotes the six-syllable mantra (oṃ maṇi padme hūṃ), and details the merits of the poṣadha (aṣṭamīvrata) fasting ritual. Alongside the Svayaṃbhūpurāṇa, the work served as a foundational scripture for Newar Buddhism.

summary: The Hetubindu is an epistemological and logical treatise by the Buddhist master Dharmakīrti, focusing on the theory of the logical reason or probans (hetu), elucidating its threefold character (trairūpya) and classifying valid reasons into identity (svabhāva), effect (kārya), and non-cognition (anupalabdhi). It systematically investigates fallacies of reason (hetvābhāsa) and marks a development in Dharmakīrti's thought wherein explicit statement of the thesis (pakṣa) is treated as dispensable because it is already established by implication.

summary: The Hetubinduṭīkā by Bhaṭṭa Arcaṭa (c. 8th century CE) is an extensive commentary on Dharmakīrti's Hetubindu, an independent treatise examining the theory of logical reasons and inference. Arcaṭa discusses essential epistemological topics of Buddhist pramāṇavāda, including the preliminary statement of purpose (prayojana), the three conditions of a valid mark (trairūpya), the threefold classification of valid probantia, and the proof of momentariness (kṣaṇikatvānumāna). Preserved in Sanskrit and Tibetan, it served as a crucial intermediate authority between Dharmakīrti and later commentators such as Dharmottara and Durveka Miśra.

summary: The Hāratīstotra is a nine-verse Buddhist devotional stotra addressed to Hāratī / Yakṣeśvarī. The text describes her seated in lalitāsana upon an eight-petaled lotus on a jeweled throne, adorned with jewelry, embracing her child with her left arm while dispelling fear with her right hand. The concluding verse promises protection of children and prosperity to anyone who recites the hymn in their household at daybreak.

summary: The Jambhalastotra is a nine-verse Sanskrit hymn attributed to Candragomin, praising Jambhala, the Buddhist deity of wealth and abundance. The poet approaches the compassionate deity as an afflicted, weeping devotee, contrasting inanimate wish-granting objects with Jambhala's living mercy and lamenting that poverty continues to afflict him. The hymn concludes with a dedication wishing that by the merit of this prayer, living beings may become like Jambhala in bestowing all desired gifts.

summary: The Jātakamālā ('Garland of Birth-Stories'), also entitled Bodhisattvāvadānamālā, is an ornate Buddhist campū composition (mixed verse and prose) by Āryaśūra, datable to approximately the 4th century CE. It retells thirty-four stories exemplifying the Bodhisattva's practice of the perfections (pāramitās), such as giving (dāna), moral discipline (śīla), and patience (kṣānti), in previous births as human, divine, or animal figures. Widely celebrated as a masterpiece of classical Sanskrit kāvya.

It culminates in a phalaśruti promising the swift attainment of awakening (buddhatva).

summary: The Karmavibhaṅgopadeśa is an anonymous Buddhist exegetical treatise (upadeśa) preserved in a Nepalese palm-leaf manuscript (dated Nepāla Saṃvat 531). Serving as an exposition and commentary to the Mahākarmavibhaṅga, it examines the mechanics of karma and karmic fruition (vipāka). summary: A concise Mahāyāna Prajñāpāramitā sūtra spoken by the Buddha to Śakra (Kauśika) on Vulture Peak in Rājagṛha. The text expounds the nondual nature of the perfection of wisdom through negative dialectical statements, eighteen modes of emptiness (aṣṭādaśaśūnyatā), and verses found in the Vajracchedikā and the opening maṅgalācaraṇa of the Mūlamadhyamakakārikā. summary: The Kaṭhināvadāna is an edifying Buddhist ritual and narrative text preserved in Nepalese manuscripts that extols the spiritual merit of offering the kaṭhina cloth to the monastic Saṃgha at the conclusion of the rains-retreat (varṣā). Opening with Mahākāśyapa questioning the Buddha on the proper time and ceremonial procedures for spreading the kaṭhina, the work outlines detailed Vinaya prescriptions for measuring, stitching, marking, and dedicating the robe before presenting past-life narratives that illustrate karmic retribution and the fruits of generosity. Several of its embedded story motifs have direct parallels in the Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya Bhaiṣajyavastu.

summary: The Kālacakragaṇitopadeśa is an astronomical handbook (karaṇa) affiliated with the Buddhist Kālacakratantra tradition. summary: A pivotal Mahāyāna sūtra dedicated to glorifying the salvific activities and cosmic compassion of Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara across various realms of saṃsāra, including Avīci hell and the preta realm. The text is historically famous as the earliest known source to teach the six-syllable mantra Oṃ maṇi padme hūṃ (the ṣaḍakṣarī mahāvidyā) and to detail its benefits and mandala ritual. Composed in northern India circa the 4th to 5th century CE, it demonstrates direct thematic engagements with contemporary Śaiva cosmologies—such as presenting Hindu deities like Maheśvara, Brahmā, and Nārāyaṇa as emanations from Avalokiteśvara's body—and provided the foundation for Avalokiteśvara worship and the Maṇi Kabum in Tibet.

summary: The Kāśyapaparivartasūtra is an early Mahāyāna scripture cast as a dialogue between the Buddha and Mahākāśyapa on Vulture Peak at Rājagṛha. It expounds the bodhisattva path, emphasizing moral purity and warning against spiritual hypocrisy, attachment to monastic privileges, and intellectual pride. summary: A collection of 32 rhymed couplets (dohās) in Apabhraṃśa composed by the Buddhist mahāsiddha Kāṇha (Kṛṣṇācārya), embedded within an anonymous continuous Sanskrit commentary entitled Dohākoṣamekhalāṭīkā. The Sanskrit commentary provides word-by-word glosses and interprets the Apabhraṃśa couplets within the framework of Anuttarayogatantra systems, frequently citing authorities such as the Hevajratantra.

summary: The Kṣaṇabhaṅgasiddhir anvayātmikā is a philosophical treatise by the eleventh-century Buddhist epistemologist Ratnakīrti of Vikramaśīla. It establishes the Buddhist doctrine of universal momentariness (kṣaṇabhaṅga) via positive pervasion (anvayavyāpti): whatever exists is causally efficient (arthakriyākārin), and causal efficiency can only occur instantaneously, not successively or simultaneously over time (kramākramābhyām). Defending the inference against Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika and Mīmāṃsā realists, Ratnakīrti deploys reductio ad absurdum (prasaṅga) and contraposition (prasaṅgaviparyaya) to show that permanent entities cannot possess causal efficacy.

summary: The Laghutantraṭīkā (also known as Lakṣābhidhānāduddhṛtalaghutantrapiṇḍārthavivaraṇa) is an important commentary by Vajrapāṇi on the introductory portion (verses 1–10 1/2) of the Cakrasaṃvaratantra (Laghusaṃvara). Together with Vajragarbha's Hevajrapiṇḍārthaṭīkā and Puṇḍarīka's Vimalaprabhā, it constitutes one of the three core commentaries of the 'Bodhisattva trilogy' foundational to the Kālacakra exegetical corpus. The work interprets the Heruka/Cakrasaṃvara system through an emergent Kālacakra framework, emphasizing internal subtle-body physiology, the retention of bodhicitta, and the integration of Yoginītantra practice within monastic discipline.

summary: The Lalitavistara ('The Extensive Account of the [Buddha's] Play') is an elaborate Mahāyāna sūtra in 27 chapters composed in mixed Buddhist Hybrid Sanskrit prose and verse. It narrates the sacred biography of Śākyamuni Buddha from his decision to descend from Tuṣita heaven, his miraculous conception and birth in Lumbinī, his luxurious princely youth, four encounters, and great renunciation, to his austerities, defeat of Māra, awakening beneath the Bodhi tree, and first turning of the wheel of Dharma in Ṛṣipatana. Blending early biographical accounts (primarily Sarvāstivādin) with a docetic Mahāyāna perspective, the sūtra depicts the Buddha's earthly career as the deliberate, compassionate sport (lalita) of an already fully enlightened being, and served as a major inspiration for classical Buddhist art and literature across Asia.

summary: A Newar Buddhist ritual manual belonging to the distinctive Nepalese 'Pārājikā' corpus. Cast as a revelation from Bodhisattva Lokeśvara (Avalokiteśvara) to Tārā on ominous portents (utpāta) and pacification procedures (śāntividhi), the text catalogues various domestic and environmental prodigies—such as eclipses, meteors, unnatural animal behavior, domestic intrusions by predators or serpents, and poisoned wells—and prescribes apotropaic rites (śānti) including homa fire offerings, recitation of the Pañcarakṣā, kalaśapūjā, and donations to the saṅgha. Despite adopting the classical Vinaya designation 'pārājikā', the work does not address monastic expulsion but rather lay and household expiatory and pacification rituals.

summary: The Madhyamakaśālistambasūtra is a unique Sanskrit adaptation of the Śālistambasūtra. The work opens with the eight negations from the dedicatory verse of Nāgārjuna's Mūlamadhyamakakārikā and dispenses with the standard introductory narrative frame between Maitreya and Śāriputra, recasting the classical Buddhist exposition of internal and external dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) in explicit Madhyamaka terminology. The latter part of the text incorporates śāstric dialectic concerning the conditioned nature of entities (paratantrāś ca bhāvā vivādapadam) and cites the Candrapradīpasūtra (Samādhirājasūtra).

summary: Candrakīrti's Madhyamakāvatāra ('Introduction to the Middle Way') is a foundational Madhyamaka treatise designed to introduce Nāgārjuna's Mūlamadhyamakakārikā along the structure of the Mahāyāna bodhisattva path. Structured around the bodhisattva stages (bhūmi), this sixth chapter corresponds to the abhimukhī-bhūmi and the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā). Chapter 6 comprises the philosophical core, expounding the refutation of intrinsic production, an extensive critique of Yogācāra positions (such as the reality of consciousness, reflexive awareness, and the ālayavijñāna), the two truths, and the sixteen forms of emptiness.

summary: The Madhyāntavibhāgakārikā ('Verses Distinguishing the Middle from the Extremes') is a foundational doctrinal treatise of the Yogācāra school, traditionally counted as one of the 'Five Treatises of Maitreya'. In 111 verses across five chapters—on characteristics (lakṣaṇa), obscurations (āvaraṇa), reality (tattva), spiritual cultivation and results (pratipakṣabhāvanā-avasthā-phala), and the supreme vehicle (yānānuttarya)—it formulates the middle way (madhyamā pratipad) as avoiding both the extreme of reification and that of nihilistic denial. The treatise provides classical expositions of unreal mental construct (abhūtaparikalpa), the three natures (trisvabhāva), and emptiness (śūnyatā) understood as the absence of subject-object duality within that construct.

summary: The Mahogratārāstuti is a short devotional hymn addressed to Mahogratārā ('Great Fierce Tārā'). Following an opening Sragdharā stanza celebrating her terrifying iconography—with protruding fangs, a garland of human heads, and a skull-cup—petition verses beseech her for refuge using the refrain 'trāhi māṃ śaraṇāgatam'. The hymn identifies Tārā with forms including Gaurī, Lakṣmī, Mahāmāyā, Umā, and Sarasvatī, concluding with a phalaśruti promising boons, learning, victory in battle, and auspiciousness to reciters on lunar days such as the 8th, 14th, and 9th.

summary: The Mahogratārāṣṭakastotra (widely transmitted in Śākta tantric literature as Tārāṣṭaka or Nīlasarasvatīstotra) is an anonymous tantric hymn of praise to the wrathful goddess Mahogratārā / Nīlasarasvatī. Composed of eight verses in ornate Sragdharā metre followed by a three-verse phalaśruti, it eulogizes her fierce iconography—standing in pratyālīḍha posture on a corpse (śava) and bearing a sword, kartrī (chopper), skull-cup (kapāla), and blue lotus—imploring her for literary brilliance, protection, and liberation. The hymn provides a clear example of shared ritual poetry spanning Newar Vajrayāna Buddhism and Śākta Tantra.

summary: The Mahābodhibhaṭṭārakastotra is an eight-verse Sanskrit devotional hymn celebrating Gautama Buddha under the epithet Mahābodhibhaṭṭāraka. Every stanza concludes with the refraining hemistich 'śrīśākyasiṃhaṃ praṇamāmi nityam'. The hymn extols the somatic perfection and auspicious major and minor marks of the Buddha—including his crown, ūrṇā, lotus-like eyes, golden hue, knee-reaching arms, and wheel-marked hands—while praising him as the supreme teacher who delivers beings from threefold suffering.

summary: The Mahācakravartināmāṣṭottaraśatastotra is a 20-verse Buddhist tantric litany and formal supplication (adhyeṣaṇā) addressed to Sarvatathāgatamahācakravartin, an esoteric manifestation of Vajrasattva associated with Trailokyavijaya. Verses 1–16 enumerate 108 devotional epithets and honorific invocations ending with 'namo 'stu te', followed by praise of the deity as the firm essence (vajradṛḍhaṃ cittam) and progenitor of all Tathāgatas (vv. 17–18), a benefit verse (phalaśruti, v. 19), and a formal prayer (adhyeṣaṇā, v. 20) entreating the lord to manifest his tantric family for the welfare of beings. Originally situated in Chapter 6 (Trilokavijayamahāmaṇḍalavidhivistara) of the Yoga Tantra scripture Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṃgraha, it also circulated as an independent liturgical hymn in the Newar Buddhist tradition.

summary: The Mahākālastotra is a short Buddhist devotional hymn in 13 anuṣṭubh stanzas addressed to the two-armed (dvibhuja) wrathful protector Mahākāla. It invokes the deity as the granter of all prosperity (sarvasampattidāyaka) and protector of practitioners (siddhasādhakarakṣaka), describing his fierce iconographic attributes including the crown of skulls, necklace of severed heads, adornment of eight serpents, tiger-skin garment, chopper (kartikā), and skull-cup (kapāla). summary: The Mahāsannipātaratnaketudhāraṇīsūtra (also known as the Ratnaketuparivarta) is an influential Mahāyāna scripture that circulated both independently and as a major component of the expansive Mahāsannipāta corpus. Set in Rājagṛha, the narrative depicts the conversion of Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, the Buddha's subjugation of Māra and his host, discourses on karmic results and bodhisattva training, and potent protective dhāraṇī incantations. summary: A Buddhist metrical avadāna in 1,077 verses forming chapter 49 of the Mahajjātakamālā. Framed as a dialogue between King Aśoka and the arhat Upagupta, the narrative recounts the past life of the Buddha as King Maṇicūḍa, who was born with a jewel in his crest. It defends the authenticity of the Mahāyāna as Buddha's word and systematically treats refuge, spiritual lineage (gotra), the arising of bodhicitta, practice, reality (tattva), the perfections, the factors of awakening and the bodhisattva's qualities and stages, culminating in buddhahood. The bhāṣya explains each verse and supplies the structure of the argument; the work was translated into Chinese (T 1604) and Tibetan (D 4020, 4026) and commented upon by Asvabhāva and Sthiramati.

summary: The Mahāyānaviṃśikā ('Twenty Verses on the Great Vehicle') is a brief Buddhist treatise traditionally attributed to Nāgārjuna that synthesizes Madhyamaka and Yogācāra doctrines. It argues that external objects lack independent reality and that the world of saṃsāra is an illusory projection arising from conceptual fabrication (kalpanā) upon mind alone (cittamātra). The text concludes by urging practitioners to rely upon the Mahāyāna vehicle as the only means to cross the ocean of delusion.

summary: The Maṅgalaṣoḍaśastuti ('Sixteen-Verse Auspicious Hymn of Praise') is a sixteen-verse Sanskrit Buddhist hymn dedicated to the Buddha Śākyamuni (Śākyasiṃha), extracted from the Bhadrakalpāvadāna, an avadānamālā collection preserved in Nepalese manuscripts. Each verse recalls a distinct narrative episode or previous life (jātaka/avadāna) of the Buddha—including Maitrakanyaka, Supriya, Sudhana, Kuśa, and Saudāsa, and concluding with his journey from Kapilavastu to venerate the Svayambhū caitya in the Kathmandu Valley—invoking his protective power with the refrain 'sa no rakṣatu'. The hymn exemplifies the ritual and liturgical repurposing of narrative avadāna literature within Newar Buddhism.

summary: The Nairātmyaparipṛcchā ('Questions on Selflessness') is a short Mahāyāna scripture consisting of a prose opening dialogue and 26 verses. Departing from standard sūtra narrative conventions, it depicts non-Buddhist wanderers (tīrthikas) approaching Mahāyāna practitioners to question how bodily actions and affective states (laughter, crying, anger, jealousy) can arise if the body is devoid of a supreme self (paramātman). The Buddhist respondents elucidate the non-duality of existence and non-existence, the distinction between conventional reality (saṃvṛti) and ultimate reality (paramārtha), and the nature of all phenomena as illusory, dream-like appearances empty of intrinsic self-nature.

summary: The Nairātmyāśīḥstuti is a seven-verse Buddhist tantric benedictory hymn celebrating the goddess Nairātmyā, the principal consort in the Hevajratantra cycle. The verses praise her terrifying dancing form adorned with bone ornaments, carrying the kartrī and kapāla, and invoke her blessing to eliminate mental afflictions and worldly evils. The concluding verse identifies her with the internal yogic subtle body, specifically the synthesis of the three channels lalanā, rasanā, and avadhūtikā.

summary: The Nairātmāṣṭakastotra is a short eight-verse hymn (aṣṭaka) in anuṣṭubh meter addressed to the tantric Buddhist goddess Nairātmyā (Nairātmā), consort of Hevajra and personification of selflessness (nairātmya). The hymn praises her absolute nature as free of conceptual construct (nirvikalpa) and without support (nirālamba), while describing her wrathful iconographic attributes (one-faced, three-eyed, dancing on a corpse, carrying a chopper and skull-cup) and her retinue of the eight maṇḍala yoginīs (Gaurī, Caurī, Vetālī, Ghasmarī, Pukkasī, Śabarī, Caṇḍālī, and Ḍombī). Preserved in the Sanskrit manuscript collections of the Kathmandu Valley, it forms part of traditional Newar Vajrayāna devotional and liturgical practice.

summary: The Narakoddhārastotra ('Hymn on Rescue from Hell') is a 15-verse Sanskrit Buddhist devotional prayer seeking salvation from the sufferings of saṃsāra and the tortures of the hell realms. The speaker confesses grievous misdeeds—including the five heinous crimes (pañcānantarya), harming sentient beings, and desecrating stūpas—and repeatedly entreats the Buddha with the refrain 'trāhi māṃ hi tathāgata' ('rescue me, O Tathāgata!'). The concluding verse hails the Lord (Lokanātha) as the supreme king of physicians (vaidyarāja) capable of curing all diseases and delivering sentient beings across the three worlds.

summary: The Niraupamyastava ('Hymn to the Incomparable One') is a devotional philosophical poem of 25 stanzas in anuṣṭubh metre composed by Nāgārjuna, forming part of his famous Catuḥstava ('Four Hymns'). Composed as an encomium praising the Buddha, the work formulates foundational Madhyamaka themes in a devotional idiom: praising the Tathāgata as having neither originated nor extinguished any dharma, having spoken not a single syllable while yet teaching all disciples, and being empty of intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva) and conceptual proliferation (vikalpa). The hymn also contains prominent discussions of the two bodies of the Buddha (dharmakāya and janmakāya/rūpakāya) and affirms the ultimate unity of the vehicles (ekayāna) grounded in the non-differentiation of the dharmadhātu.

summary: The Nyāyabindu ('Drop of Logic') is Dharmakīrti's concise foundational primer on Buddhist epistemology and logic, articulating the core doctrines of the Dignāga–Dharmakīrti school. Written in terse prose aphorisms (sūtras), the work is structured into three chapters: direct perception (pratyakṣa), inference for oneself (svārthānumāna), and inference for others (parārthānumāna). It defines perception as non-conceptual (kalpanāpoḍha) and non-erroneous (abhrānta), formulates the threefold requirement of the logical reason (trairūpya), classifies valid reasons into essential nature (svabhāva), effect (kārya), and non-cognition (anupalabdhi), and provides a taxonomy of logical fallacies. Due to its clarity and pedagogical conciseness, it became the primary introductory manual of Buddhist logic in India and Tibet.

summary: The Nyāyapraveśakasūtra (commonly known as the Nyāyapraveśa), authored by Dignāga's pupil Śaṅkarasvāmin (c. 6th century CE), is an influential introductory manual of Buddhist logic and epistemology (hetuvidyā). It systematically defines the members of formal proof (sādhana) and refutation (dūṣaṇa), the three characteristics of a valid logical reason (trairūpya), the varieties of logical fallacies (pakṣābhāsa, hetvābhāsa, dṛṣṭāntābhāsa), and valid cognition through perception and inference. Translated into Chinese by Xuanzang (T1630), it became a foundational treatise for the East Asian Buddhist logical tradition (yinming), and was preserved and commented upon in medieval India, notably by Jaina scholars.

summary: The Nāgānanda ('Joy of the Serpents') is a five-act Sanskrit drama (nāṭaka) attributed to King Harṣa of Kanauj (7th century CE), dramatizing the Buddhist legend of the Vidyādhara prince Jīmūtavāhana. The opening acts combine standard courtly kāvya romance with Jīmūtavāhana's courtship and marriage to Princess Malayavatī, while the fourth and fifth acts center on his Bodhisattva-like self-sacrifice: offering his own flesh on the slaughter stone to Garuḍa to rescue the young Nāga Śaṅkhacūḍa. Moved by Jīmūtavāhana's radical compassion and non-violence, Garuḍa renounces the slaughter of serpents and revives those previously consumed. Famous for invoking both the Buddha (munīndra / jina) and the Hindu goddess Gaurī, the work is an exceptional surviving exemplar of classical Buddhist dramatic literature.

summary: The Paramārthastava ('Hymn to Ultimate Reality') is a short hymn of eleven verses attributed to Nāgārjuna and canonical as the fourth praise in the Catuḥstava quartet. It articulates Madhyamaka apophasis within devotional verse: because the Buddha is unarisen (anutpanna), unlocated (asthita), and beyond language (vākpathātīta), he cannot be praised in an ultimate sense (paramārtha). Consequently, praise can only take place conditionally via conventional designation (lokaprajñapti), culminating in the realization that in emptiness there is neither praised nor praiser.

summary: The Pañcakrama ('Five Stages') is the foundational manual of the completion stage (niṣpannakrama) according to the Ārya tradition of the Guhyasamāja Tantra. It outlines five sequential yogic stages of subtle-body meditation leading to awakening: speech isolation (vajrajāpa), mind purification (sarvaśuddhiviśuddhi / cittaviśuddhi), self-consecration / illusory body (svādhiṣṭhāna / māyādeha), clear light (abhisaṃbodhi / prabhāsvara), and nondual union (yuganaddha). Composed c. 8th–9th century CE, chapters 1 and 3–5 are attributed to the tantric Nāgārjuna, while chapter 2 is attributed to Śākyamitra.

summary: Pañcarakṣādevīstotrāṇi is a cycle of five five-verse hymns (25 verses total) celebrating the five protective goddesses of the Pañcarakṣā pentad: Mahāpratisarā, Mahāmantrānusāriṇī, Mahāmāyūrī, Mahāśītavatī, and Mahāsāhasrapramardinī. Each hymn extols the apotropaic efficacy of the deity and her dhāraṇī in dispelling snakebites, illnesses, hostile planetary influences (graha), and calamities. The cycle forms a core component of traditional Newar Buddhist devotional and liturgical practice.

summary: A short Sanskrit poem of 15 anuṣṭubh stanzas addressed to Dharmaratna. The poet laments the infirmities of old age: trembling, failing sight that spectacles (upacakṣus) no longer help, loss of memory, and his books lying unread in the library to be gnawed by worms and mice. Recalling the Buddhist teaching that everything in saṃsāra ends in decay, except the imperishable liberation taught by the Muni, he voices regret (paścāttāpa) for his lost youth and his inability to compose further poetry at the age of 87.

summary: The Piṇḍīkrama (also known as Piṇḍīkramasādhana or Piṇḍīkṛtasādhana) is a generation-stage liturgical manual of the Ārya exegesis of the Guhyasamāja Tantra, traditionally attributed to Nāgārjuna. Although often transmitted alongside the Pañcakrama, it is an independent manual for the Ārya school's practice.

summary: The Prajñāpāramitāhṛdayasūtra ('Heart Sūtra') is one of the most widely recited and influential texts of Mahāyāna Buddhism, condensing the vast Prajñāpāramitā literature into an essential doctrinal summary. summary: The Prajñāpāramitāhṛdayasūtra ('Heart of the Perfection of Wisdom Sūtra') is one of the most widely recited and commented-upon texts in Mahāyāna Buddhism. This e-text preserves the complete longer recension (vistaramātṛkā), which includes the full narrative setting (nidāna) on Vulture Peak in Rājagṛha and concludes with the Buddha rising from samādhi to praise Avalokiteśvara's exposition. The bodhisattva expounds to Śāriputra the emptiness of intrinsic existence (svabhāvaśūnyatā) of all five aggregates, sense spheres, and Noble Truths, concluding with the famous mantra: gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā.

summary: Candrakīrti's Prasannapadā ('Clear Words'), also titled Madhyamakaśāstravṛtti, is a 7th-century CE Sanskrit prose commentary on the 27 chapters of Nāgārjuna's fundamental Madhyamakaśāstra (Mūlamadhyamakakārikā). It is the only fully surviving Indian commentary on Nāgārjuna's root verses preserved in Sanskrit. Candrakīrti defines the Prāsaṅgika-Madhyamaka approach by defending Buddhapālita's method of reductio ad absurdum (prasaṅga) against Bhāvaviveka's use of autonomous inference (svatantra), making the work an essential foundation for the study of Indian and Tibetan Madhyamaka philosophy.

summary: The Pratītyasamutpādahṛdayakārikā ('Verses on the Heart of Dependent Origination') is a concise seven-stanza Madhyamaka treatise that condenses the twelve links (nidāna) of dependent arising into three interrelated categories: defilements (kleśa), karma, and suffering (duḥkha). It demonstrates that empirical entities arise entirely through conditioned causal processes without any transmigrating soul or independent entity (sattva). Employing eight classical analogies (such as a lamp, an echo, a reflection in a mirror, and an imprint of a seal), the text establishes that cyclic rebirth takes place without substantial transmigration (asaṅkrama), culminating in the celebrated assertion that in ultimate reality nothing is to be subtracted and nothing added.

summary: The Pratītyasamutpādahṛdayakārikā with Pratītyasamutpādahṛdayavyākhyāna is an epitome of the doctrine of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) traditionally ascribed to Nāgārjuna. It reduces the twelve links of existence into three fundamental categories: afflictions (kleśa), karma, and suffering (duḥkha), explaining how they perpetuate cyclic existence like an endlessly turning wheel without any permanent agent or substantial soul transmigrating between lives. Emphasizing that purely empty factors arise from empty conditions, the text concludes with well-known verses declaring that in ultimate reality nothing is to be removed and nothing added.

summary: The Pratītyasamutpādādivibhaṅganirdeśasūtra is a canonical Buddhist discourse delivered by the Buddha at Jetavana in Śrāvastī. It is divided into two parts: the fundamental exposition (ādi), which articulates the standard twelvefold formula of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) from ignorance (avidyā) to aging and death (jarāmaraṇa), and the detailed analysis (vibhaṅga), which provides concise definitions of each link.

summary: The Pāramitāsamāsa ("Compendium of the Perfections") is a kāvya-style verse treatise in six chapters on the six perfections of the bodhisattva: generosity, morality, patience, vigour, meditation and wisdom. summary: A tantric Sanskrit hymn in 67 verses venerating Gaṇapati followed by the Eight Mothers (Aṣṭamātṛkā: Brahmāṇī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī, Indrāṇī/Śakreśvarī, Cāmuṇḍā, and Mahālakṣmī). Each goddess is invoked in conjunction with one of the directional sacred seats (pīṭhas/kṣetras, such as Prayāga, Vārāṇasī, Kolāpura, Aṭṭahāsa, and Jayantī) and corresponding sacred trees (udumbara, tāla, vaṭa, kadamba, nimba, karañja). Preserved in the Newar Buddhist tradition, the hymn concludes with a phalaśruti (vv. 61–67) promising protection from disease, conflicts, premature death, and hostile sorcery.

summary: A 15-verse Sanskrit Buddhist hymn of praise (stotra) in anuṣṭubh metre addressed to Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara (invoked as Lokanātha and Lokanāyaka). Verse 2 commemorates the Newar legend of the twelve-year drought in Nepal (dvādaśābdeṣu anāvṛṣṭiḥ) during the reign of Licchavi king Narendradeva (7th century CE), in which Avalokiteśvara (associated with Bungadyo / Karuṇāmaya) was established in Nepal to relieve famine and suffering. Most stanzas conclude with the prayerful refrain 'rakṣa māṃ lokanāyaka'.

summary: The Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā ('Verses on the Accumulation of Precious Qualities') is a metrical summary of early Prajñāpāramitā doctrine composed in Buddhist Hybrid Sanskrit. It expounds foundational Mahāyāna teachings, emphasizing the emptiness (śūnyatā) of the aggregates, the practice of non-abiding (asthānayoga), and the bodhisattva's dedication to awakening through compassion without grasping. While the root verses represent an early stratum of Prajñāpāramitā literature (c. 100 BCE – 100 CE), this e-text preserves the 32-chapter Sanskrit recension associated with Haribhadra.

summary: The Ratnakīrtinibandhāvalī is a collection of ten philosophical monographs (nibandhas) composed by Ratnakīrti. Major subjects addressed include the proof of the Buddha's omniscience (Sarvajñasiddhi), the refutation of God as creator (Īśvarasādhanadūṣaṇa), the apoha nominalist theory of word meaning (Apohasiddhi), positive and negative proofs of universal momentariness (Kṣaṇabhaṅgasiddhi), the refutation of enduring entities (Sthirasiddhidūṣaṇa), the logic of invariable concomitance and reduction of valid cognitions (Vyāptinirṇaya, Pramāṇāntarbhāvaprakaraṇa), and an ultimate idealist critique of external objects and other minds (Citrādvaitaprakāśavāda, Santānāntaradūṣaṇa).

Preserved within the Newar Buddhist liturgical corpus of the Kathmandu Valley, it offers an anatomical sequence of veneration, praising in turn the hair, face, crown, eyes, voice, body, garments, arms, hands, navel, and wheel-marked feet. Although designated in its colophon as a hymn to Avalokiteśvara, the refrains consistently praise the 'Daśabala' and the phalaśruti terms it a Sugatastava.

summary: The Saddharmalaṅkāvatārasūtra is an influential Mahāyāna Buddhist sūtra that synthesizes Yogācāra consciousness-only (vijñaptimātratā / cittamātra) doctrines with the tathāgatagarbha teaching. Framed as an exposition delivered by the Buddha on Mount Malaya in Laṅkā to the bodhisattva Mahāmati and king Rāvaṇa, it expounds the eight consciousnesses (especially ālayavijñāna), the five dharmas, the three intrinsic natures (trisvabhāva), the two kinds of selflessness (dharmanairātmya and pudgalanairātmya), and the doctrine of vegetarianism (māṃsabhakṣaṇaparivarta). The text exerted foundational influence across Mahāyāna philosophical schools, Tibetan scholasticism, and East Asian Chan/Zen traditions.

summary: The Saddharmapuṇḍarīkasūtra ('The White Lotus of the True Dharma') is one of the most celebrated and influential Mahāyāna scriptures. It propounds the doctrine of the One Vehicle (ekayāna), declaring that the apparent three vehicles (śrāvakayāna, pratyekabuddhayāna, and bodhisattvayāna) are provisional pedagogical devices (upāyakauśalya) and that all beings are destined for unexcelled awakening. Renowned for its rich parables—such as the burning house, the prodigal son, the medicinal herbs, and the gem concealed in the garment—the sūtra also reveals the Buddha's lifespan to be immeasurable and his parinirvāṇa an expedient display.

Framed as a discourse at Jetavana where the Buddha instructs Śāriputra on how devotees should fashion icons after the Teacher's parinirvāṇa, the text establishes canonical proportions (pramāṇa) for images of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. summary: The Samādhirājasūtra ('King of Samādhis Sūtra', often cited by Indian Madhyamaka commentators as Candrapradīpasūtra) is an influential Mahāyāna scripture in 40 chapters expounding the meditative absorption (samādhi) that reveals the fundamental equality and emptiness of all phenomena (sarvadharmasvabhāvasamatā). Delivered by the Buddha on Vulture Peak to the youth Candraprabha, the text combines exposition of non-arising and ultimate reality with teachings on ethical discipline, ascetic practices (dhūtaguṇa), dhāraṇī formulas, and past-life narratives (jātakas). It was widely quoted as a scriptural authority on emptiness by Candrakīrti, Śāntideva, and Prajñākaramati, and served as a foundational sūtra source for contemplative traditions in Tibet, particularly Sūtra Mahāmudrā.

summary: The Samājasādhanavyavastholi is a foundational ritual treatise on the generation stage (utpattikrama) of the Guhyasamājatantra according to the Ārya (Nāgārjuna) school. It structures the Guhyasamāja sādhana by establishing correspondences between Buddhist cosmogony—the periodic dissolution and reappearance of the physical receptacle (bhājanaloka) and sentient beings (sattvaloka)—and the yogic generation of the maṇḍala and its thirty-two deities. The text served as an essential authority for later commentarial traditions, prominently utilized by Tsongkhapa in his exposition of the generation stage.

summary: The Saptabuddhastotra is an anonymous Sanskrit Buddhist hymn of praise (stotra) preserved in the Nepalese Newar manuscript tradition. Over nine verses in Sragdharā meter, it systematically enumerates each of the seven Buddhas of antiquity (Vipaśyin, Śikhin, Viśvabhū, Krakucchanda, Kanakamuni, Kāśyapa, and Śākyamuni) and the future Buddha Maitreya, specifying the birthplace, clan/lineage, lifespan, and bodhi tree of each. The concluding verse dedicates the accumulated merit to the destruction of afflictions and the attainment of nirvāṇa.

summary: The Saptajinastava ('Praise of the Seven Conquerors') is a short Buddhist hymn of praise composed in nine verses. The first seven stanzas venerate the lineage of the seven past Buddhas (Vipaśyin, Śikhin, Viśvabhū, Krakucchanda, Kanakamuni, Kāśyapa, and Śākyamuni), followed by a stanza honoring the future Buddha Maitreya, and concluding with a dedication of merit (puṇyapariṇāmanā). The hymn is known from medieval Chinese and Tibetan translations.

summary: The Saptavidhānuttarastotra is an anonymous twelve-verse devotional hymn dedicated to Avalokiteśvara (invoked as Lokanātha). It adapts the classical Mahāyāna framework of the 'sevenfold supreme worship' (saptavidhā anuttarā pūjā)—salutation, veneration, refuge, confession, and merit-dedication—into a praise poem concluding with an aspiration for rebirth in Sukhāvatī. The hymn belongs to the liturgical corpus maintained in Nepalese Newar Buddhism.

summary: The Saptaśatikā Prajñāpāramitā ('Perfection of Wisdom in 700 Lines', also designated Mañjuśrīparivartāparaparyāyā or Puṇyakṣetranirdeśa) is an influential Mahāyāna scripture belonging to the Prajñāpāramitā corpus. Set in Śrāvastī's Jeta Grove, it consists of profound dialogues between the Buddha, Śāriputra, and the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī emphasizing the unreality of dualistic categories, the unoriginated nature (anutpāda) of all dharmas, and the non-apprehending contemplation of the Tathāgata.

summary: The Saptākṣarastotra is an anonymous eight-verse Buddhist hymn (ślokāṣṭaka) addressed to Āryāvalokiteśvara. The text explicitly invokes Avalokiteśvara as Lokanātha, Matsyendra, and Viṣṇu, praises him alongside the four Buddhist consorts (Locanā, Māmakī, Tārā, and Pāṇḍarā), and describes him wearing Amitābha on his crown while offering protection against yakṣas, rākṣasas, vetālas, and nāgas.

summary: The Dohākoṣa of the siddha Saraha is a seminal collection of rhymed Apabhraṃśa couplets (dohās) teaching Sahajayāna and Mahāmudrā realisation. The poetry harshly critiques Vedic Brahmanism, Jain asceticism, and scholastic Buddhist classifications, pointing instead to the non-dual, spontaneously innate nature of the mind (sahaja). In this e-text, the dohās are preserved within the Sanskrit prose commentary (Dohākoṣapañjikā / Sahajāmnāyapañjikā) attributed to Advayavajra, which elucidates the tantric and philosophical meaning of each verse.

summary: The Sarvabuddhaviṣayāvatārajñānālokālaṃkārasūtra ('The Ornament of the Light of Wisdom that Enters the Domain of All Buddhas') is an influential Mahāyāna sūtra presented through dialogues between the Buddha and Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta concerning the nature of awakening, the transcendent realm of the buddhas, and ultimate reality. The text emphasizes that all dharmas are unoriginated (anutpāda), non-dual, and that the fundamental nature of mind is luminous (prakṛtiprabhāsvara). Extensively cited in key Indian treatises including the Ratnagotravibhāga, the sūtra was known through three Chinese versions and a Tibetan translation.

summary: The Sarvadurgatipariśodhanatantra ('Tantra of the Elimination of All Evil Destinies') is an influential Buddhist Yogatantra of the Vairocana cycle, dating roughly to the late 7th to 8th century CE. Set in the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, the tantra opens with Śakra pleading with Śākyamuni to deliver the god Vimalamaṇiprabha, who has fallen into the lower realms upon his death. Centering on Sarvavid Vairocana and his maṇḍalas, the text provides elaborate ritual instructions—including initiations, sādhanas, apotropaic rites, and especially mortuary and post-mortem ceremonies—designed to purify negative karmic imprints and ensure liberation from adverse transmigrations.

summary: The Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṅgraha is the foundational root tantra of the Yogatantra class in Indian esoteric Buddhism, dating to the late 7th century CE. Centered on Mahāvairocana and the five Buddha families (kulas) within the Vajradhātu maṇḍala, it expounds the enlightenment of Sarvārthasiddhi via the five progressive realizations (pañcākārābhisambodhi) along with extensive rituals for initiation (abhiṣeka), mudrās, and mantras. It forms the primary doctrinal and ritual bedrock for East Asian esoteric Buddhism (Zhenyan and Shingon) and directly influenced subsequent Indo-Tibetan tantric traditions.

summary: The Sekoddeśa consists of 174 verses traditionally considered an excerpt from the fifth chapter of the lost Kālacakra root tantra (Paramādibuddha). Presented as a dialogue between the Buddha and King Sucandra of Śambhala, it provides an exposition of the Kālacakra initiation system, including the seven worldly initiations and the higher supramundane empowerments. The text details subtle-body physiology, visionary manifestations appearing in the sky, and the realization of imperishable bliss (akṣarasukha).

Set in the Sudharmā assembly hall of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, the narrative recounts how Śākyamuni Buddha enters meditative absorption (samādhi), from whose crown protuberance (uṣṇīṣa) emanates this protective incantation. The text provides extensive salutations to buddhas, bodhisattvas, and brahmanical deities, followed by powerful averting and binding formulas (pratyaṅgirā) designed to protect practitioners against evil spirits, demonic afflictions, curses, diseases, and untimely death.

summary: The Sragdharāpañcakastotra is a short five-verse Sanskrit devotional hymn composed in the sragdharā metre, preserved in the Newar Buddhist manuscript tradition of Nepal. It praises the primordial Ādibuddha as the ultimate unmanifest, pristine mental caitya (cittacaitya) and primordial flame (jyotīrūpa), from which the Five Tathāgatas (Vairocana, Akṣobhya, Ratnasambhava, Amṛtaruc/Amitābha, and Amoghasiddhi) and all beings proceed. The hymn is framed as an act of complete devotional surrender and dedication of merit uttered by Śākyamuni Buddha.

summary: The Smaller Sukhāvatīvyūhasūtra (saṃkṣiptamātṛkā), widely revered in East Asia as the Amitābha Sūtra, is a foundational scripture of Pure Land Buddhism. Set in Śrāvastī, Śākyamuni Buddha describes the western Buddha-field Sukhāvatī and its presiding Buddha Amitāyus (Amitābha) to his disciple Śāriputra, portraying in sensory detail its jeweled pavilions, radiant lotus ponds, music, and divine birds that ceaselessly proclaim the Dharma. The sūtra teaches that living beings who hear Amitāyus's name and hold it single-mindedly without distraction will be welcomed by Amitābha at the point of death and reborn in his realm, a promise affirmed by the Buddhas of the six directions.

summary: The Larger Sukhāvatīvyūha is a foundational Mahāyāna sūtra and the principal scriptural authority for Pure Land Buddhism. Set on Vulture Peak (Gṛdhrakūṭa) in Rājagṛha, the Buddha Śākyamuni narrates to Ānanda how the monk Dharmākara, in the presence of the Buddha Lokeśvararāja, generated the resolve for awakening and made forty-eight great vows to establish the western realm of Sukhāvatī and become the Buddha Amitābha (Amitāyus). The sūtra expounds the visual and spiritual splendors of this paradise, delineates the requirements for rebirth there through faith, recollection, and merits, and includes instructions addressed to the bodhisattva Ajita (Maitreya) on dispelling doubt.

summary: The Suvarṇaprabhāsasūtra ('Sūtra of the Golden Light') is an influential Mahāyāna canonical scripture that synthesizes doctrinal expositions of emptiness (śūnyatā) and the boundless lifespan of the Tathāgata with rituals of repentance and state protection. A pivotal episode centers on the bodhisattva Ruciraketu's vision of a golden drum radiating stanzas on confession and purification (deśanā). Protective deities including the Four Heavenly Kings (Caturmahārāja), Sarasvatī, Śrī, and Dṛḍhā pledge to guard righteous sovereigns and realms that uphold the sūtra, while subsequent chapters recount past-life narratives of the Buddha, notably the Vyāghrīparivarta (Mahāsattva jātaka) where the bodhisattva sacrifices his life to feed a starving tigress and her cubs.

summary: The Suvikrāntavikrāmiparipṛcchā (also known as the Sārdhadvisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā, or Perfection of Wisdom in 2,500 Lines) is a canonical Mahāyāna sūtra in seven chapters. Set at the Veṇuvana in Rājagṛha, it features an extensive dialogue between the Buddha and the Bodhisattva Suvikrāntavikrāmin detailing the nature and cultivation of prajñāpāramitā. The sūtra expounds the core doctrine of the non-apprehension (anupalabdhi) and lack of intrinsic existence (asvabhāvatva) of all dharmas, maintaining that true bodhisattva practice avoids attachment to conceptual markers or spiritual attainments.

summary: The Svastyayanagāthā is a 17-verse benedictory and apotropaic hymn preserved in Buddhist Hybrid Sanskrit within the Chatravastu narrative of the Mahāvastu. It represents the northern Buddhist Sanskrit parallel to the well-known Theravāda Ratana Sutta (Sn / Khp), chanted by the Buddha as an act of truth to expel malicious non-human spirits and restore welfare. Each stanza extols specific transcendent virtues of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, culminating in the protective refrain 'etena satyena susvasti bhotu manuṣyato vā amanuṣyato vā'. Transmitted also as an independent protective text, it is preserved in Tibetan translation in the Kangyur under the title bDe legs su 'gyur ba'i tshigs su bcad pa (Toh 818, Toh 1102).

summary: The Svayambhūpurāṇa is the foundational mythic chronicle and pilgrimage guide (sthala-māhātmya) of Newar Buddhism in the Kathmandu Valley. It recounts the myth of the primordial lake (Nāgadaha) drained through the Chobhar gorge by the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, followed by the appearance of the primordial lotus and the self-existent flame (svayambhūjyotis) of the Dharmadhātu enshrined within the Svayambhū Mahācaitya (Swayambhunath). The work incorporates visits of the previous Buddhas of antiquity, legends of local tīrthas, deities, and nāgas, and the transformation of the valley into a Buddhist kingdom. This 10-chapter recension represents the intermediate (madhyama) version of the text.

summary: The Svayaṃbhūstava is a seven-verse Sanskrit Buddhist hymn of praise (stotra) addressed to Svayambhū, the primordial self-originated Buddha (Ādibuddha) manifest as flame or light (jyotīrūpa) at the Svayambhū Mahācaitya in Nepal. Reflecting medieval Nepalese syncretic devotion, the stotra identifies Svayambhū with the Three Jewels, the Bodhisattvas, the lokapālas, and major Hindu devas (Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa), as well as the source of cosmic creation via the five wisdoms (pañcajñāna). A concluding phalaśruti attributes the text to the Four Great Kings (Cāturmahārāja) and promises sovereignty and liberation to those who recite it.

summary: The Sāmānyadūṣaṇa ('Refutation of Universals') by Aśoka is a short polemical treatise defending Buddhist nominalism against the realist ontology of universals. Following Buddhist epistemological arguments, Aśoka argues that an eternal, unitary, and pervasive universal (sāmānya) cannot be established by perception or inference. The text concludes with the celebrated five-fingers argument: one who claims to perceive a sixth common entity over and above the five distinct fingers might just as well perceive horns on their own head.

summary: The Tattvaratnāvaloka is a concise 20-verse tantric philosophical treatise by Vāgīśvarakīrti. The work surveys and critiques diverse definitions of the spiritual goal (sādhya) and ultimate reality (tattva)—contrasting non-Buddhist views and standard Pāramitāyāna models with multiple Mantrayāna interpretations—and culminates in an exposition of the fourth initiation (caturthābhiṣeka). Vāgīśvarakīrti also composed an autocommentary on the text.

summary: The Tattvaratnāvalī ('Jeweled Garland of Reality') is an 11th-century doxographical treatise composed by the scholar-siddha Advayavajra (Maitrīpa). It classifies the Buddhist path into three vehicles (Śrāvakayāna, Pratyekabuddhayāna, and Mahāyāna) and four philosophical tenets (Vaibhāṣika, Sautrāntika, Yogācāra, and Madhyamaka), dividing the Mahāyāna into Pāramitānaya and Mantranaya. The treatise is famous for setting out early bipartite divisions within Yogācāra (Sākāra and Nirākāra) and Madhyamaka (Māyopamādvayavāda and Sarvadharmāpratiṣṭhānavāda), making it a key primary source for late Indian Buddhist doxographical literature (siddhānta).

summary: The Trisvabhāvanirdeśa ('Exposition of the Three Natures') is a concise verse work of 38 kārikās by Vasubandhu presenting the classical Yogācāra doctrine of the three natures: the imagined (parikalpita), dependent (paratantra), and consummate (pariniṣpanna). Using the simile of a magician conjuring an elephant from a piece of wood, Vasubandhu demonstrates how subject-object duality is an unreal mental construction upon causally dependent mental processes, and how liberation entails the cessation of this duality and the realization of non-dual reality (dharmadhātu).

summary: The Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā ('Diamond-Cutter Perfection of Wisdom Sūtra'), commonly known as the Diamond Sūtra or Triśatikā ('Three Hundred Lines'), is one of the most celebrated and influential scriptures in Mahāyāna Buddhism. Structured as a dialogue between the Buddha and the venerable Subhūti in the Jetavana grove at Śrāvastī, it systematically dismantles attachment to conceptual signs and ontological categories, teaching that bodhisattvas must practice generosity and cultivate supreme enlightenment without abiding in notions of self, living being, or dharma. The text is renowned for its characteristic dialectical formula asserting that a dharma is designated as such precisely because it is empty of intrinsic existence. First translated into Chinese by Kumārajīva in 401/402 CE, the sūtra became a cornerstone of East Asian Buddhist traditions—particularly Chan/Zen—and is celebrated for the 868 CE Dunhuang woodblock scroll, the world's earliest dated complete printed book.

summary: The Vajradevīstotra is a 20-verse Vajrayāna hymn praising the goddess Vajradevī, specifically addressed as Vajravārāhī, Vajrayoginī, and Jñānaḍākinī. The opening verses present her fierce iconographic form: red-complexioned, three-eyed, nude, adorned with skull ornaments and the five bone mudrās, and carrying a khaṭvāṅga and kartikā while dancing. Subsequent verses praise her as the Mother of all Buddhas (sarvabuddhamātṛ), dispeller of Māra, and grantor of supreme bliss (mahāsukha) and spiritual accomplishments (ṛddhisiddhi).

summary: The Vajramahākālastotra is a nine-stanza Vajrayāna hymn composed in the Sragdharā meter, traditionally attributed to Nāgārjuna. Dedicated to the wrathful protector Mahākāla—invoked repeatedly throughout the text under his aspect or retinue identity of Kṣetrapāla ('field-protector')—each verse begins with alliterative chains of tantric seed-syllables (bījas) such as hāṃ, pheṃ, kṣaṃ, and klīṃ. The text details the deity's terrifying charnel-ground iconography and concludes with a phalaśruti promising health, renown, peace, and the removal of all obstacles.

summary: The Vajrapāṇināmāṣṭottaraśatastotra is a 21-verse Buddhist Sanskrit devotional hymn invoking the 108 epithets of the bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, identified here with Vajrasattva and primordial Bodhicitta. Verses 1–16 systematically invoke the deity under the attributes and virtues of the sixteen Vajrabodhisattvas of the Vajradhātu-maṇḍala (from Vajrasattva to Vajramuṣṭi), followed by verses 17–21 extolling his status as the origin of all Buddhas and declaring the spiritual fruit (phalaśruti) of reciting this litany. Derived from the culmination of the fundamental Yoga Tantra scripture Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṃgraha, the work long enjoyed independent circulation in the devotional liturgy of Newar Buddhism.

summary: The Vajrasattvaniṣpādanasūtra (also known as the Vajrasattvasādhana) is a foundational generation-stage (utpattikrama) meditation manual of the Ārya tradition of Guhyasamāja tantra exegesis, attributed to the tantric commentator Candrakīrti (c. 9th–10th century CE). It delineates the generation of the thirty-two deities of the Guhyasamāja maṇḍala centered on Vajrasattva in accordance with the process of human rebirth and embryonic development (bhavotpattikrama). Structured across three successive meditations—samādhirāja, maṇḍalarājāgrī, and karmarājāgrī—the practice systematically correlates ritual visualizations with canonical scriptural quotations cited across the seventeen chapters of the root Guhyasamājatantra.

summary: The Vajrasattvastotra is a short, eight-verse Newar Buddhist devotional hymn. While the opening two verses praise Vajrasattva as the supreme guide, embodiment of the Vajradhātu mandala, and dispeller of the darkness of delusion, subsequent verses invoke Lokanātha, Śākyamuni (Śākyasiṃha), Amoghapāśa, the Dharmadhātu caitya alongside four female consorts/prajñās (Māmakī, Locanā, Tārā, Padminī), and incorporate the widely cited Tārā praise formula ('namas tāre ture vīre...'). It serves as a composite liturgical stotra in Newar Vajrayāna ritual manuals such as the Gurumaṇḍalārcana.

summary: The Vajrasattvapārājikā is an anonymous Newar Buddhist manual on expiation (prāyaścitta) and ritual purity, framed by homage to Vajrasattva and to the ācārya as Vajradhara. Despite the Vinaya term pārājikā in its title, it is addressed to Vajrācārya and lay communities, not to celibate monastics. It adapts Dharmaśāstra-style rules on liability and penance for homicide and cow-killing (govadha), birth and death impurity (sūtaka), purification (śaucācāra, including pañcagavya) and ancestral rites (śrāddha). The Sanskrit is irregular.

The verses depict esoteric internal yogic processes, the dissolution of duality symbolized by sun and moon, and the arising of innate bliss (sahaja). It concludes by emphasizing that definitive understanding of spiritual stages is obtained through direct oral instruction from a qualified master (gurumukha).

summary: A sixteen-verse Vajrayāna liturgical hymn (stuti) condensing the esoteric realization (piṇḍārtha) of Trikāyavajrayoginī, the triple-bodied, severed-headed form of the goddess precursor to Chinnamastā. The text equates the deity with non-dual supreme bliss (mahāsukha), transcendent wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), emptiness devoid of extremes, and the central yogic channel (avadhūtī). Preserved as part of the Guhyasamayasādhanamālā collection from Nepal, the hymn is traditionally attributed to the mahāsiddha Virūpa.

summary: An anonymous Tantric Buddhist hymn of adoration (praṇāma) in twenty-one verses (ekaviṃśikā) praising the goddess Vajrayoginī. Each verse concludes with the refrain 'namaste vajrayogini', addressing her esoteric yogic aspects: seated on the evaṃkāra, embodying innate bliss (sahajānanda), bearing skull-cup (kapāla), khaṭvāṅga, and chopper (kartrī), and residing in the eight cremation grounds. The hymn notably expresses an ecumenical and syncretic perspective (vv. 13–14), describing Vajrayoginī as manifesting as Śakti in Śaivism, Caṇḍī in sacred pilgrimage sites, Veda in the Vedic stream, and Kubjikā in the Kula tradition.

summary: The Vajrayoginyāḥ stutipraṇidhānam is an esoteric Vajrayāna hymn of praise and aspiration (stuti-praṇidhāna) dedicated to Trikāyavajrayoginī (the severed-headed form of Vajrayoginī). summary: The Vajrayānadarśanamīmāṃsā is a modern systematic treatise in Sanskrit composed by Bhikṣu Wangchuk Dorjee Negi examining the philosophy and hermeneutics of Vajrayāna Buddhism. Drawing upon major Tantras, classic Indian commentaries, and Tibetan scholastic sources, the author addresses the status of Tantra as buddhavacana, its relationship to the turnings of the Dharma wheel, and the doctrine of the two stages (utpattikrama and niṣpannakrama). The treatise provides an exposition of the integration of Madhyamaka emptiness, intrinsically luminous mind, and tantric yogic praxis.

summary: A short four-verse Vajrayāna Buddhist hymn belonging to the Cakrasaṃvara/Heruka tradition. Verses 1 and 2 praise the male deity Heruka (addressed as Ubhayacittaheruka and Sahajātmaheruka) visualized within the internal centres (dhātumaṇḍala) and subtle channels (nāḍikā) of the body. summary: The Vasudhārādhāraṇī is a widely recited Mahāyāna Buddhist dhāraṇī-sūtra centered on Vasudhārā, the goddess of wealth and grain. In the Kauśāmbī setting, the Buddha instructs the impoverished householder Sucandra on the protective incantation and ritual practices revealed by the ancient tathāgata Vajradharasāgaranirghoṣa to overcome poverty and dispel harm. This e-text preserves a unique recension copied in 1638 CE (Vikrama Saṃvat 1695) in Gujarat, documenting the cross-sectarian adoption and ritual use of the Buddhist prosperity spell by Jaina communities.

summary: The Vasudhārānāmadhāraṇīstotra is an anonymous Buddhist devotional hymn praising the goddess Vasudhārā, the embodiment of wealth, prosperity, and spiritual abundance in Newar Mahāyāna-Vajrayāna tradition. Composed in 24 anuṣṭubh verses, the hymn lists 108 sacred names and epithets across the first 20 stanzas, invoking Vasudhārā simultaneously as a granter of worldly riches and as an embodiment of Mahāyāna perfections (Prajñāpāramitā, Dānapāramitā, Vīryapāramitā, Kṣāntipāramitā). The concluding stanzas (vv. 21–24) provide a phalaśruti describing the ritual efficacy of reciting the hymn thrice daily to eradicate grave karmic transgressions and attain rebirth in Sukhāvatī.

summary: The Vigrahavyāvartanī ('Dispeller of Disputes') is a core philosophical work by Nāgārjuna defending the Madhyamaka doctrine of universal emptiness (śūnyatā) against epistemological objections, particularly those framed by early Nyāya and realist Abhidharma thought. Consisting of 70 dialectical verses in the āryā metre and two concluding dedicatory stanzas, verses 1–20 present the opponent's objections (pūrvapakṣa), arguing that if words and means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) lack intrinsic reality (svabhāva), the Buddhist refutation of inherent existence is itself void and self-defeating. In verses 21–70 (uttarapakṣa), Nāgārjuna replies that empty words operate effectively like illusory creations acting upon illusions, famously declaring (kārikā 29) that he advances no independent ontological thesis (pratijñā) to suffer logical contradiction, before concluding in verses 71–72 with adoration of the Buddha.

summary: The Vimalakīrtinirdeśa is an influential Mahāyāna sūtra set in Vaiśālī, centered on the lay bodhisattva Vimalakīrti, who feigns illness to receive visitors and instruct them. In a series of witty dialogues with major arhat disciples and bodhisattvas, Vimalakīrti dismantles dualistic attachments regarding renunciation, purity, and emptiness (śūnyatā), culminating in his famous silence to signify direct entry into non-duality (advayadharmamukha-praveśa). Long celebrated in East Asian Buddhism and Tibet via early translations, the complete Indic Sanskrit text was identified in a palm-leaf manuscript preserved at the Potala Palace in Lhasa.

summary: Guṇaprabha's Vinayasūtra is the definitive scholastic digest of the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya, condensing canonical narrative and disciplinary legal codes into concise aphorisms. This first chapter, the Pravrajyāvastu, sets forth monastic regulations and formal legal acts (karmavācanā) regarding novice reception (śrāmaṇeratvopanayana) and full ordination (upasaṃpad). Accompanied here by Guṇaprabha's auto-commentary (Vinayasūtravṛtti or Svavyākhyāna), it served as an authoritative reference work for Buddhist monastic jurisprudence in late Indian and Tibetan Buddhism.

summary: A Mahāyāna sūtra transmitted within the Ratnakūṭa collection that contrasts the monastic prātimokṣa rules of śrāvakas with the ethical conduct of bodhisattvas. The Buddha explains that while the śrāvaka discipline centers on strict detachment to avoid any rebirth in saṃsāra, bodhisattva discipline is guided by skillful means (upāyakauśalya) and intention, prioritizing the welfare and gathering of beings. Consequently, offenses rooted in aversion or hatred are considered severe for a bodhisattva because they cause abandonment of beings, whereas infractions rooted in desire can serve to gather beings and are deemed comparatively less obstructive. The sūtra concludes with an exposition by Mañjuśrī on the unconditioned, inherently pure nature of all dharmas.

summary: The Viṃśatikāvijñaptimātratāsiddhi ('Proof of Mere Representation in Twenty Verses') is a foundational treatise of Yogācāra-Vijñānavāda philosophy composed by Vasubandhu in the 4th to 5th century CE. In twenty-two concise kārikās, Vasubandhu defends the thesis that external objects do not exist independently of cognition (vijñaptimātra), refuting realist objections regarding spatiotemporal determinacy, intersubjective consensus, and causal efficacy through comparisons with dreams and hell visions. The work also articulates a famous critique of atomism (paramāṇuvāda), arguing that indivisible partless atoms cannot coalesce into composite extended bodies without logical contradiction.

summary: The Viṃśatikākārikā ('Twenty Verses on Representation-Only') is a foundational Yogācāra-Vijñānavāda polemical treatise composed by Vasubandhu. The text refutes the reality of mind-independent external physical objects (bāhyārtha) through a rigorous critique of atomism (paramāṇuvāda), demonstrating that atomic partlessness and spatial extension are mutually incompatible. Vasubandhu defends the thesis that all experiential phenomena are appearances only (vijñaptimātra), answering realist objections by showing that spatial-temporal determination, intersubjective consistency, and practical efficacy can function without external objects, as seen in dreams, collective karmic hallucinations, and demonic mental projections.
