summary: The Saṅkalpakalpadruma is a Sanskrit devotional-poetic work by Jīva Gosvāmin composed as an address to his own mind (manaḥ-śikṣā). The work employs the allegory of a wish-fulfilling tree (kalpadruma) divided into four parts: root (janmādi-līlā, the manifest narrative pastimes of Kṛṣṇa), trunk (nitya-līlā, the eternal eightfold daily pastimes or aṣṭakālīya-līlā), branches (sarvartu-līlā, seasonal pastimes across the six seasons), and fruit (phala-niṣpatti, the ultimate attainment of loving service).

summary: The Sarvabuddhaviṣayāvatārajñānālokālaṃkārasūtra ('The Ornament of the Light of Wisdom that Enters the Domain of All Buddhas') is an influential Mahāyāna sūtra presented through dialogues between the Buddha and Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta concerning the nature of awakening, the transcendent realm of the buddhas, and ultimate reality. The text emphasizes that all dharmas are unoriginated (anutpāda), non-dual, and that the fundamental nature of mind is luminous (prakṛtiprabhāsvara). Extensively cited in key Indian treatises including the Ratnagotravibhāga, the sūtra was known through three Chinese versions and a Tibetan translation.

summary: The Jātakastava ('Praise of the Buddha\'s Former Births') by Jñānayaśas is a 20-stanza Mahāyāna devotional hymn (stotra) composed in the classical Śārdūlavikrīḍita metre. Framed by an opening confession of inadequate poetic capacity (verses 1–3) and a concluding dedication of merit for universal enlightenment (verses 19–20), stanzas 4–18 succinctly celebrate the Bodhisattva's extreme self-sacrificing deeds in previous lives—including feeding the tigress, giving away his wife and children, jumping into fire as the hare, giving up his tusks as Ṣaḍdanta, and slicing off his flesh as King Śibi. The text is preserved in the Tengyur (Toh. 1178).

summary: The Śivapūjāstava is a 47-verse liturgical hymn of the Śaiva Siddhānta tradition composed by Jñānaśambhu (c. 12th century). summary: The Vṛttamālāstuti is a Buddhist devotional hymn and versified manual of Sanskrit metrics (chandaśśāstra) by Jñānaśrīmitra. Comprising 154 stanzas praising the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī (Mañjughoṣa), the work illustrates approximately 150 classical metres by weaving the metrical name directly into each stanza while exemplifying its metrical structure. It was translated into Tibetan by Pang Lotsāwa Lodrö Tenpa (Dpal-ldan blo-gros brtan-pa) along with Śoṅ-ston Rdo-rje rgyal-mtshan.

summary: The Jaiminigṛhyasūtra is the domestic ritual manual of the Jaiminīya (or Talavakāra) śākhā of the Sāmaveda. Structured in two praśnas comprising 24 and 9 khaṇḍas respectively, it begins with the standard model of the pārvaṇasthālīpāka offering and details domestic life-cycle rites (saṃskāras) such as upanayana, godāna, vivāha, and śrāddha, concluding with a navagrahaśānti. It constitutes an indispensable source for the domestic ritual liturgy of the Sāmaveda preserved primarily in South India (Tamil Nadu and Kerala).

summary: The foundational aphorisms of the Pūrva-Mīmāṃsā school attributed to Jaimini, accompanied by its earliest surviving commentary, the Śābarabhāṣya of Śabarasvāmin. Together they establish the epistemological foundations of Vedic exegesis, arguing for the intrinsic validity of cognition (svataḥprāmāṇya), the eternal authorlessness of the Veda (apauruṣeyatva), the inherent relation between word and referent, and the concept of unseen ritual efficacy (apūrva). This partial e-text encompasses adhyāyas 1 through 7, treating the sources of dharma, ritual classifications, subsidiary relations (śeṣatva), and the opening rules governing the transfer of ritual details (atideśa).

summary: The Mīmāṃsāsūtra (or Pūrvamīmāṃsāsūtra), traditionally attributed to Jaimini, is the foundational text of the Pūrva-Mīmāṃsā darśana. Arranged into twelve books (adhyāyas), hence known as the Dvādaśalakṣaṇī, the aphorisms formulate the rules of interpretation (nyāya) for the ritual injunctions (vidhi) of the Vedic corpus. The work provides systematic epistemological arguments for the intrinsicality of knowledge (svataḥprāmāṇya) and the eternality of language and the Veda, establishing hermeneutic canons that deeply influenced Dharmaśāstra, Vedānta, and Indian legal interpretation.

summary: The Candrāloka is an elementary verse treatise on Sanskrit poetics (alaṃkāraśāstra) composed by Jayadeva Pīyūṣavarṣa in ten chapters (mayūkhas) in straightforward anuṣṭubh meter. It methodically surveys poetic causes and definitions, word-powers (śaktivṛtti), poetic faults (doṣas), virtues (guṇas), figures of speech (alaṃkāras), and sentiment (rasa). The fifth mayūkha, treating figures of speech, is celebrated for its didactic technique wherein each definition serves simultaneously as an illustration of the figure defined; this chapter served as the direct basis for Appayya Dīkṣita's influential Kuvalayānanda.

summary: The Gītagovinda of Jayadeva (composed in late 12th-century Bengal) is a celebrated lyrical kāvya celebrating the passionate love, separation (viraha), and joyful reconciliation of Kṛṣṇa and Rādhā. Comprising 12 cantos structured around 24 rhymed aṣṭapadīs framed by narrative and descriptive stanzas in classical metres, the work innovatively bridges classical Sanskrit kāvya traditions with vernacular song performance. Its synthesis of theological bhakti and refined erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra) deeply influenced Gauḍīya and pan-Indian Vaiṣṇavism.

summary: The Meghadūta ('Cloud Messenger') of Kālidāsa is the foundational lyric poem of the sandeśakāvya genre in classical Sanskrit literature, composed entirely in the mandākrāntā meter. Exiled to Mount Rāmagiri for neglecting his duties, an attendant yakṣa begs a passing monsoon cloud to deliver a message of love and reassurance to his pining wife in the celestial city of Alakā. The poem comprises two sections: the Pūrvamegha, charting the cloud's scenic journey across the rivers, mountains, and cities of northern and central India, and the Uttaramegha, depicting the mythological splendors of Alakā and conveying the yakṣa's tender message. This e-text preserves the 111-stanza Kashmiri recension commented on by Vallabhadeva.

summary: Kālidāsa's Raghuvaṃśa ('The Dynasty of Raghu') is a classic Sanskrit mahākāvya chronicling the legendary solar dynasty of Ayodhyā. Cantos 1–6 cover the reign and ascetic devotion of King Dilīpa and Queen Sudakṣiṇā to the sacred cow Nandinī, the birth and world-conquering digvijaya of King Raghu, Raghu's munificent gift-giving at the Viśvajit sacrifice, and the bridegroom-choice (svayaṃvara) assembly in which Princess Indumatī chooses Raghu's son Aja. summary: A pivotal Mahāyāna sūtra dedicated to glorifying the salvific activities and cosmic compassion of Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara across various realms of saṃsāra, including Avīci hell and the preta realm. The text is historically famous as the earliest known source to teach the six-syllable mantra Oṃ maṇi padme hūṃ (the ṣaḍakṣarī mahāvidyā) and to detail its benefits and mandala ritual. Composed in northern India circa the 4th to 5th century CE, it demonstrates direct thematic engagements with contemporary Śaiva cosmologies—such as presenting Hindu deities like Maheśvara, Brahmā, and Nārāyaṇa as emanations from Avalokiteśvara's body—and provided the foundation for Avalokiteśvara worship and the Maṇi Kabum in Tibet.

summary: The Kāśyapaparivartasūtra is an early Mahāyāna scripture cast as a dialogue between the Buddha and Mahākāśyapa on Vulture Peak at Rājagṛha. It expounds the bodhisattva path, emphasizing moral purity and warning against spiritual hypocrisy, attachment to monastic privileges, and intellectual pride. The text famously articulates the Middle Way between the extremes of eternalism and annihilationism and contains the influential simile comparing the dogmatic reification of emptiness to a medicine that itself becomes a deadly disease.

summary: The Kāśyapaparivartasūtra (also known as the Kāśyapaparivarta or Ratnakūṭasūtra) is an archaic and foundational Mahāyāna scripture presented as a dialogue between Śākyamuni Buddha and Mahākāśyapa on Vulture Peak. It expounds core bodhisattva ethics, the Middle Way (madhyamā pratipad) avoiding eternalism and annihilationism, and the meditation on emptiness (śūnyatā), featuring the famous warning that reifying emptiness as a dogmatic view turns medicine into incurable poison. It also delivers severe critiques of counterfeit, self-serving monastics, providing essential scriptural authority frequently cited across Madhyamaka, Yogācāra, and Tibetan scholastic traditions.

summary: The Kṣaṇabhaṅgasiddhir anvayātmikā is a philosophical treatise by the eleventh-century Buddhist epistemologist Ratnakīrti of Vikramaśīla. It establishes the Buddhist doctrine of universal momentariness (kṣaṇabhaṅga) via positive pervasion (anvayavyāpti): whatever exists is causally efficient (arthakriyākārin), and causal efficiency can only occur instantaneously, not successively or simultaneously over time (kramākramābhyām). Defending the inference against Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika and Mīmāṃsā realists, Ratnakīrti deploys reductio ad absurdum (prasaṅga) and contraposition (prasaṅgaviparyaya) to show that permanent entities cannot possess causal efficacy.

summary: The Bhairavānukaraṇastotra ('Hymn on the Assimilation to Bhairava') is a 48-verse non-dual Śaiva hymn composed by Kṣemarāja in āryā metre. Rather than offering purely devotional praises, the hymn systematically decodes the terrifying Agamic iconography of Svacchandabhairava—his many weapons, ornaments of skulls and elephant skin, charnel-ground setting, and retinue—interpreting them as symbolic expressions of the dynamic powers of supreme, unconditioned consciousness (cidbhairava). The stotra illustrates the Trika and Krama synthesis of ritual visualization, aesthetic sentiment, and non-dual recognition (pratyabhijñā).

summary: The Bodhavilāsa ('Play of Awakened Consciousness') is a concise Pratyabhijñā manual in 42 anuṣṭubh verses by the Kashmirian master Kṣemarāja (early 11th c. CE). Functioning as a versified epitome of the core doctrine set out in his Pratyabhijñāhṛdaya, the work expounds how autonomous universal consciousness (citi) contracts into individual minds (citta), continuously performs the five cosmic operations (pañcakṛtya), and recovers its innate liberation through steady contemplative discernment (vimarśa).

summary: The Pratyabhijñāhṛdaya ('Heart of Recognition') is an influential introductory manual of non-dual Kashmir Śaivism composed in the first half of the 11th century CE by Kṣemarāja, the principal pupil of Abhinavagupta. Composed specifically for practitioners and novices lacking training in formal logic (tarka), the treatise distills the core metaphysics and soteriology of Utpaladeva's Īśvarapratyabhijñā into twenty concise aphorisms accompanied by Kṣemarāja's own explanatory commentary. It outlines the cosmic dynamics of Citi (supreme consciousness), which freely manifests the universe, contracts itself into limited individual experients (paśu), and achieves liberation through the intuitive recognition of its inherent oneness with Śiva.

summary: Pallava 93 of Kṣemendra's Bodhisattvāvadānakalpalatā comprises 111 classical Sanskrit verses retelling the legend of Sumāgadhā, daughter of the merchant Anāthapiṇḍada. Married into a non-Buddhist Jain (kṣapaṇaka) household in Puṇḍravardhana, Sumāgadhā is appalled by the behavior of the naked ascetics and miraculously invites the Buddha from Jetavana. The Buddha flies to Puṇḍravardhana with his retinue of arhats, converts her in-laws and the local populace through miracles and Dharma discourse, and reveals the karmic origins of her fortune from previous lifetimes.

summary: The Darpadalana ('Crushing of Pride') is a seven-chapter satirical and didactic poem (upadeśakāvya) composed by Kṣemendra. Each chapter (vicāra) targets one of seven traditional causes of conceit (madahetavaḥ)—noble birth (kula), wealth (vitta), erudition (śruta), physical beauty (rūpa), valor (śaurya), munificence (dāna), and asceticism (tapas)—demonstrating through general moral reflections and illustrative narratives (dṛṣṭānta) how excessive vanity leads to downfall and ridicule.

summary: Kalāvilāsa is a satirical poem in ten cantos composed by Kṣemendra. Framed as instruction delivered by Mūladeva to his disciple Candragupta, the work catalogues and satirizes widespread forms of deceit, greed, and hypocrisy in society—exposing corrupt bureaucrats and scribes (kāyasthas), merchants, quack physicians, astrologers, courtesans, and false ascetics—before concluding with an exposition of genuine, auspicious arts.

summary: The Narmamālā ('Garland of Mirth' or 'Garland of Satires') is a satirical poem in three chapters (parihāsas) composed in 11th-century Kashmir during the reign of King Ananta. It presents a caustic caricature and expose of corrupt scribe-officials (Kāyasthas and diviras), detailing their greed, oppression of the public, administrative malpractice, religious charlatanism, and domestic vices. Together with the Deśopadeśa, it is a key satirical source for socio-political life in medieval Kashmir.

summary: The Pratītyasamutpādāvadāna is the 75th pallava of Kṣemendra's Bodhisattvāvadānakalpalatā. summary: The Sevyasevakopadeśa is a didactic and satirical poem (upadeśakāvya) composed by the Kashmiri writer Kṣemendra. It offers a critique of courtly dependence, describing the degradation, anxiety, and humiliation endured by servants and dependents (sevaka) at the hands of arrogant patrons and masters (sevya). The work ultimately praises self-reliance, moral autonomy, and inner contentment (saṃtoṣa).

summary: The Sudhanakinnaryavadāna constitutes the 64th chapter (pallava) of Kṣemendra's 11th-century kāvya work, the Bodhisattvāvadānakalpalatā. It narrates the romance of Prince Sudhana and the Kinnarī princess Manoharā, recounting their encounter, subsequent separation, Sudhana's perilous supernatural quest to find her in the Kinnara kingdom, and their eventual reunion. Framed in the context of the Buddha's past life, it explains karmic bonds relating to Yaśodharā.

summary: The Vaiśeṣikasūtra is the foundational treatise of the Vaiśeṣika school of classical Indian philosophy, traditionally attributed to Maharṣi Kaṇāda. Organised into ten adhyāyas of two āhnikas each, it elaborates an atomistic and pluralistic realist ontology structured around fundamental categories (padārtha): substance (dravya), quality (guṇa), motion/action (karman), generality (sāmānya), particularity (viśeṣa), and inherence (samavāya). The work investigates physical causation, the elementary constituents of matter, and perception and inference, maintaining that spiritual liberation (niḥśreyasa) arises from discriminative knowledge of reality induced by dharma.

summary: The Kaṭhināvadāna is a Buddhist narrative work belonging to the Sanskrit avadāna literature preserved in Nepalese manuscripts. It integrates Vinaya ritual prescriptions concerning the kaṭhina robe ceremony—detailing the cutting, sewing, ritual marking, and offering of monastic robes at the end of the rains retreat (varṣāvāsa)—with didactic avadāna stories illustrating the karmic merit of giving to the Saṅgha. The narrative episodes draw heavily upon and share motifs with canonical Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya sources such as the Bhaiṣajyavastu and the Anavataptagāthā.

summary: The Kaṭhinavastu is the eighth chapter of the Mūlasarvāstivāda-Vinayavastu, governing the ceremonial production, acceptance, and formal 'spreading' (kaṭhināstāra) of robes made from cloth offered by the laity after the annual rains-retreat (varṣā). It specifies the special monastic dispensations and privileges (anuśaṃsā) granted to participating monks during the kaṭhina season, the communal legal acts (karman) required for its validity, and the eight distinct circumstances that terminate those privileges (kaṭhinoddhāra). Preserved substantially in Sanskrit in the Gilgit manuscript collection, it corresponds to the Pali Kaṭhinakkhandhaka and canonical Tibetan and Chinese translations.

summary: The Kaivalyopaniṣad is a celebrated text belonging to the Śaiva Upaniṣad corpus, preserved in recensions attached to both the Atharvaveda and the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda. Framed as a dialogue in which Brahmā instructs the Vedic seer Āśvalāyana on Brahmavidyā, it expounds the attainment of kaivalya (isolation / supreme liberation) through renunciation, faith, and inward meditation. It harmonizes non-dual Advaitic metaphysics with theistic contemplation of Rudra-Śiva (Umāsahāya), identifying the cosmic Absolute with the innermost transcendent witness (sākṣin, cinmātra) abiding in the cave of the heart.

summary: The Bhāvanākrama ('Stages of Meditation') by Kamalaśīla (c. 740–795 CE) is an influential triad of treatises formulating the graduated Mahāyāna path according to the Yogācāra-Madhyamaka synthesis. Composed in Tibet in connection with the Samyé (bSam yas) debate, it defends the classical Indian gradualist method of spiritual development against the sudden, non-conceptualizing quietism attributed to the Chinese Chan master Heshang Moheyan. Across the three works, Kamalaśīla systematizes the cultivation of compassion (karuṇā), the awakening mind (bodhicitta), and the balanced union (yuganaddha) of calm abiding (śamatha) and analytical discernment (vipaśyanā) leading to the non-conceptual realization of emptiness.

summary: The Sāṃkhyasūtra (or Sāṃkhyapravacanasūtra) is an aphoristic treatise in six adhyāyas articulating Sāṃkhya metaphysics, traditionally attributed to Kapila. The first three books expound core ontological doctrines (puruṣa, prakṛti, the evolutes, and the mechanics of bondage and liberation), the fourth provides illustrative parables and allegories, and the final two refute rival philosophical schools and recapitulate the system. Appended to the root text in this file is the Tattvasamāsa, a concise mnemonic compendium detailing the twenty-five tattvas and auxiliary categories of Sāṃkhya, arranged here in two sections: Tattvapāda and Prakīrṇapāda.

summary: The Karatoyāmāhātmya is an early medieval regional sthalamāhātmya in 85 verses extolling the sacred Karatoyā river and the holy precinct of Pauṇḍravardhana (modern Mahasthangarh, Bogra District, Bangladesh). Set as a dialogue between Śiva and Pārvatī reported by Sūta to the sages, the text relates the mythic origin of the Karatoyā from the water poured onto Śiva's hands during his marriage to Pārvatī and surveys the holy bathing places, shrines, and lingas established by Paraśurāma in Pauṇḍrakṣetra. Verses from the text are cited in medieval dharmaśāstra and lexical commentaries as early as Sarvānanda's Ṭīkāsarvasva (1159 CE) and Devaṇabhaṭṭa's Smṛticandrikā, confirming its currency in the twelfth century.

summary: The Karmavastu is the tenth chapter of the Vinayavastu of the Mūlasarvāstivāda school, treating the validity and taxonomy of ecclesiastical legal acts (saṅghakarman). It categorizes monastic proceedings according to whether the monastic assembly is harmonious/complete (samagra) or fractured/incomplete (vyagra), and whether the execution adheres to the Dharma (dharmeṇa) or violates it (adharmeṇa). The chapter details procedures including motions (jñapti), single and fourfold proclamations (karmavācanā), and suspension (utkṣepaṇakarman) and rehabilitation (osāraṇakarman) of monks.

summary: The Karmavibhaṅgopadeśa is an anonymous Buddhist exegetical treatise (upadeśa) preserved in a Nepalese palm-leaf manuscript (dated Nepāla Saṃvat 531). Serving as an exposition and commentary to the Mahākarmavibhaṅga, it examines the mechanics of karma and karmic fruition (vipāka). The text defends and elucidates key doctrinal positions—such as why making offerings to a stūpa after the Buddha's parinirvāṇa remains profoundly meritorious despite the absence of an embodied recipient—by citing canonical Āgama/Nikāya, Abhidharma, and avadāna parallels.

summary: The Kaṭhopaniṣad is a classical mukhya Upaniṣad of the Kaṭha school of the Black (Kṛṣṇa) Yajurveda, framed as an initiatory dialogue between the boy Naciketas and Yama, the lord of death. When granted three boons, Naciketas bypasses earthly riches and longevity to demand knowledge of what transpires beyond death, prompting Yama to distinguish the path of spiritual good (śreyas) from the path of worldly pleasure (preyas) and reveal the immortal nature of the inner self (ātman). The text is renowned for its chariot allegory in Vallī 3—correlating the body with a chariot, the intellect with the charioteer, the mind with reins, and the senses with horses—and for providing one of the earliest textual formulations of proto-Sāṃkhya ontological gradations and the definition of yoga as steady sensorial restraint.

summary: The Arthaśāstra is ancient India's foundational treatise on statecraft, political economy, judicial administration, and diplomatic strategy. Divided into fifteen books (adhikaraṇas), it systematically covers the education and discipline of the king, ministerial appointments, internal civil and revenue administration, civil and criminal law (dharmasthīya and kaṇṭakaśodhana), espionage, interstate relations (the mandala theory and the sixfold foreign policy, ṣāḍguṇya), military logistics and warfare, and the methodological hermeneutics of treatises (tantrayukti). Treating artha (material welfare and power) as the foundation of royal and societal flourishing, it provides an exceptionally detailed blueprint for state institutions in classical India.

summary: A concise Mahāyāna Prajñāpāramitā sūtra spoken by the Buddha to Śakra (Kauśika) on Vulture Peak in Rājagṛha. The text expounds the nondual nature of the perfection of wisdom through negative dialectical statements, eighteen modes of emptiness (aṣṭādaśaśūnyatā), and verses found in the Vajracchedikā and the opening maṅgalācaraṇa of the Mūlamadhyamakakārikā. It concludes with a series of protective mantras and dhāraṇīs honoring Prajñāpāramitā, bridging exoteric Prajñāpāramitā philosophy with esoteric protective practice.

summary: The Vṛttaratnākara of Kedārabhaṭṭa is a widely known manual of classical Sanskrit prosody (chandaśśāstra). Structured in six concise chapters of 136 verses, it covers metrical definitions and the trika/gaṇa syllabic foot notation, mātrāvṛtta (moraic) metres, samavṛtta, ardhasamavṛtta, viṣamavṛtta, and the six metrical pratyayas (combinatorial algorithms such as prastāra, naṣṭa, and uddiṣṭa). Each metrical rule is composed in the very metre that it defines, serving simultaneously as definition and illustrative instance.

summary: The Kauśikapaddhati is a ritual manual (paddhati) by Keśava setting forth the procedural application of the Kauśikasūtra, the primary ritual handbook of the Śaunakīya Atharvaveda. Keśava arranges the aphoristic sūtras into a systematic, sequential ritual program for Atharvavedic priests, detailing domestic rites (saṃskāras), therapeutic rituals (bhaiṣajya), propitiatory ceremonies (śānti), and sorcery (abhicāra). Together with Dārila's earlier bhāṣya, Keśava's paddhati is the principal traditional authority for interpreting Atharvavedic ritual practice.

summary: The Sāṃkhyatattvapradīpikā (or Sāṃkhyārthatattvapradīpikā) is an introductory compendium of Sāṃkhya philosophy by Keśava, son of Sadānanda, following the system of Vijñānabhikṣu. It systematically defines prakṛti, puruṣa, and the evolutes before analyzing cognition and the eight states of the intellect (bhāvas). It concludes by demonstrating how knowledge alone frees the spirit from embodiment.

summary: The Kiraṇatantra is one of the foundational canonical scriptures of the dualist Śaiva Siddhānta, presented as an exposition revealed by Śiva to Garuḍa. This e-text contains the first six chapters of its doctrinal section (Vidyāpāda) along with the extensive philosophical commentary (Kiraṇavṛtti) of Bhaṭṭa Rāmakaṇṭha II (c. late 10th century CE). The text articulates the core Saiddhāntika ontological categories of Lord (pati), individual soul (paśu), and bonds (pāśa—mala, karma, and māyā), establishing the necessity of ritual initiation (dīkṣā) and defending dualist theology against rival Buddhist, Advaita, and Sāṅkhya positions.

summary: The Kośāmbakavastu is the ninth section of the Vinayavastu of the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya. It relates the famous schismatic dispute among the monks residing at Kauśāmbī, originating from an infraction over a communal water vessel in the privy and escalating into a bitter factional rift between scholars of the sūtras and masters of the vinaya. The text details the disciplinary procedures of suspension (utkṣepaṇīyakarma) for refusing to see or atone for an offense, the prescribed conduct of suspended monks, their subsequent rehabilitation (osāraṇā), and the performance of the concord ceremony (sāmagrīpoṣadha) restoring communal harmony.

summary: The Kubjikāmatatantra (also known as the Kulālikāmnāya or Śrīmata) is the foundational scripture of the Kubjikā cult within the Western Transmission (Paścimāmnāya) of Kaula Śākta-Śaivism, dating to approximately the 9th or 10th century CE. Preserved predominantly in early Nepalese manuscript witnesses, its 25 chapters articulate esoteric cosmology, initiation rituals, mantra systems (notably the Navātman and Aghorī mantras), and an early five-cakra model of the subtle body centered on the worship of the goddess Kubjikā ('the Crooked One') as kuṇḍalinī energy.

summary: The Kalpanāmaṇḍitikā (or Dṛṣṭāntapaṅkti) of Kumāralāta is an early Buddhist narrative collection composed in mixed ornate prose and verse (campū style). It presents illustrative moral tales (dṛṣṭānta/avadāna) teaching karma, devotion to the Buddha and Saṅgha, and early Dārṣṭāntika doctrinal stances. While preserved completely only in Kumārajīva's Chinese translation (T 201) under an erroneous attribution to Aśvaghoṣa, Central Asian manuscript discoveries confirmed Kumāralāta's authorship of the original Sanskrit text.

summary: The Vakroktijīvita by Rājānaka Kuntaka is a landmark treatise in Sanskrit poetics that presents vakrokti ('oblique' or 'striking expression') as the essential life-principle (jīvita) of all literature. Composed in kārikā verses alongside Kuntaka's own prose commentary (svavṛtti) and hundreds of illustrative literary citations, the work systematizes creative poetic deviation (vakratā) across six hierarchical levels of linguistic organization: phoneme/letter arrangements (varṇavinyāsa), lexical stems (pada-pūrvārdha), inflectional morphology (pratyayāśraya), sentential composition (vākya), thematic episodes (prakaraṇa), and overall plot structure (prabandha). Responding to the dominant dhvani theory of Ānandavardhana, Kuntaka seeks to integrate alaṅkāra, guṇa, mārga, and rasa into an all-encompassing aesthetic framework centered on the imaginative faculty and creative activity of the poet (kavi-vyāpāra).

summary: The Ṛgvedavedāṅgajyotiṣa (also known as Ārcajyotiṣa) is the Ṛgvedic recension of the Vedāṅgajyotiṣa, the earliest surviving Indian text on mathematical astronomy and calendrical calculation, traditionally attributed to Lagadha. In 35 concise anuṣṭubh verses, it lays out a lunisolar calendar designed to determine the precise times for Vedic sacrifices, based on a five-year yuga consisting of 62 synodic months (including two intercalary months) and 1,830 civil days. The text details the coordinate system of 27 nakṣatras with their presiding deities, the positions of the solstices and equinoxes, rules for calculating tithis and nakṣatra portions, and seasonal variations in daytime length measurable by a water-clock (clepsydra).

summary: The Advayasiddhi ('Attainment of Non-Duality') is a concise Tantric treatise in 36 verses attributed to Lakṣmīṅkarā. It represents an early Sahajayāna orientation, teaching that enlightenment is directly attainable within the innate body without external asceticism, rituals, or conventional caste distinctions, while emphasizing guru devotion and the omnipresence of Vajrasattva. The work is counted as one of the Siddhi texts of Indian Vajrayāna.

summary: The Lalitavistara ('The Extensive Account of the [Buddha's] Play') is an elaborate Mahāyāna sūtra in 27 chapters composed in mixed Buddhist Hybrid Sanskrit prose and verse. It narrates the sacred biography of Śākyamuni Buddha from his decision to descend from Tuṣita heaven, his miraculous conception and birth in Lumbinī, his luxurious princely youth, four encounters, and great renunciation, to his austerities, defeat of Māra, awakening beneath the Bodhi tree, and first turning of the wheel of Dharma in Ṛṣipatana. Blending early biographical accounts (primarily Sarvāstivādin) with a docetic Mahāyāna perspective, the sūtra depicts the Buddha's earthly career as the deliberate, compassionate sport (lalita) of an already fully enlightened being, and served as a major inspiration for classical Buddhist art and literature across Asia.

summary: The Liṅgapurāṇa is one of the eighteen Mahāpurāṇas and a principal scripture of medieval Śaivism, distinguished by its strong Pāśupata orientation. This first section, the Pūrvabhāga (adhyāyas 1–108), presents the cosmogony and the primordial revelation of Śiva as an infinite pillar of cosmic fire (liṅgodbhava) confounding Brahmā and Viṣṇu. It treats the twenty-eight avatars of Śiva in the Kali yugas (concluding with Lakulīśa), ritual installation and worship of the liṅga, royal and householder gift rituals (ṣoḍaśamahādāna), sacred geography (Vārāṇasī), and Śaiva yoga disciplines alongside standard Purāṇic genealogies.

summary: The Vaidyajīvana ('Physician's Life') is an Āyurvedic treatise composed in ornate poetic verse (kāvya) by the poet-physician Lolimbarāja (17th cent.). In five vilāsas, it treats fevers, bowel and digestive disorders, women's diseases and aphrodisiacs, pulmonary consumption, and general ailments. Uniquely within Indian medical literature, the medical prescriptions and dietary rules are formulated as playful, erotic addresses to the author's beloved.

summary: A seminal foundation text of early Advaita Vedānta comprising 215 verses across four prakaraṇas: Āgama, Vaitathya, Advaita, and Alātaśānti. Developing the Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad's analysis of the four states of consciousness (waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and the fourth, turīya) correlated with the constituent morae of Oṃ, the text formulates the doctrine of ajātivāda (absolute non-origination) and asparśayoga. It represents the earliest extant systematic treatise of Advaita philosophy and is celebrated for its dialectical engagement with and creative absorption of Madhyamaka and Yogācāra terminology.

summary: The Anuvyākhyāna is Madhva's versified dialectical supplement to his own prose Brahmasūtrabhāṣya, expounding Dvaita (Tattvavāda) Vedānta across four adhyāyas. Composed in a concise and vigorously polemical style reminiscent of Kumārila Bhaṭṭa's Ślokavārttika, the work systematically refutes Advaita and rival schools while demonstrating the absolute supremacy of Viṣṇu and the reality of difference (bheda). It is regarded as Madhva's chief philosophical masterpiece and serves as the foundation for Jayatīrtha's celebrated sub-commentary, the Nyāyasudhā.

summary: The Śiśupālavadha ('The Slaying of Śiśupāla') is a canonical 20-canto court epic (mahākāvya) composed by the poet Māgha. Expanding an episode from the Sabhāparvan of the Mahābhārata, the narrative recounts the slaying of the insolent king Śiśupāla of Chedi by Kṛṣṇa during Yudhiṣṭhira's Rājasūya sacrifice. Celebrated in traditional Sanskrit literary criticism alongside Kālidāsa and Bhāravi, the work is renowned for its vigorous political debate (Canto 2), rich descriptive set pieces (Cantos 4–13), and intricate verbal pyrotechnics and visual poetry (citrakāvya, Canto 19).

summary: The Mālinīvijayottaratantra is the primary canonical scripture (mukhyaśāstra) of the Śaiva Trika tradition, datable to approximately the 8th to 9th century CE. It presents itself as a condensed successor to the wider Siddhayogeśvarīmata revelation, expounding the thirty-six principles (tattvas), esoteric phonology (the mātṛkā and mālinī orders of the Sanskrit alphabet), initiation rites (dīkṣā), mudrās, and an influential system of non-dual yoga and apperceptive levels (pramātṛs). The work served as the principal scriptural authority for Abhinavagupta's monumental synthesis in the Tantrāloka and was the subject of his Mālinīvijayavārttika.

summary: The Mānavagṛhyasūtra is the domestic ritual manual belonging to the Mānava school of the Maitrāyaṇīya recension of the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda. Arranged into two divisions (puruṣas) containing 23 and 18 sections (khaṇḍas) respectively, it outlines the standard domestic sacraments (saṃskāras) from initiation and wedding rituals to ancestor worship (śrāddha) and domestic oblations. It is particularly renowned among Indologists for preserving ancient non-Śrauta folk cults, including an early rite for pacifying the four Vināyakas (2.14).

summary: The Mārkaṇḍeyapurāṇa is considered one of the oldest and most narrative-driven of the eighteen Mahāpurāṇas, characterized by its general lack of sectarian bias. It opens with the sage Jaimini consulting four enlightened birds in the Vindhya mountains to resolve four perplexities left unresolved in the Mahābhārata, proceeding through discourses on cosmogony, dharma, eschatology, yoga, and the manvantara lineages. Structured across thirteen thematic sections, the work extols the Buddha's peerless compassion, bodily marks, intellectual qualities, moral perfection, and liberating teachings in an elegant kāvya idiom. As testified by the 7th-century Chinese pilgrim Yijing, the work was committed to memory and chanted daily in Buddhist monastic communities throughout India and rapidly spread to Central Asia, Tibet, and China.

While treating mantra-śāstra, phonological symbolism (mātṛkā), yantras, and ritual worship, it is notable for its alchemical (rasaśāstra) chapters (paṭalas 1, 5, and 8), which detail mercurial preparations, the transmutation of base metals into silver and gold, and the consecration of mercurial liṅgas (rasaliṅga). The work also addresses Kaula ritual practices, esoteric physiology, and the ritual purification of wine.

summary: The Mṛtyuvañcanatārāsādhana is a concise Vajrayāna visualization manual devoted to White Tārā (Sitatārā) for averting untimely death and extending lifespan. summary: The Vibhramaviveka ('Discrimination of Error') is a verse treatise in 164 kārikās by Maṇḍana Miśra examining the epistemology of perceptual error (khyātivāda). It critically evaluates rival classical theories—specifically Yogācāra ātmakhyāti, Mādhyamika asatkhyāti, and Prābhākara akhyāti—before analyzing anyathākhyāti / viparītakhyāti and demonstrating how the ultimate nature of error points toward indeterminability (anirvacanīyatva). The treatise is a fundamental document for the synthesis between late Mīmāṃsā epistemology and early Advaita Vedānta.

The work opens with the eight negations from the dedicatory verse of Nāgārjuna's Mūlamadhyamakakārikā and dispenses with the standard introductory narrative frame between Maitreya and Śāriputra, recasting the classical Buddhist exposition of internal and external dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) in explicit Madhyamaka terminology. The latter part of the text incorporates śāstric dialectic concerning the conditioned nature of entities (paratantrāś ca bhāvā vivādapadam) and cites the Candrapradīpasūtra (Samādhirājasūtra).

summary: The Mahākarmavibhaṅga (also referred to in manuscripts as Karmavibhaṅga or Karmavibhaṅgasūtra) is an early Buddhist discourse detailing the retributions of specific actions across cycles of rebirth. Expanding substantially upon the framework of the canonical Cūḷakammavibhaṅga-sutta (Majjhima-nikāya 135) and its Āgama parallels, the text presents 80 categories of wholesome and unwholesome deeds, frequently illustrating doctrinal points with narrative exempla and avadānas. The work was historically influential across Buddhist Asia and served as the direct textual source for the 160 relief panels carved on the hidden basement of Borobudur in Java.

summary: The Mahāmāyūrīvidyārājñī ('Great Peacock Queen of Spells') is one of the earliest and most celebrated Buddhist rakṣā (protective) and dhāraṇī scriptures, subsequently included as one of the Five Protective Deities (Pañcarakṣā). Framed around the story of the novice monk Svāti being bitten by a poisonous snake while gathering wood for the bathhouse, the Buddha imparts the Mahāmāyūrī spell to Ānanda for protection against snakebites, poisons, malevolent spirits, and disasters. The scripture is also renowned for preserving an extensive geographical list of local tutelary yakṣas across the Indian subcontinent and adjacent regions.

summary: The Mahāmantrānusāriṇī ('Follower of the Great Mantra') is a Buddhist apotropaic scripture belonging to the popular Pañcarakṣā ('Five Protections') collection and classified by Peter Skilling as an independent Mahāsūtra closely related to the Vaiśālīpraveśa-sūtra. Set in Rājagṛha and Vaiśālī, the Buddha instructs Ānanda to stand at the city threshold (indrakīla) of plague-ridden Vaiśālī and recite protective formulas and verses in the name of the Buddhas, Arhats, and gods to expel diseases and malevolent spirits. The text blends protective incantations (mantrapadas) with verses radiating universal loving-kindness (maitrī) to secure the well-being of all living beings.

summary: The Mahāpratisarāvidyārājñī ('The Queen of Spells, the Great Amulet') is the primary and most widespread scripture in the Buddhist Pañcarakṣā ('Five Protections') collection. Preserved across two chapters—an initial narrative detailing the origins and efficacy of the spell (prathamakalpa) and an extensive ritual manual (rakṣāvidhānakalpa)—the sūtra teaches the dhāraṇī of Mahāpratisarā for averting physical and spiritual dangers such as poison, illness, untimely death, weapons, and lower rebirths. The work is particularly known for its instructions on manufacturing, consecrating, and wearing written dhāraṇī amulets on the body.

summary: The Mahāpratisarāmahāvidyārājñī ('Great Queen of Spells, the Great Amulet') is a widely influential Buddhist apotropaic scripture, forming the principal text in the Pañcarakṣā ('Five Protectors') pentad. Set atop Mount Vajrameru, it features the Buddha expounding potent dhāraṇīs, mantra syllables, and detailed ritual instructions for preparing and wearing protective amulets. The text integrates nine testimonial narratives illustrating the dhāraṇī's power to grant protection against poison, execution, disease, demonic affliction, and premature death.

summary: The Mahāpratisarāvidyāvidhi is a short Vajrayāna ritual manual describing the preparation and design of a protective amulet-diagram (rakṣācakra) centered on Mahāpratisarā, the preeminent deity of the Pañcarakṣā pentad. The text sets forth specific geometric concentric circles (puṭa) to be drawn on birch bark (bhūrjatvac) or cloth, inscribed with seed-syllables, dhāraṇī formulas, names of guardian deities, and ritual emblems. Once inscribed and worn by the practitioner, the cakra is held to provide complete protection against calamities, evil spirits, and illness while fostering pacification (śānti) and prosperity (puṣṭi).

summary: The Ratnaketuparivarta (Mahāsaṃnipātaratnaketudhāraṇīsūtra) is a Mahāyāna sūtra of the Mahāsaṃnipāta collection. It opens with the conversion of Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana despite Māra's obstruction and goes on to the Buddha's subjugation of Māra and his hosts, the revelation of protective dhāraṇīs and the protection of the Dharma. The Sanskrit text survives in a Gilgit manuscript with a donor colophon of the Paṭola Ṣāhi king Vikramādityanandi.

summary: The Mahāsannipātaratnaketudhāraṇīsūtra (also known as the Ratnaketuparivarta) is an influential Mahāyāna scripture that circulated both independently and as a major component of the expansive Mahāsannipāta corpus. Set in Rājagṛha, the narrative depicts the conversion of Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, the Buddha's subjugation of Māra and his host, discourses on karmic results and bodhisattva training, and potent protective dhāraṇī incantations. This digital text reproduces the incomplete Sanskrit text recovered from the Gilgit manuscript and edited by Nalinaksha Dutt, containing chapters 1–6 and 10–11 of the thirteen chapters preserved in classical Tibetan and Chinese translations.

summary: The Mahāsudarśanāvadāna is a Buddhist narrative preserved in the Gilgit manuscripts recounting a former existence of the Buddha as the righteous universal monarch (cakravartin) Mahāsudarśana. Endowed with the seven royal jewels and four supernatural faculties, the king establishes boundless charity, erecting magnificent palaces and ponds for all beings in his city of Kuśāvatī. Moving beyond temporal sovereignty, he renounces sensuality, cultivates the four immeasurable minds (brahmavihāras), enters the meditative absorptions (dhyānas), and attains rebirth in the Brahmā realm, with the Buddha identifying the tale as an exposition of the accumulation of merit (saṃbhāra) necessary for supreme awakening.

summary: The Mahāvadānasūtra ('The Great Legend Sūtra') is a canonical discourse of the Sarvāstivāda tradition belonging to the Dīrghāgama (part of the Ṣaṭsūtrakanipāta), corresponding to the Pali Mahāpadāna-sutta (DN 14) and the Chinese Dà běn jīng (T 1 / T 2). Spoken by Śākyamuni Buddha at Śrāvastī, it records the lineage, lifespan, tree of awakening, and chief disciples of the seven Buddhas of the past, and provides an extensive exemplary narrative of the conception, birth, renunciation, awakening, and first teaching of the previous Buddha Vipaśyin. This critical edition by Takamichi Fukita (2003) reedits and substantially supplements Ernst Waldschmidt's earlier pioneering edition using all available Northern Turkestan manuscript fragments.

summary: The Mahāvastu ('The Great Story') is an extensive Buddhist Hybrid Sanskrit canonical text preserved by the Lokottaravāda sub-sect of the Mahāsāṃghika school, nominally forming the opening section of their Vinayapiṭaka. It presents an expansive biography of the Buddha Gautama, tracing his past lives, his bodhisattva path across the ten spiritual stages (daśabhūmi), his vow under previous Buddhas such as Dīpaṃkara, and his final awakening and initial teaching career. Rich in jātakas, avadānas, and early doctrinal discourses, the work was compiled and expanded over several centuries (c. 2nd century BCE to 4th century CE) and stands as a key witness for early Lokottaravāda supramundane buddhology and proto-Mahāyāna concepts.

summary: The Mattavilāsaprahasana ('The Farce of Drunken Sport') is a 7th-century one-act Sanskrit satire (prahasana) by the Pallava monarch Mahendravarman I, set in Kāñcīpuram. The plot follows a drunken Kāpālika ascetic, Satyasoma, and his consort Devasomā, who misplace their skull begging bowl (kapāla) and wrongly accuse a Buddhist monk, Nāgasena, of having stolen it. A Pāśupata ascetic is called in to arbitrate the dispute until a madman arrives with the bowl, which he had recovered from a stray dog, clearing the monk of blame. The play satirizes contemporary sectarian friction and religious hypocrisy among Kāpālikas, Pāśupatas, Buddhists, and Jains, and survives as a staple piece in Kerala's classical Kūṭiyāṭṭam theater.

summary: The Madhyāntavibhāgakārikā ('Verses Distinguishing the Middle from the Extremes') is a foundational doctrinal treatise of the Yogācāra school, traditionally counted as one of the 'Five Treatises of Maitreya'. In 111 verses across five chapters—on characteristics (lakṣaṇa), obscurations (āvaraṇa), reality (tattva), spiritual cultivation and results (pratipakṣabhāvanā-avasthā-phala), and the supreme vehicle (yānānuttarya)—it formulates the middle way (madhyamā pratipad) as avoiding both the extreme of reification and that of nihilistic denial. The treatise provides classical expositions of unreal mental construct (abhūtaparikalpa), the three natures (trisvabhāva), and emptiness (śūnyatā) understood as the absence of subject-object duality within that construct.

summary: The Abhisamayālaṅkāranāmaprajñāpāramitopadeśaśāstra is a central Mahāyāna verse treatise of 273 kārikās in eight chapters outlining the hidden path-structure implicit in the Prajñāpāramitā sūtras (specifically the Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā). It classifies the spiritual path into eight clear realizations (aṣṭāv abhisamayāḥ) and seventy doctrinal topics (saptati padārthāḥ) leading from initial bodhicitta to complete omniscient buddhahood. Attributed to Maitreyanātha and transmitted to Asaṅga, it constitutes the foundational scholastic curriculum text for Prajñāpāramitā exegesis across Tibetan monastic institutions.

summary: The Maitreyavyākaraṇa ('Prophecy Concerning Maitreya') is a metrical Buddhist scripture in anuṣṭubh verse setting forth the future advent of the bodhisattva Maitreya as the next buddha of the current cosmic era. Framed as an exposition delivered by Śākyamuni Buddha to his disciple Śāriputra, the text describes the utopian state of Jambudvīpa and the capital Ketumatī ruled by the righteous universal monarch (cakravartin) Śaṅkha, Maitreya's birth into a brāhmaṇa family, his renunciation, enlightenment under the Nāga tree, and the three major preaching assemblies (saṃnipāta). It concludes by enjoining devotees to cultivate devotion toward the Three Jewels and practice Buddhist morality to ensure rebirth in Maitreya's presence.

summary: The Maitreyavyākaraṇa is an Indian Buddhist prophetic scripture (vyākaraṇa) in anuṣṭubh verse predicting the advent of the future Buddha Maitreya. summary: The Kāvyaprakāśa is a foundational eleventh-century Sanskrit treatise on poetics (alaṃkāraśāstra) composed by the Kashmiri scholar Mammaṭa and completed by Allaṭa. Arranged into ten chapters (ullāsas) combining kārikā verses and an authoritative prose exposition (vṛtti), the work synthesizes the dhvani (suggestion) and rasa aesthetics of Ānandavardhana and Abhinavagupta with earlier taxonomic models of poetic figures and faults. It covers the definition and objectives of poetry, the three primary semantic functions of words (abhidhā, lakṣaṇā, and vyañjanā), stylistic blemishes (doṣas), excellences (guṇas), and phonological as well as semantic figures (śabdālaṃkāra and arthālaṃkāra), functioning as the preeminent textbook of classical Sanskrit literary theory.

summary: The Kāvyaprakāśa is an 11th-century masterpiece of Sanskrit poetics (alaṃkāraśāstra) authored by the Kashmiri scholar Mammaṭa and completed in its tenth chapter by Allaṭa. Divided into ten chapters (ullāsas), it systematically synthesizes the dhvani (poetic suggestion) theory developed by Ānandavardhana and Abhinavagupta with the older traditions of poetic faults (doṣa), qualities (guṇa), and figurative ornaments (alaṃkāra). Combining terse theoretical kārikās with an auto-commentarial vṛtti and hundreds of illustrative verses drawn from classical literature, it served as the foremost textbook of literary theory across the subcontinent and inspired dozens of subcommentaries.

summary: The Brahmasiddhi is a philosophical treatise of Advaita Vedānta by Maṇḍanamiśra, written in a mixture of kārikās and prose auto-commentary. Structured into four chapters—Brahmakāṇḍa, Tarkakāṇḍa, Niyogakāṇḍa, and Siddhikāṇḍa—the work establishes nondual Brahman as the sole ultimate reality, offers an epistemological critique of the perception of difference (bheda), and rejects the Mīmāṃsā theory that Vedic authority is tethered to action-oriented injunction (niyoga).

summary: The Nādabindūpaniṣad is a minor Yoga Upaniṣad centered on meditation on the sacred syllable Oṃ (praṇava) through the symbolic visualization of the cosmic bird (haṃsa). It sets forth the twelve kalās (mātrās) of the praṇava, their associated deities and realms, and describes the spiritual rebirth or post-mortem destination attained by a practitioner who departs physical life during meditation on each respective measure. In this shorter 20-verse recension, the text concludes with dissolution of mental modifications into the transcendental, partless Brahman (paraṃ brahma) and the realization of supreme beatitude.

summary: The Acintyastava ('Hymn to the Inconceivable [Buddha]') is a philosophical stotra of 59 anuṣṭubh verses attributed to Nāgārjuna, belonging to the Catuḥstava collection. Styled as praise of the Buddha, it articulates quintessential Madhyamaka philosophy by equating dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) with the non-substantiality (naiḥsvābhāvya) of all factors of existence. It examines the relativity of existence and non-existence, the four extremes of the tetralemma (catuṣkoṭi), the illusion-like character of conventional experience, the distinction between provisional (neyārtha) and definitive (nītārtha) teachings, and ultimate reality as transcending all discursive proliferation.

summary: The Dharmasaṃgraha is a concise Sanskrit Buddhist glossary consisting of 140 numbered entries categorizing doctrinal concepts and numerical dharmas (mātṛkā). summary: The Lokātītastava ('Hymn to the World-Transcendent One') is a short hymn of 28 anuṣṭubh stanzas attributed to Nāgārjuna, traditionally ordered as the first text in the Catuḥstava collection. Framed as praise of the Buddha who has transcended worldly categories, it systematically presents foundational Madhyamaka philosophy: the five skandhas are revealed as dreamlike and illusory, subject and object lack intrinsic nature, and dependent arising (pratītyasamutpāda) is directly equated with emptiness (śūnyatā). Esteemed and cited by Candrakīrti and later commentators, it is considered one of the authentic works of Nāgārjuna.

summary: The Mūlamadhyamakakārikā ('Root Verses on the Middle Way'), comprising 448 verses in 27 chapters, is the foundational philosophical treatise of the Madhyamaka school of Mahāyāna Buddhism composed by Nāgārjuna. Through systematic dialectic, Nāgārjuna deconstructs essentialist claims regarding causality, motion, faculties, aggregates, the self, time, karma, and nirvāṇa, establishing that no entity possesses inherent existence (svabhāva). Identifying dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) with emptiness (śūnyatā) and conventional designation (prajñapti), the work articulates the Middle Way free from the extremes of eternalism and annihilationism.

summary: The Madhyamakaśāstra (widely known as Mūlamadhyamakakārikā) is Nāgārjuna's foundational philosophical treatise and the central text of the Madhyamaka school of Mahāyāna Buddhism. summary: The Mahāyānaviṃśikā ('Twenty Verses on the Great Vehicle') is a brief Buddhist treatise traditionally attributed to Nāgārjuna that synthesizes Madhyamaka and Yogācāra doctrines. It argues that external objects lack independent reality and that the world of saṃsāra is an illusory projection arising from conceptual fabrication (kalpanā) upon mind alone (cittamātra). The text concludes by urging practitioners to rely upon the Mahāyāna vehicle as the only means to cross the ocean of delusion.

summary: The Pañcakrama ('Five Stages') is the foundational manual of the completion stage (niṣpannakrama) according to the Ārya tradition of the Guhyasamāja Tantra. It outlines five sequential yogic stages of subtle-body meditation leading to awakening: speech isolation (vajrajāpa), mind purification (sarvaśuddhiviśuddhi / cittaviśuddhi), self-consecration / illusory body (svādhiṣṭhāna / māyādeha), clear light (abhisaṃbodhi / prabhāsvara), and nondual union (yuganaddha). Composed c. 8th–9th century CE, chapters 1 and 3–5 are attributed to the tantric Nāgārjuna, while chapter 2 is attributed to Śākyamitra.

summary: The Piṇḍīkrama (also known as Piṇḍīkramasādhana or Piṇḍīkṛtasādhana) is a generation-stage liturgical manual of the Ārya exegesis of the Guhyasamāja Tantra, traditionally attributed to Nāgārjuna. Consisting of 226 verses and interspersed ritual mantras, it details the purification of conceptual thought (vikalpa), the erection of the protective circle, the generation of the Akṣobhyaguhyasamāja maṇḍala, and subsequent internal and external offerings. Although often transmitted alongside the Pañcakrama, it is an independent manual for the Ārya school's practice.

summary: The Pratītyasamutpādahṛdayakārikā ('Verses on the Heart of Dependent Origination') is a concise seven-stanza Madhyamaka treatise that condenses the twelve links (nidāna) of dependent arising into three interrelated categories: defilements (kleśa), karma, and suffering (duḥkha). It demonstrates that empirical entities arise entirely through conditioned causal processes without any transmigrating soul or independent entity (sattva). Employing eight classical analogies (such as a lamp, an echo, a reflection in a mirror, and an imprint of a seal), the text establishes that cyclic rebirth takes place without substantial transmigration (asaṅkrama), culminating in the celebrated assertion that in ultimate reality nothing is to be subtracted and nothing added.

summary: The Pratītyasamutpādahṛdayakārikā with Pratītyasamutpādahṛdayavyākhyāna is an epitome of the doctrine of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) traditionally ascribed to Nāgārjuna. It reduces the twelve links of existence into three fundamental categories: afflictions (kleśa), karma, and suffering (duḥkha), explaining how they perpetuate cyclic existence like an endlessly turning wheel without any permanent agent or substantial soul transmigrating between lives. Emphasizing that purely empty factors arise from empty conditions, the text concludes with well-known verses declaring that in ultimate reality nothing is to be removed and nothing added.

summary: The Vigrahavyāvartanī ('Dispeller of Disputes') is a core philosophical work by Nāgārjuna defending the Madhyamaka doctrine of universal emptiness (śūnyatā) against epistemological objections, particularly those framed by early Nyāya and realist Abhidharma thought. Consisting of 70 dialectical verses in the āryā metre and two concluding dedicatory stanzas, verses 1–20 present the opponent's objections (pūrvapakṣa), arguing that if words and means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) lack intrinsic reality (svabhāva), the Buddhist refutation of inherent existence is itself void and self-defeating. In verses 21–70 (uttarapakṣa), Nāgārjuna replies that empty words operate effectively like illusory creations acting upon illusions, famously declaring (kārikā 29) that he advances no independent ontological thesis (pratijñā) to suffer logical contradiction, before concluding in verses 71–72 with adoration of the Buddha.

summary: The Vigrahavyāvartanīkārikā ('Verses on Turning Back Disputes') is a seminal epistemological treatise by Nāgārjuna defending the Madhyamaka doctrine of universal emptiness (sarvadharmaśūnyatā) against realist objections, notably from the Nyāya school. Verses 1–20 set forth the opponent's paradox: if all things lack intrinsic nature (svabhāva), Nāgārjuna's own statement lacks reality and cannot negate anything, or else valid means of knowing (pramāṇa) must be conceded. Verses 21–71 provide Nāgārjuna's counter-arguments, showing that negation and conceptual discourse function precisely because of dependently originated emptiness, and that pramāṇa and prameya are mutually established rather than inherently real.

summary: The Hitopadeśa is a celebrated Sanskrit collection of animal fables and gnomic maxims composed in prosimetric campū form by Nārāyaṇa under the patronage of Prince Dhavalacandra [3882, 3887]. Drawing largely on the Pañcatantra as well as the Kāmandakīyanītisāra and the epics [19], the work is framed as practical instruction in statecraft and ethics given by the sage Viṣṇuśarman to the errant sons of King Sudarśana of Pāṭaliputra [21, 28]. It is divided into four thematic books: Mitralābha (Gaining Friends), Suhṛdbheda (Alienating Friends), Vigraha (War), and Sandhi (Peace) [18, 2076, 3889]. Renowned for its direct syntax and pragmatic political wisdom (nīti), it has served for centuries as an essential introductory reader for students of Sanskrit.

summary: The Nagaropamasūtra ('Discourse on the Simile of the City') is a canonical discourse of the Sarvāstivāda Saṃyuktāgama (Nidānasaṃyukta 14; paralleled in the Pāli Nagara Sutta, SN 12.65). In this discourse, the Buddha explains how prior to awakening he investigated the twelve links of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda), comparing his discovery of the ancient path to an explorer finding an overgrown trail leading to a majestic forgotten city. In Central Asian Sanskrit manuscript transmission, the discourse was preserved as an independent apotropaic text (rakṣā), enlarged with a narrative and ritual appendix extolling its recitation for protection against perils.

summary: The Nairātmyaparipṛcchā ('Questions on Selflessness') is a short Mahāyāna scripture consisting of a prose opening dialogue and 26 verses. Departing from standard sūtra narrative conventions, it depicts non-Buddhist wanderers (tīrthikas) approaching Mahāyāna practitioners to question how bodily actions and affective states (laughter, crying, anger, jealousy) can arise if the body is devoid of a supreme self (paramātman). The Buddhist respondents elucidate the non-duality of existence and non-existence, the distinction between conventional reality (saṃvṛti) and ultimate reality (paramārtha), and the nature of all phenomena as illusory, dream-like appearances empty of intrinsic self-nature.

summary: The Rājanighaṇṭu (also known as Nighaṇṭurāja or Abhidhānacūḍāmaṇi) by Narahari is a comprehensive Āyurvedic materia medica and medical lexicon. summary: The Pāṇḍulohitakavastu is the eleventh chapter (vastu) of the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinayavastu, governing disciplinary legal acts (karmans) carried out by the monastic saṅgha against contentious or recalcitrant monks. Named after the factions led by the monks Pāṇḍuka and Lohitaka, it details five disciplinary measures: censure (tarjanīyakarman), demotion to subordination (nigarhaṇīyakarman), temporary banishment (pravāsanīyakarman), formal reconciliation with aggrieved laity (pratisaṃharaṇīyakarman), and suspension (utkṣepaṇīyakarman) for refusing to see, atone for, or renounce an offense or false view. It also describes the saṅgha legal procedures for probation (parivāsa), retrospective resetting of seniority (mūlāpakarṣa), penance (mānāpya), and eventual reinstatement/rehabilitation (āvarhaṇa) for saṃghāvaśeṣa offenses.

summary: The Pārivāsikavastu is the thirteenth section of the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinayavastu, setting forth the legal prescriptions and behavioral obligations for monks undergoing disciplinary penance for saṅghāvaśeṣa offenses. It details the sangha procedures for conferring probation (parivāsa), penance (mānāpya/mānatva), and setting back to the initial probation (mūlāpakarṣa) when an offense has been concealed. It also lays down the specific rules of conduct governing probationary monks (pārivāsika) in interactions with monks of regular standing (prakṛtisthaka), as well as the formal declarations required to suspend and resume probation.

summary: The Śāstradīpikā of Pārthasārathi Miśra (fl. c. late 11th century CE) is a major classical commentary on Jaimini's Mīmāṃsāsūtra adhering strictly to the Bhāṭṭa school of Kumārila Bhaṭṭa. Its introductory section, the Tarkapāda (Adhyāya 1, Pāda 1), constitutes one of the foundational works of Mīmāṃsā epistemology and metaphysics, defending the intrinsic validity of knowledge (svataḥprāmāṇya), perception, realism concerning universals, and the eternal, uncreated nature of sound and the Vedas against Buddhist, Nyāya, and Advaita opponents. This file contains the Sanskrit text of the Tarkapāda from sūtras 1.1.1 to 1.1.23, ending at the conclusion of the section on the eternality of language (śabdanityatā).

summary: The Pāśupatasūtra is the foundational scriptural text of the Pāñcārthika Pāśupatas, the oldest documented initiatory Śaiva ascetic order (Atimārga). Organized around five cardinal doctrines (pañcārtha: kārya, kāraṇa, yoga, vidhi, and duḥkhānta), it outlines the ascetic path from initiatory vows to eccentric, antinomian behavior intended to solicit public disdain, culminating in total communion with Rudra-Śiva. Kauṇḍinya's Pañcārthabhāṣya provides a detailed theological, ritual, and philosophical commentary that systematizes Pāśupata metaphysics and spiritual practice.

summary: The Pāśupatasūtra is the foundational textual authority of the Pāśupata order, the earliest attested sectarian Śaiva tradition. In five chapters, the work details the five primary ontological and practical principles (pañcārtha): cause (kāraṇa, Śiva/Paśupati), effect (kārya, the bound soul and created world), yoga (contemplative union with Rudra), vidhi (ascetic practices, including smearing ashes, ritual laughter and dance, simulated madness, and inducing public contempt), and duḥkhānta (the final cessation of suffering and attainment of divine powers/fellowship with Śiva).

summary: The Avayavinirākaraṇa ('Refutation of the Composite Whole') is a short polemical treatise by the late Buddhist logician Aśoka. Defending the Dignāga–Dharmakīrti pramāṇa tradition against Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika realists, Aśoka refutes the objective reality of the avayavin (a single composite whole posited as distinct from its parts). Applying the core Buddhist criterion that assigning contradictory properties (such as motion and rest, or visibility and obscuration) to an entity necessitates numerical multiplicity, he demonstrates that gross objects are mental superimpositions upon aggregates of partless atomic particulars.

summary: The Sāmānyadūṣaṇa ('Refutation of Universals') by Aśoka is a short polemical treatise defending Buddhist nominalism against the realist ontology of universals. Following Buddhist epistemological arguments, Aśoka argues that an eternal, unitary, and pervasive universal (sāmānya) cannot be established by perception or inference. The text concludes with the celebrated five-fingers argument: one who claims to perceive a sixth common entity over and above the five distinct fingers might just as well perceive horns on their own head.

summary: The Paippalādasaṃhitā is one of the two surviving recensions of the Atharvaveda (alongside the Śaunakasaṃhitā). Arranged into twenty kāṇḍas, it contains healing charms, protective spells, rituals for prosperity and defense, royal rites, and speculative cosmological hymns. Long known in modern scholarship only through a single, heavily corrupt birch-bark manuscript from Kashmir discovered in 1875, it was rediscovered in the late 1950s when Durgamohan Bhattacharyya located living communities and palm-leaf manuscripts in Odisha.

summary: The Parātriṃśikāvivaraṇa (also entitled Parātriṃśikātattvavivaraṇa) is Abhinavagupta's philosophical commentary on the verses of the Parātriṃśikā. Building on Somānanda's earlier exegesis, Abhinavagupta articulates a metaphysics of absolute consciousness (saṃvid, anuttara) and the Goddess Parā, presenting a philosophy of the Word across its levels. The text provides theoretical grounding for phonematic cosmic emanation, the seed-syllable SAUḤ, and the Kaula contemplative path.

summary: The Paraśurāmakalpasūtra is an aphoristic manual of the Śākta Śrīvidyā (Kaula) ritual tradition. Arranged in ten chapters (khaṇḍas), it sets forth instructions for initiation (dīkṣā), daily and occasional rites, fire offerings (homa), and the esoteric worship of Lalitā Tripurasundarī, the Śrīcakra, and associated deities including Mahāgaṇapati, Śyāmā (Mātaṅgī), Vārāhī, and Parā. It sets forth the procedural and legal rules governing the suspension (sthāpana) of the fortnightly poṣadha (uposatha) Prātimokṣa recitation rite and the invitation rite (pravāraṇā) when a monk is deemed impure or charged with an ecclesiastical offense. The work systematically classifies valid (dhārmika) and invalid (adhārmika) suspensions, outlines appropriate dispute procedures, and defines four kinds of saṃghas.

It details the historical origin of the rite, the delimitation and consecration of monastic precincts (sīmā), the calculation of quorums, formal confession of infractions and declaration of communal purity (pariśuddhi), and the recitation of the Prātimokṣasūtra. summary: The Pratītyasamutpādamahāyānasūtra is a brief Mahāyāna scripture set in the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, where the bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara petitions the Buddha to deliver a teaching yielding boundless merit for the assembly. In response, the Buddha recites the famed dependent arising verse (ye dharmā hetuprabhavā...) and equates dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) directly with the Dharma body (dharmakāya) of all Tathāgatas, stating that whoever perceives dependent arising sees the Tathāgata. He teaches that fashioning even miniature caityas, bodhi trees, and umbrellas and reciting or depositing this verse inside them yields vast, Brahma-like merit (brāhmaṃ puṇyam) leading to rebirth in the Brahmaloka and the Śuddhāvāsa heavens. The sūtra serves as a crucial canonical justification for the widespread medieval Asian Buddhist practice of depositing the ye dharmā creed into stūpas, plaques, and images as a dharmakāya relic (dharmadhātu).

summary: The Pravāraṇāvastu is the third chapter (vastu) of the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinayavastu, regulating the pravāraṇā ('invitation' / mutual admonition) rite held at the conclusion of the three-month rains-retreat (varṣā). In this ceremony, each monastic invites fellow members of the saṅgha to declare any transgression he may have committed—whether seen, heard, or suspected—enabling communal confession, amends, and reconciliation before the community departs. The text details the qualifications and appointment of the presiding pravāraka monk, the formal legal transactions (karmavācanā), provisions for sick monks participating by proxy, and regulations for postponing or staying the ceremony.

Rather than commenting sequentially on Kaṇāda's Vaiśeṣikasūtra, it presents an independent systematic categorization of reality into six fundamental ontological categories (padārthas: dravya, guṇa, karma, sāmānya, viśeṣa, and samavāya), establishing the conceptual foundation for all subsequent classical Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika philosophy.

summary: The Praśnopaniṣad is a classical Upaniṣad associated with the Pippalāda śākhā of the Atharvaveda, composed in mixed prose and verse. It is organized around six philosophical questions addressed by the sage Pippalāda to six seekers concerning the cosmic generation of creatures, the primacy and functions of prāṇa (vital breath), deep sleep, the meditation on the sacred praṇava Oṃ, and the sixteen-part person (ṣoḍaśakala puruṣa). The accompanying Praśnopaniṣadbhāṣya attributed to Śaṅkara expounds these teachings from an Advaita Vedāntic perspective, distinguishing lower knowledge (aparam brahma) from higher realization of the non-dual Self (param brahma).

summary: The Pudgalavastu is the twelfth section (vastu) of the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinayavastu, setting forth ecclesiastical regulations for dealing with individuals (pudgala) guilty of saṃghāvaśeṣa offenses. Starting from the case of the monk Udāyī, the text classifies offending monks according to their degree of awareness, acknowledgment, and concealment of faults, prescribing corresponding sanctions such as probation (parivāsa), retroactive probation (mūlaparivāsa), demotion (mūlāpakarṣa), and the six-day penance (mānāpya). The Sanskrit text is preserved in the Gilgit manuscript discovery.

summary: The Rāṣṭrapālaparipṛcchā ('Questions of Rāṣṭrapāla') is an influential Mahāyāna sūtra included as assembly 18 in the Mahāratnakūṭa collection. Framed as a discourse at Gṛdhrakūṭa between the Buddha and the bodhisattva Rāṣṭrapāla, the text champions the ascetic ideal of forest dwelling (āraṇyaka) and dhūtaguṇa practice while mounting a severe critique against corrupt, comfortable urban monks of the decadent age (paścimakāla). The second half recounts fifty former-life tales (pūrvayoga) illustrating the Bodhisattva's extreme acts of self-sacrifice, culminating in the story of Prince Puṇyaraśmi.

summary: The Mahāgaṇapatistotra is a 16-verse ornate stotra in praise of the tantric form of Mahāgaṇapati, composed in classical metres by the ascetic master Rāghavacaitanya. The verses systematically encode the Mahāgaṇapati mantra, yantra, dhyāna, and iconographic details—depicting the ten-armed red Ganapati embracing his consort upon a jewelled lotus throne in the ocean of sugarcane juice. The running prose ṭippaṇī, composed by the author's disciple, explicitly decodes the esoteric bījas and ritual symbols embedded within the verses.

summary: The Kāvyamīmāṃsā ('Inquiry into Poetry') by Rājaśekhara is a classic of Sanskrit literary theory focused on the practical training and culture of a poet (kaviśikṣā). Although planned on an encyclopedic scale of eighteen books, only the first book, the Kavirahasya ('The Poet's Secret') in eighteen chapters, is extant. The work offers valuable documentation of early medieval Indian literary life, describing the allegorical personification of poetry (Kāvyapuruṣa), the nature of innate poetic talent (pratibhā), royal assemblies and salons (kavisabhā), the classification of borrowing and plagiarism (haraṇa), poetic conventions (kavisamaya), and Pan-Indian cultural geography (deśavibhāga).

summary: The Rāmodanta is an anonymous pedagogical Sanskrit poem summarizing the complete narrative of the Rāmāyaṇa in simple anuṣṭubh verse. Widely used across South India—particularly Kerala—as an introductory reader, it traditionally served as a student's first narrative text following the memorization of basic grammatical declensions and conjugations (such as the Siddharūpa). The original recension comprises 156 verses, encoded by the kaṭapayādi chronogram 'cinmayaḥ' (156) in the final verse, while popular later print editions expanded the text to 199 verses organized into seven kāṇḍas.

summary: The Haṃsadūta ('The Swan Messenger') is a Sanskrit messenger poem (dūtakāvya) in 142 verses composed by Rūpa Gosvāmī. Modeled after Kālidāsa's Meghadūta, the poem describes Lalitā, a confidante of Rādhā, dispatching a swan from the banks of the Yamunā to Kṛṣṇa in Mathurā following his departure from Vraja. The bulk of the composition conveys Lalitā's message depicting Rādhā's distress in separation (vipralambha-śṛṅgāra) and reproaching Kṛṣṇa for abandoning the gopīs, synthesizing courtly lyric conventions with Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava devotional theology.

summary: The Bhaktirasāmṛtasindhu ('Ocean of the Nectar of Devotional Rasa'), composed by Rūpa Gosvāmin, is the foundational work of Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava devotional theology and aesthetics. Adapting the classical rasa theory of Bharata's Nāṭyaśāstra and medieval alaṃkāraśāstra, Rūpa establishes devotion (bhakti) directed toward Kṛṣṇa not merely as a bhāva (transient emotional state), but as the supreme aesthetic and ontological sentiment (bhakti-rasa). Organised in four quadrants (pūrva, dakṣiṇa, paścima, and uttara vibhāgas), the text comprehensively systematises the categories of devotional practice (sādhana, bhāva, prema), the constituent components of aesthetic emotion (vibhāva, anubhāva, sāttvikabhāva, vyabhicāribhāva), the primary rasas (śānta, dāsya, sakhya, vātsalya, madhura), and the secondary devotional sentiments along with discordant mixtures (rasābhāsa).

summary: The Laghubhāgavatāmṛta is a theological treatise composed by Rūpa Gosvāmī summarizing and systematizing Vaiṣṇava ontology. The first part (Pūrvakhaṇḍa or Śrī-Kṛṣṇāmṛta) provides a scriptural classification of divine forms and avataric descents (svayaṃrūpa, tad-ekātma-rūpa, vilāsa, svāṃśa, āveśa, and prakāśa), demonstrating that Kṛṣṇa is the original supreme divinity (avatārī) rather than a subordinate incarnation of Viṣṇu. The shorter second part (Uttarakhaṇḍa or Śrī-Bhaktāmṛta) establishes a gradated hierarchy of devotees of Kṛṣṇa, culminating in the gopīs of Vraja and preeminently Śrī Rādhā.

summary: The Nāṭakacandrikā ('Moonlight of Drama') is a 16th-century dramaturgical treatise by Rūpa Gosvāmī. Synthesizing Bharata's Nāṭyaśāstra and especially the Rasapūrvasudhākara (Rasārṇavasudhākara)—while consciously rejecting the formulation of the Sāhitya-darpaṇa—the work systematizes plot structure (sandhi, sandhyaṅga), hero types, and emotional states for dramatic poetry. It serves as dramaturgical theory and draws dramatic examples from Lalitamādhava and other plays, establishing Kṛṣṇa as the ideal dramatic hero.

summary: The Ujjvalanīlamaṇi ('The Blazing Sapphire') is an influential treatise on devotional aesthetics and theology by Rūpa Gosvāmin. Written as a continuation of the madhura-rasa section of his Bhaktirasāmṛtasindhu, the work presents an analysis of madhura-rasa (the erotic-devotional sentiment) in relation to Kṛṣṇa. Rūpa treats classifications of hero and heroine (nāyaka- and nāyikā-bheda), supporting characters, excitant factors (vibhāva), involuntary physical responses (anubhāva), and permanent emotions (sthāyibhāva) to explain loving relations between Kṛṣṇa and the gopīs of Vraja, culminating in the preeminence of Rādhā.

summary: The Muktācarita ('The Tale of the Pearl') is a campū-kāvya combining Sanskrit prose and verse, composed by Raghunāthadāsa Gosvāmī. Framed as a dialogue between Kṛṣṇa and his queen Satyabhāmā in Dvārakā, Kṛṣṇa recounts an incident from his youth in Vraja during the Dīpāvalī festival: when the gopīs refuse to give him pearls to ornament his beloved cows, Kṛṣṇa plants pearls in the earth and harvests bountiful pearl creepers, whereas the envious gopīs sow pearls with milk and butter but reap only thorny bushes. The work focuses on the witty banter, mock disputes, and commercial bargaining over the jewels between Kṛṣṇa, Subala, Madhumaṅgala, Rādhā, and Lalitā, illustrating the intimate erotic-devotional theology (mādhura-līlā) of the Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava tradition.

summary: The Rasārṇava is one of the principal classical treatises of Indian alchemy (Rasaśāstra), framed as a tantric dialogue between Bhairava and Devī. Across 18 chapters (paṭalas), it provides extensive descriptions of laboratory equipment (yantras), crucibles (mūṣās), furnaces, and mineralogical operations including the purification and fixation of mercury (rasabandha) and flame tests for metals. The physical transmutations are explicitly situated within a tantric soteriological framework aiming at bodily immortality (dehasiddhi) and living liberation (jīvanmukti).

summary: The Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā ('Verses on the Accumulation of Precious Qualities') is a metrical summary of early Prajñāpāramitā doctrine composed in Buddhist Hybrid Sanskrit. summary: The Kṣaṇabhaṅgasiddhi Vyatirekātmikā ('Proof of Universal Momentariness by Negative Concomitance') is a philosophical monograph by Ratnakīrti, defending the epistemological arguments of his master Jñānaśrīmitra. Complementing his Kṣaṇabhaṅgasiddhi Anvayātmikā, this treatise argues from negative contraposition: non-momentary (enduring) entities cannot exercise causal efficiency (arthakriyāsāmarthya) either in succession (krama) or simultaneously (akrama), and therefore cannot exist. Ratnakīrti pays particular attention to defusing the Nyāya objection that an inference with a non-existent subject incurs the fallacy of lack of substratum (āśrayāsiddhi).

summary: The Ratnakīrtinibandhāvalī is a collection of ten philosophical monographs (nibandhas) composed by Ratnakīrti. Major subjects addressed include the proof of the Buddha's omniscience (Sarvajñasiddhi), the refutation of God as creator (Īśvarasādhanadūṣaṇa), the apoha nominalist theory of word meaning (Apohasiddhi), positive and negative proofs of universal momentariness (Kṣaṇabhaṅgasiddhi), the refutation of enduring entities (Sthirasiddhidūṣaṇa), the logic of invariable concomitance and reduction of valid cognitions (Vyāptinirṇaya, Pramāṇāntarbhāvaprakaraṇa), and an ultimate idealist critique of external objects and other minds (Citrādvaitaprakāśavāda, Santānāntaradūṣaṇa).

summary: The Alaṅkārasarvasva is an influential 12th-century Kashmiri treatise on Sanskrit poetics by Ruyyaka (c. 1135–1150 CE). Composed in concise sūtras accompanied by a prose vṛtti, the work provides an analytical and exhaustive classification of over eighty figures of sense and sound (alaṅkāra), integrating traditional rhetorical taxonomies with the dhvani framework established by earlier theorists. Its introductory Bhūmikā offers a critical historical review of earlier poetic theories (including Bhāmaha, Udbhaṭa, Vāmana, Rudraṭa, and Bhaṭṭa Nāyaka), demonstrating that ornamental figures are functionally related to suggested sense.

summary: The Vyaktivivekavyākhyā is a commentary by Ruyyaka on Mahimabhaṭṭa's Vyaktiviveka. This text contains the second chapter (dvitīya vimarśa), which analyzes poetic defects (doṣas) and syntactic improprieties (śabdānaucitya), examining five major faults: vidheyāvimarśa (faulty predication/emphasis), prakramabheda (lack of syntactic parallelism), kramabheda (misplaced word order), paunaruktya (redundancy), and vācyāvacana / avācyavacana (omission or unwarranted inclusion of expressions). Although Mahimabhaṭṭa composed the root work as a polemic against Ānandavardhana's dhvani doctrine by seeking to subsume suggestion into logical inference (anumāna), Ruyyaka's commentary provides indispensable grammatical and rhetorical elucidations while critically scrutinizing Mahimabhaṭṭa's positions.

summary: The Sāṃkhyaparibhāṣā is a late, syncretistic definitional manual composed in mixed prose and verse. Although titled as a Sāṃkhya work, it integrates Sāṃkhya cosmological categories (the twenty-five tattvas) with Advaita Vedānta concepts—explicitly citing the classical Advaita guru lineage from Gauḍapāda to Śaṅkara and the fourfold spiritual prerequisites (sādhanacatuṣṭaya)—as well as elements of Yoga and Haṭhayoga praxis. summary: The Sāṃkhyasūtravivaraṇa (also titled Kāpilasūtravṛtti in its closing colophon) is an anonymous post-classical commentary on the Tattvasamāsa, a concise 23-sūtra mnemonic compendium of orthodox Sāṃkhya topics traditionally ascribed to Kapila. The commentary glosses each sūtra in lucid prose, defining the eight creative causes (aṣṭau prakṛtayaḥ), sixteen modifications (ṣoḍaśa vikārāḥ), spirit (puruṣa), the three guṇas, cosmic emergence and dissolution (sañcara and pratisañcara), down to the three valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa). It represents a concise late scholastic handbook expounding the classical Sāṃkhya dualist ontology and epistemology.

summary: The Sāmavedasaṃhitā is the liturgical verse collection (ārcika) providing the textual base (yoni) for the melodies (sāman) intoned by the Udgātṛ priest during Śrauta sacrificial rituals, particularly the Soma sacrifices. Preserved here in the standard Kauthuma recension, the collection comprises 1,875 mantras divided into the Pūrvārcika (single stanzas arranged by deity—principally Agni, Indra, and Soma Pavamāna—followed by the Āraṇyaka/Mahānāmnī section) and the Uttarārcika (strophes and triplets arranged according to ritual execution). With the exception of approximately 75 stanzas, all verses are drawn from the Ṛgvedasaṃhitā (predominantly Mandalas VIII and IX), frequently showing distinct dialectal and phonetic variations adapted to musical chant.
