summary: The Saṃghāṭasūtra is a Mahāyāna Buddhist sūtra set on Vulture Peak near Rājagṛha, consisting of dialogues between the Buddha and the bodhisattvas Sarvaśūra and Bhaiṣajyasena. It emphasizes the spiritual perils of cyclic existence, the visionary experiences of dying and intermediate states, karmic retribution and purification, and the boundless merit accrued from hearing, reciting, or copying the text. It was exceptionally widely copied in northwestern India and Central Asia, surviving in numerous Sanskrit manuscripts from Gilgit and Dunhuang, as well as Khotanese, Sogdian, Tibetan, and Chinese translations.

summary: The Saṃghāṭasūtra is a canonical Mahāyāna scripture framed as a discourse delivered by the Buddha at Gṛddhrakūṭa to the bodhisattvas Sarvaśūra and Bhaiṣajyasena. The text is celebrated as a classic witness to the Mahāyāna 'cult of the book', repeatedly emphasizing the limitless karmic merit, protection, and purification accrued through hearing, reciting, copying, and worshiping the sūtra itself. Multiple birch-bark copies were recovered from the Gilgit cache; it also circulated in Central Asia, surviving in Khotanese fragments as well as early Chinese (T. 423 by 月婆首那 / Upaśūnya, 538 CE) and Tibetan translations.

summary: The Saddharmalaṅkāvatārasūtra is an influential Mahāyāna Buddhist sūtra that synthesizes Yogācāra consciousness-only (vijñaptimātratā / cittamātra) doctrines with the tathāgatagarbha teaching. Framed as an exposition delivered by the Buddha on Mount Malaya in Laṅkā to the bodhisattva Mahāmati and king Rāvaṇa, it expounds the eight consciousnesses (especially ālayavijñāna), the five dharmas, the three intrinsic natures (trisvabhāva), the two kinds of selflessness (dharmanairātmya and pudgalanairātmya), and the doctrine of vegetarianism (māṃsabhakṣaṇaparivarta). The text exerted foundational influence across Mahāyāna philosophical schools, Tibetan scholasticism, and East Asian Chan/Zen traditions.

summary: The Saddharmapuṇḍarīkasūtra ('The White Lotus of the True Dharma') is one of the most celebrated and influential Mahāyāna scriptures. It propounds the doctrine of the One Vehicle (ekayāna), declaring that the apparent three vehicles (śrāvakayāna, pratyekabuddhayāna, and bodhisattvayāna) are provisional pedagogical devices (upāyakauśalya) and that all beings are destined for unexcelled awakening. Renowned for its rich parables—such as the burning house, the prodigal son, the medicinal herbs, and the gem concealed in the garment—the sūtra also reveals the Buddha's lifespan to be immeasurable and his parinirvāṇa an expedient display.

summary: The Samādhirājasūtra ('King of Samādhis Sūtra', often cited by Indian Madhyamaka commentators as Candrapradīpasūtra) is an influential Mahāyāna scripture in 40 chapters expounding the meditative absorption (samādhi) that reveals the fundamental equality and emptiness of all phenomena (sarvadharmasvabhāvasamatā). Delivered by the Buddha on Vulture Peak to the youth Candraprabha, the text combines exposition of non-arising and ultimate reality with teachings on ethical discipline, ascetic practices (dhūtaguṇa), dhāraṇī formulas, and past-life narratives (jātakas). It was widely quoted as a scriptural authority on emptiness by Candrakīrti, Śāntideva, and Prajñākaramati, and served as a foundational sūtra source for contemplative traditions in Tibet, particularly Sūtra Mahāmudrā.

summary: The Samādhirājasūtra (also known as the Candrapradīpasūtra) is a major Mahāyāna scripture centered on the meditative realization of the essential sameness of all phenomena (sarvadharmasvabhāvasamatā), through which all virtues of buddhahood and the bodhisattva path are perfected. It expounds the emptiness and non-substantiality of dharmas, the transcendent nature of the Tathāgata's dharmakāya, and the ideal ethical and ascetic conduct of bodhisattvas. The text is frequently cited by classical Indian Madhyamaka authors such as Candrakīrti and Śāntideva and plays a prominent role in Tibetan contemplative traditions.

summary: The Āptamīmāṃsā ('Critique of the Trustworthy Authority'), also known as the Devāgamastotra after its opening words, is a philosophical treatise by Samantabhadra. Beginning as a theological inquiry into what qualifies an individual as a truly omniscient, authoritative teacher (āpta), it establishes that miracles and external divine manifestations cannot establish authority; rather, true authority belongs only to one who has eradicated internal passions and whose teachings cannot be invalidated by reason or experience. Samantabhadra applies the sevenfold conditional predication (syādvāda / saptabhaṅgī) and many-sided ontology (anekāntavāda) to refute one-sided (ekānta) philosophical positions across rival Indian traditions, creating the dialectical framework that shaped subsequent Jain logic.

summary: The Samyaksambuddhabhāṣitapratimālakṣaṇa (also known as the Pratimālakṣaṇa) is a manual of Buddhist iconometry. Framed as a discourse at Jetavana where the Buddha instructs Śāriputra on how devotees should fashion icons after the Teacher's parinirvāṇa, the text establishes canonical proportions (pramāṇa) for images of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. Across 54 verses, it details precise measurements in bodily units (aṅgula, mātrā, vyāma) for the uṣṇīṣa, cranial contours, facial features, torso, and limbs, as well as distinct facial types for various classes of divine, human, and semi-divine beings.

summary: The Sarvadurgatipariśodhanatantra ('Tantra of the Elimination of All Evil Destinies') is an influential Buddhist Yogatantra of the Vairocana cycle, dating roughly to the late 7th to 8th century CE. Set in the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, the tantra opens with Śakra pleading with Śākyamuni to deliver the god Vimalamaṇiprabha, who has fallen into the lower realms upon his death. Centering on Sarvavid Vairocana and his maṇḍalas, the text provides elaborate ritual instructions—including initiations, sādhanas, apotropaic rites, and especially mortuary and post-mortem ceremonies—designed to purify negative karmic imprints and ensure liberation from adverse transmigrations.

summary: The Sarvamatasaṃgraha is a concise Sanskrit doxography composed from an Advaita Vedānta perspective. It opens with an epistemological overview (pramāṇanirūpaṇa) detailing means of valid cognition, followed by an exposition of heterodox (Cārvāka/Lokāyata, Jaina, and Buddhist schools) and orthodox schools (including Nyāya, Sāṅkhya, Yoga, Pūrva-Mīmāṃsā, and Uttara-Mīmāṃsā). The systems conclude with non-dual Brahma-realization as the ultimate purport of philosophy.

summary: The Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṅgraha is the foundational root tantra of the Yogatantra class in Indian esoteric Buddhism, dating to the late 7th century CE. Centered on Mahāvairocana and the five Buddha families (kulas) within the Vajradhātu maṇḍala, it expounds the enlightenment of Sarvārthasiddhi via the five progressive realizations (pañcākārābhisambodhi) along with extensive rituals for initiation (abhiṣeka), mudrās, and mantras. It forms the primary doctrinal and ritual bedrock for East Asian esoteric Buddhism (Zhenyan and Shingon) and directly influenced subsequent Indo-Tibetan tantric traditions.

summary: The Sarvopakāriṇī ('The All-Benefiting Gloss') is a concise, anonymous Sanskrit commentary on the Tattvasamāsa (also called Samāsasūtra or Kāpilasūtra), an ancient mnemonic outline of classical Sāṃkhya philosophy. It comments systematically on the 22 sūtras of this recension, expounding the 25 principles (tattvas), the forward and reverse evolutions of the guṇas (sañcāra and pratisañcara), the three kinds of suffering, the sources of valid cognition (pramāṇa), and the nature of liberation (mokṣa). Its opening lines preserve a notable scholastic tradition asserting that this 22-sūtra work represents the original seed of the system taught by Kapila as an avatāra of Nārāyaṇa, in contrast to the six-chapter Sāṃkhyasūtra composed by Kapila as an avatāra of Vaiśvānara.

summary: The Rasārṇavasudhākara ('Nectar-Moon to the Ocean of Rasa') is an encyclopedic 14th-century Sanskrit treatise on dramaturgy and aesthetics composed by King Siṃhabhūpāla II of the Recherla dynasty. Arranged into three comprehensive 'rays' (vilāsas)—Rañjakollāsa (dealing with dramatic personae, the typology of hero and heroine, and their aesthetic embellishments), Rasollāsa (treating the primary sentiments, transient emotions, excitant/ensuant factors, and the nature of aesthetic delight), and Nāṭakollāsa (treating plot structure, junctures/sandhis, and dramatic genres)—it synthesizes the traditions of Bharata's Nāṭyaśāstra, Dhanañjaya's Daśarūpaka, and Bhoja's Śṛṅgāraprakāśa. The work is especially prized by later commentators (notably Mallinātha and the Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava theorists such as Rūpa Gosvāmin) for its rigorous definitions and rich repertoire of illustrative quotations drawn from classical poetry and drama.

summary: The Nyāyāvatāra is a concise 32-verse Jain treatise on epistemology and logic (pramāṇaśāstra) treating perception (pratyakṣa), inference (anumāna), verbal testimony, internal pervasion (antarvyāpti), and the doctrine of perspectives (naya) in the context of anekāntavāda. Historically ascribed to Siddhasena Divākara, the text is also attributed to Siddhasena Mahāmati, who engaged systematically with Buddhist logic. Siddharṣigaṇin's commentary, the Nyāyāvatāravivṛti, provides an exposition of each verse, defending Jain epistemological positions against rival objections.

summary: The Sarvatathāgatoṣṇīṣasitātapatrānāmāparājitāpratyaṅgirāmahāvidyārājñī is an influential Mahāyāna/Vajrayāna apotropaic dhāraṇī scripture centered on the goddess Sitātapatrā ('The White Parasol'). Set in the Sudharmā assembly hall of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, the narrative recounts how Śākyamuni Buddha enters meditative absorption (samādhi), from whose crown protuberance (uṣṇīṣa) emanates this protective incantation. The text provides extensive salutations to buddhas, bodhisattvas, and brahmanical deities, followed by powerful averting and binding formulas (pratyaṅgirā) designed to protect practitioners against evil spirits, demonic afflictions, curses, diseases, and untimely death.

summary: The Revākhaṇḍa is a sacred geographical and pilgrimage text celebrating the holy sites along the course of the Narmadā (Revā) River in Central India. Structured largely around dialogues between the sage Mārkaṇḍeya and Yudhiṣṭhira, the work delineates pilgrimage and circumambulation along both the northern and southern banks, detailing origin legends, shrines, and devotional benefits. As noted by the contributor, Jürgen Neuss, this 116-chapter recension is the genuine Skandapurāṇa Revākhaṇḍa, distinct from the 232-chapter text of the Vāyupurāṇa tradition wrongly assigned to SkP 5.3 in the Veṅkaṭeśvara edition (Bombay: 1910).

summary: The Sukhāvatīvyūhasūtra (commonly designated the Smaller or Shorter Sukhāvatīvyūha, and known in East Asian tradition as the Amitābhasūtra / Amituo jing) is a foundational Mahāyāna scripture of Pure Land Buddhism. Set in the Jeta Grove at Śrāvastī, Śākyamuni Buddha describes to Śāriputra the wondrous adornments and spiritual delights of Sukhāvatī, the western realm presided over by the Buddha Amitāyus. The sūtra proclaims that those who hear Amitāyus's name and maintain focused mindfulness on it will be reborn in Sukhāvatī, a message attested by the buddhas of all directions.

summary: The Śāktavijñāna is a brief 30-verse manual of esoteric Śaiva-Śākta yoga attributed to Somānanda. It expounds thirteen stages or modes (trayodaśavidha) of kuṇḍalinī practice taught across the Trika scriptures: locus (sthāna), penetration (praveśa), form (rūpa), contemplative focus (lakṣa), diagnostic signs (lakṣaṇa), elevation (utthāpana), awakening (bodhana), rest in the centers (cakraviśrāma), ascent through the levels (bhūmikāgamana), penultimate state (antāvasthā), supreme rest in Śiva (viśrāma), radical transformation (pariṇāma), and subsequent return (āgamana).

summary: The Kathāsaritsāgara ('Ocean of the Streams of Story') is an encyclopedic 11th-century Sanskrit narrative poem composed in Kashmir by Somadeva for Queen Sūryavatī. Arranged into 18 lambakas and 124 taraṅgas, it preserves a major Kashmiri verse recension of Guṇāḍhya's lost Paiśācī epic, the Bṛhatkathā. The central frame tale follows Prince Naravāhanadatta's romantic adventures and quest to attain sovereignty over the Vidyādharas, embedding numerous cycles of folk tales, fables, and romances, including the Vetālapañcaviṃśatikā.

summary: The Rasendracūḍāmaṇi ('Crest-Jewel of the Lord of Essences [Mercury]') is an alchemical and iatrochemical treatise composed by Somadeva. It systematically describes the layout and staffing of the alchemical laboratory (rasaśālā), technical apparatus (yantras), crucibles (mūṣās), furnaces (koṣṭhīs), pits (puṭas), as well as the pharmaceutical processing, purification, incineration, and digestion (jāraṇa) of mercury, metals, and minerals.

summary: The Stūpalakṣaṇakārikā is an architectural and ritual verse treatise composed by Bhadravyūha of the Mahāsāṃghika-Lokottaravādin school, setting forth the canonical dimensions, proportions, and structural units of Buddhist stūpas alongside a systematic doctrinal mapping of its components onto Buddhist dharmas (such as the 37 bodhipakṣikadharmas, the four noble truths, and the elements). It is accompanied by the anonymous Stūpalakṣaṇakārikāvivecana, a detailed prose commentary that interprets each stanza with reference to the Lokottaravādin Prakīrṇakavinaya and related monastic traditions. Preserved in a single early Nepalese palm-leaf manuscript, the work constitutes one of the rare surviving Sanskrit treatises on non-Tantric Buddhist stūpa architecture and architectural symbolism.

summary: The Vāsavadattā of Subandhu (dated to the sixth century) is a classical Sanskrit prose romance (kathā). The narrative recounts how Prince Kandarpaketu and Princess Vāsavadattā experience dreams of each other, seek each other out, elope, undergo separation after Vāsavadattā is petrified into stone by an ascetic's curse, and are reunited once the touch of Kandarpaketu restores her to life. The work is famed for its extreme rhetorical display, notably pervasive paronomasia (śleṣa) across almost every syllable and sentence, which served as a major stylistic predecessor to Bāṇabhaṭṭa's prose romances.

summary: The Subhāṣitaratnakaraṇḍakathā is a late Buddhist homiletic poem of 191 verses ending with a pāramitāparikathā. It offers didactic exhortations on the rarity of human rebirth, dharma hearing, merit-making (puṇya), and the practice of the perfections (pāramitās). Although traditionally attributed to Āryaśūra, the work is recognized by modern scholarship as a late Buddhist text on merit (spätbuddhistischer Text zur Verdienstlehre).

summary: The Larger Sukhāvatīvyūha is the primary canonical scripture of the Mahāyāna Pure Land tradition focusing on the Buddha Amitābha (Amitāyus) and his western realm, Sukhāvatī. Delivered by Śākyamuni Buddha on Vulture Peak near Rājagṛha, the sūtra relates the ancient past-life story of the monk Dharmākara, who took great bodhisattva vows to establish a supreme realm. The text depicts the wondrous topography, assemblies, and spiritual benefits of Sukhāvatī, while specifying the criteria for rebirth therein—chiefly generating the aspiration for awakening (bodhicittotpāda), sincere faith, ethical observance, and mindful recollection of Amitābha.

summary: The Smaller Sukhāvatīvyūhasūtra (saṃkṣiptamātṛkā), widely revered in East Asia as the Amitābha Sūtra, is a foundational scripture of Pure Land Buddhism. Set in Śrāvastī, Śākyamuni Buddha describes the western Buddha-field Sukhāvatī and its presiding Buddha Amitāyus (Amitābha) to his disciple Śāriputra, portraying in sensory detail its jeweled pavilions, radiant lotus ponds, music, and divine birds that ceaselessly proclaim the Dharma. The sūtra teaches that living beings who hear Amitāyus's name and hold it single-mindedly without distraction will be welcomed by Amitābha at the point of death and reborn in his realm, a promise affirmed by the Buddhas of the six directions.

summary: The Larger Sukhāvatīvyūha is a foundational Mahāyāna sūtra and the principal scriptural authority for Pure Land Buddhism. Set on Vulture Peak (Gṛdhrakūṭa) in Rājagṛha, the Buddha Śākyamuni narrates to Ānanda how the monk Dharmākara, in the presence of the Buddha Lokeśvararāja, generated the resolve for awakening and made forty-eight great vows to establish the western realm of Sukhāvatī and become the Buddha Amitābha (Amitāyus). The sūtra expounds the visual and spiritual splendors of this paradise, delineates the requirements for rebirth there through faith, recollection, and merits, and includes instructions addressed to the bodhisattva Ajita (Maitreya) on dispelling doubt.

summary: The Sumāgadhāvadāna is an independent Buddhist narrative work (avadāna) in mixed prose and verse relating the story of Sumāgadhā, daughter of the prominent merchant and patron Anāthapiṇḍada of Śrāvastī. Married into the household of Vṛṣabhadatta in Puṇḍravardhana (Bengal), whose family reveres the Nirgranthas (Jains), she is repelled by the naked ascetics and miraculously summons the Buddha and his disciples from her roof. The aerial arrival and marvelous transformations of the Buddha and the arhats convert her husband's family and the entire city to Buddhism. The text concludes with karmic explanations by the Buddha, including Sumāgadhā's past lives and the ten prophetic dreams of King Kṛkin.

summary: The Suvarṇaprabhāsasūtra ('Sūtra of the Golden Light') is an influential Mahāyāna canonical scripture that synthesizes doctrinal expositions of emptiness (śūnyatā) and the boundless lifespan of the Tathāgata with rituals of repentance and state protection. A pivotal episode centers on the bodhisattva Ruciraketu's vision of a golden drum radiating stanzas on confession and purification (deśanā). Protective deities including the Four Heavenly Kings (Caturmahārāja), Sarasvatī, Śrī, and Dṛḍhā pledge to guard righteous sovereigns and realms that uphold the sūtra, while subsequent chapters recount past-life narratives of the Buddha, notably the Vyāghrīparivarta (Mahāsattva jātaka) where the bodhisattva sacrifices his life to feed a starving tigress and her cubs.

After spurning the advances of the corrupt chief minister's wife, Suvarṇavarṇa is falsely accused and condemned to death, but is saved through the miraculous spiritual intervention of the Elder Ānanda and eventually renounces worldly life. summary: The Suvikrāntavikrāmiparipṛcchā (also known as the Sārdhadvisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā, or Perfection of Wisdom in 2,500 Lines) is a canonical Mahāyāna sūtra in seven chapters. Set at the Veṇuvana in Rājagṛha, it features an extensive dialogue between the Buddha and the Bodhisattva Suvikrāntavikrāmin detailing the nature and cultivation of prajñāpāramitā. The sūtra expounds the core doctrine of the non-apprehension (anupalabdhi) and lack of intrinsic existence (asvabhāvatva) of all dharmas, maintaining that true bodhisattva practice avoids attachment to conceptual markers or spiritual attainments.

summary: The Svalpākṣarā prajñāpāramitā ('Perfection of Wisdom in Few Syllables') is a short scripture belonging to the late, tantric phase of the Prajñāpāramitā literature. summary: The Svayambhūpurāṇa is the foundational mythic chronicle and pilgrimage guide (sthala-māhātmya) of Newar Buddhism in the Kathmandu Valley. It recounts the myth of the primordial lake (Nāgadaha) drained through the Chobhar gorge by the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, followed by the appearance of the primordial lotus and the self-existent flame (svayambhūjyotis) of the Dharmadhātu enshrined within the Svayambhū Mahācaitya (Swayambhunath). The work incorporates visits of the previous Buddhas of antiquity, legends of local tīrthas, deities, and nāgas, and the transformation of the valley into a Buddhist kingdom. This 10-chapter recension represents the intermediate (madhyama) version of the text.

summary: The Taittirīyopaniṣad is a principal Upaniṣad of the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda, comprising three chapters: Śikṣāvallī, Brahmavallī (or Brahmānandavallī), and Bhṛguvallī. It covers traditional phonetic instruction, meditative upāsanās, the fivefold sheath analysis (pañcakośa), and the quintessential definition of absolute reality as satyaṃ jñānam anantaṃ brahma. summary: A Buddhist discourse extolling the karmic fruit and spiritual merit generated by fashioning, commissioning, and worshipping images of the Buddha (tathāgatabimba / buddhapratimā). The Buddha recounts the former life of Prince Suvarṇaprabha, who in the era of the past Buddha Vipaśyin was a destitute farmer who fashioned a Buddha image and as a consequence experienced countless rebirths as a universal emperor (cakravartin), Indra, and Brahmā before attaining arhatship. The sūtra systematically lists permissible image materials (clay, stone, ivory, wood, gold, bronze, brass/tin, silver, crystal, and gems) and provides rare early epigraphic/ritual textual evidence for enshrining either bodily relics (sadhātuka) or the Pratītyasamutpāda stanza (sapratītyasamutpāda) inside Buddha statues.

summary: The Tattvamīmāṃsā is a late classical Sāṃkhya prose treatise composed around 1800 CE by Ācārya Kṛṣṇamitra. Structuring its inquiry around the classical framework of the Sāṃkhyakārikā, the work opens by establishing the necessity of philosophical inquiry due to the threefold misery (duḥkhatraya) and refuting both mundane and ritualistic Vedic remedies. It methodically expounds the twenty-five principles (tattvas) divided into primordial source (mūlaprakṛti), evolutes that produce further principles, mere modifications, and the transcendent conscious self (puruṣa), concluding with an exposition of the eight fundamental dispositions (bhāvas) and liberation through discriminative insight ('nāsmi na me nāham').

summary: The Tattvasamāsa ('Compendium of Principles') is a very brief mnemonic outline consisting of between 23 and 27 aphorisms (sūtras) that summarize the central ontological, cosmological, and psychological categories of classical Sāṃkhya philosophy. It lists the fundamental categories including the eight material causes (prakṛti), the sixteen evolutes (vikāra), the conscious subject (puruṣa), the three constituents (guṇa), cosmic evolution and dissolution, and the faculties and conditions governing bondage and release. Traditionally attributed to the mythic sage Kapila, the surviving text represents a medieval scholastic syllabus that served as the basis for several commentaries, such as those by Kṣemānanda, Bhāvāgaṇeśa, and the author of the Kramadīpikā.

summary: The Toḍalatantra is a concise Śākta scripture in ten chapters (paṭalas) preserved chiefly in eastern India. It expounds subtle yogic anatomy, microcosm-macrocosm homologies, and the pūjā, mantras, and iconography of Kālī, Tārā, and the Mahāvidyās along with their male Bhairava consorts. In its tenth chapter, it presents a well-known synthesis equating each of the ten Mahāvidyās with one of Viṣṇu's ten avatāras (such as Kālī with Kṛṣṇa and Tārā with the fish incarnation).

summary: The Triskandhasūtra ('Sūtra of the Three Heaps') is a Mahāyāna liturgical text used for purifying infractions of the bodhisattva vows and moral downfalls. Its title refers to three key ritual actions: confession of moral faults (pāpadeśanā), rejoicing in merits (anumodanā / puṇyānumodanā), and the dedication of merit (pariṇāmanā). While it circulates independently as a ritual text, the liturgy also constitutes the confession pericope within the Vinayaviniścaya-Upāliparipṛcchāsūtra.

summary: The Udānavarga is a canonical northern Buddhist anthology of aphoristic stanzas (udāna) arranged topically across 33 chapters (vargas), primarily preserved in the Sarvāstivāda and Mūlasarvāstivāda traditions. Functioning as the Sanskrit counterpart to the Pāli Dhammapada, the Pāli Udāna, and the Gāndhārī Dharmapada, it shares an ancient core of stanzas while expanding the collection to over a thousand verses. Preserved in Sanskrit manuscripts from Central Asian oasis sites along the Northern and Southern Silk Roads as well as in Tibetan and Chinese translations, it is a crucial witness to early Buddhist verse anthologies and sectarian transmission.

summary: The Pādatāḍitaka ('The Kick') by the late Gupta-era poet Śyāmilaka is the longest and most celebrated of the four satirical monologue plays preserved in the Caturbhāṇī. Spoken entirely by a viṭa (cosmopolitan man-about-town), the play recounts his journey through the streets of Sārvabhaumanagara (Ujjayinī) to convene a council of rogues to prescribe a comedic expiation (prāyaścitta) for a high-caste gentleman kicked on the head by a courtesan during a lovers' quarrel. Rich in social satire, vivid urban character sketches, and linguistic wit, it provides unparalleled insight into late classical Indian courtly and demi-monde life.

summary: The Nyāyavārttikatātparyapariśuddhi (also known as Nyāyanibandha) is Udayana's sub-commentary on Vācaspati Miśra's Nyāyavārttikatātparyaṭīkā, constituting a commentary on Gautama's Nyāyasūtra. This opening section (Adhyāya 1, Āhnika 1) examines the definition and nature of the sixteen Nyāya categories (padārtha), beginning with the instruments of valid knowledge (pramāṇa), the knowables (prameya), and the prerequisites of philosophical debate through final ascertainment (nirṇaya). Udayana vigorously defends Nyāya realism, epistemology, and natural theology against contemporary Buddhist epistemological and anti-realist objections.

summary: The Kāvyālaṃkārasārasaṃgraha ('Compendium of the Essence of Poetic Ornaments') by the Kashmiri rhetorician Udbhaṭa is a major foundational treatise of Sanskrit poetics (alaṃkāraśāstra). In six chapters (vargas), it defines, illustrates, and classifies poetic figures of sound and sense, modifying Bhāmaha's schema and introducing new categories such as punaruktavadābhāsa, kāvyahetu, and kāvyadṛṣṭānta. The accompanying Laghuvṛtti by Pratīhārendurāja is the earliest surviving commentary on the work, providing valuable syntactic analysis, philosophical contextualization (integrating Mīmāṃsā and Nyāya tenets), and critical discussion of the emerging dhvani doctrine.

summary: The Upasaṃpadājñapti is a liturgical legal formulary (karmavācanā) of the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya governing entry into the Buddhist monastic order. It sets out the motions (jñapti) and acts (karman) for the taking of lay vows (upāsakasaṃvara), the going forth from the household life (pravrajyā / novice ordination), and the higher monastic ordination (upasaṃpadā). The text details the formal examination of the candidate for disqualifying impediments (antarāyikā dharmāḥ), the request for preceptor and teachers, the unanimous declaration of the assembled saṅgha, and the subsequent instructions on fundamental monastic rules.

summary: The Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā along with its auto-commentary (vṛtti) by Utpaladeva constitutes the foundational philosophical treatise of the Pratyabhijñā ('Recognition') system of non-dual Kashmir Śaivism. Structured into four sections (adhikāras on knowledge, action, scriptural authority, and a summary of tattvas), the work argues dialectically against Buddhist epistemologists and other rivals to establish that all reality and individual consciousness are identical with the autonomous, self-luminous Lord (Maheśvara / Śiva), and that liberation consists in the explicit recognition of this identity.

summary: The Ajaḍapramātṛsiddhi ('Proof of a Conscious Knower') is one of three short treatises comprising Utpaladeva's Siddhitrayī, written to establish the foundational tenets of non-dual Pratyabhijñā philosophy. In 27 kārikās, Utpaladeva argues against Buddhist momentariness and static Vedāntic consciousness, maintaining that both cognition and practical causal efficacy (arthakriyā) require an active, self-reflective subject (vimarśa, ahaṃbhāva) rather than an insentient (jaḍa) continuum. In this edition, the lost original auto-commentary is replaced by a concise Sanskrit Vṛtti composed in Śāka 1841 by Kashmiri scholar Harabhaṭṭa Śāstrī.

summary: The Ayodhyākāṇḍa (Book 2) and Āraṇyakāṇḍa (Book 3) form the central narrative axis of the Rāmāyaṇa. In Book 2, Queen Kaikeyī's demands force King Daśaratha to abort Rāma's royal consecration and send him into fourteen-year exile with Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa; Daśaratha dies of grief, and Bharata rejects the throne, governing from Nandigrāma with Rāma's wooden sandals on the seat of state. summary: The Ayodhyākāṇḍa forms the second book of Vālmīki's Rāmāyaṇa and depicts the succession crisis in Ayodhyā. Following Daśaratha's plan to crown Rāma as yuvarāja, Queen Kaikeyī, goaded by Mantharā, demands two boons: the exile of Rāma to the forest for fourteen years and the installation of Bharata as king. Rāma unhesitatingly departs with Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa, which precipitates Daśaratha's demise from grief; Bharata adamantly refuses the throne, follows Rāma to Citrakūṭa to plead for his return, and ultimately agrees to govern from Nandigrāma as regent for Rāma's wooden sandals (pādukā).

summary: The Kāvyālaṅkārasūtra along with its auto-commentary (Kāvyālaṅkārasūtravṛtti or Kavipriyā) by Vāmana (fl. late 8th to early 9th century CE, Kashmir) constitutes the defining work of the Rīti school of classical Sanskrit poetics. Vāmana formulated the famous thesis that style (rīti) is the soul of poetry ('rītir ātmā kāvyasya', 1.2.6), distinguishing three primary styles (Vaidarbhī, Gauḍī, and Pāñcālī) based on the presence of specific poetic qualities (guṇas). Organised into five adhikaraṇas (Śārīra, Doṣadarśana, Guṇavivecana, Ālaṅkārika, and Prāyogika), the work presents a comprehensive taxonomy of poetic purpose, flaws (doṣas), aesthetic qualities (ten verbal and ten semantic guṇas), figures of speech (alaṅkāras), and rules for grammatical purity in poetry (śabdaśuddhi).

summary: The Vāmanapurāṇa is one of the eighteen traditional Mahāpurāṇas, nominally named after Viṣṇu's dwarf avatāra who subdues Bali. Despite its formal classification as a Vaiṣṇava Purāṇa, the majority of its narrative content is eclectic, with substantial sections devoted to Śaiva and Śākta mythology, including the myths of Satī and Pārvatī, Śiva's penance, the birth of Kārttikeya, and the goddess's battles with Mahiṣāsura and Andhaka. It also contains detailed sacred geography and pilgrim itineraries (māhātmya), focusing heavily on Kurukṣetra, Sthāṇutīrtha, and Prayāga. Modern scholars assign the compilation of the surviving recension to between the 9th and 11th centuries CE.

Framed as a discourse delivered by the bard Lomaharṣaṇa to the ṛṣis assembled in Kurujāṅgala, it provides an elaborate eulogy of Kurukṣetra and its sacred lakes, notably Brahmasaras (identified with Rāmahrada and Samantapañcaka) and Sannihita-saras, alongside sacred sites along the Sarasvatī and Dṛṣadvatī rivers. The text blends pilgrimage itineraries with local mythology, celebrating Sthāṇutīrtha and recounting both Vaiṣṇava legends (the Vāmana avatāra) and Śaiva myths.

summary: The Kāmasūtra of Vātsyāyana is the foundational Sanskrit treatise on kāma (erotic desire, pleasure, and aesthetic enjoyment), one of the traditional goals of human life (puruṣārtha). Divided into seven adhikaraṇas, the text surveys general principles of life, sexual union, courtship and marriage, the domestic conduct of wives, extramarital affairs, courtesans, and erotic/aphrodisiac recipes. Beyond physical intimacy, the work presents a detailed manual on urban sociology and the cultured lifestyle of the sophisticated citizen (nāgaraka), serving as the canonical source for all subsequent Indian erotic literature.

summary: The Vaikhānasadharmasūtra constitutes the dharmasūtra portion (Praśnas 8–10) of the Vaikhānasasmārtasūtra, belonging to the Taittirīya recension of the Black Yajurveda. Across three praśnas, the work details the duties and occupations of the four social classes (varṇas) and life-stages (āśramas), providing classical Sanskrit literature's most elaborate typology of hermits (vānaprasthas/vaikhānasas) and ascetics (bhikṣus). Combining late Vedic smārta jurisprudence with pronounced early Vaiṣṇava devotional features (such as the worship of Nārāyaṇa), the work is generally assigned to the 3rd or 4th century CE.

summary: The Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā ('Diamond-Cutter Perfection of Wisdom') is a foundational Mahāyāna sūtra presented as a discourse between the Buddha and Subhūti in the Jeta Grove at Śrāvastī. It expounds the core doctrine of emptiness (śūnyatā) through radical deconstructive paradoxes, asserting that while bodhisattvas resolve to liberate all sentient beings, in ultimate reality no entities or self-subsisting dharmas exist. This e-text provides the critical transcription of an early Greater Gandhāran birchbark manuscript from Bamiyan (Schøyen Collection MS 2385/1/1, c. 5th–6th century CE), containing sections 1 through 16c before breaking off.

summary: The Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā is a Mahāyāna Buddhist sūtra cast as a dialogue between the Buddha and the elder Subhūti in the Jetavana at Śrāvastī. The text deconstructs conceptual attachment and reification using iterative paradoxical formulas ('A is not A, therefore it is called A'), emphasizing that dharmas, bodhisattvas, and awakening itself lack svabhāva and must be practiced without fixed ideation (saṃjñā). summary: The Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā ('Diamond-Cutter Perfection of Wisdom Sūtra'), commonly known as the Diamond Sūtra or Triśatikā ('Three Hundred Lines'), is one of the most celebrated and influential scriptures in Mahāyāna Buddhism. Structured as a dialogue between the Buddha and the venerable Subhūti in the Jetavana grove at Śrāvastī, it systematically dismantles attachment to conceptual signs and ontological categories, teaching that bodhisattvas must practice generosity and cultivate supreme enlightenment without abiding in notions of self, living being, or dharma. The text is renowned for its characteristic dialectical formula asserting that a dharma is designated as such precisely because it is empty of intrinsic existence. First translated into Chinese by Kumārajīva in 401/402 CE, the sūtra became a cornerstone of East Asian Buddhist traditions—particularly Chan/Zen—and is celebrated for the 868 CE Dunhuang woodblock scroll, the world's earliest dated complete printed book.

summary: The Vajravidāraṇīdhāraṇī (also known as Vajravidāraṇādhāraṇī) is an apotropaic and purificatory dhāraṇī sūtra delivered by Vajrapāṇi through the spiritual power (anubhāva) of the Buddha. The scripture contains the root dhāraṇī along with heart (hṛdaya) and secondary heart (upahṛdaya) mantras intended to subdue harmful entities (grahas, bhūtas), neutralize sorcery, and clear karmic obscurations. It holds a major place in Indo-Tibetan Vajrayāna ritual as a primary text for ablution and purification (khrus chog).

summary: The Bṛhatsaṃhitā ('Great Compendium') of Varāhamihira (ca. 6th century CE) is the fundamental classic of the saṃhitā (natural omen, divination, and mundane astrology) branch of Indian jyotiṣa. Arranged into 106 chapters and comprising nearly 4,000 stanzas, it serves as an encyclopaedia of classical Indian material and ritual life, treating topics such as planetary movements, eclipses, meteorology, ground water and rainfall, temple and residential architecture (vāstuvidyā), iconometry (pratimālakṣaṇa), gemmology (ratnaparīkṣā), perfumery (gandhayukti), agriculture, and physiognomy. It is an indispensable primary source for the history of science, material culture, and religious society in Gupta-era India.

summary: The Varṣāvastu ('Chapter on the Rains Retreat') is the fourth chapter of the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinayavastu, regulating the mandatory three-month monastic retreat (varṣā or varṣāvāsa) observed during the monsoon. It sets out the formal legal procedures (saṃghakarman) for entering the retreat, the election and duties of the assigner of dwelling places (śayanāsanagrāhaka), the distribution of rooms and seats by casting voting markers or tallies (śalākā), communal regulations during the retreat, and the precise conditions under which a monk may temporarily cross the monastic boundary (sīmā) for up to seven days. Preserved in Sanskrit in the Gilgit manuscripts as well as in Tibetan (Toh 1) and Chinese (T 1445) translations, it closely corresponds to the Vassūpanāyikakkhandhaka of the Theravāda Pali Vinaya.

summary: The Laghusiddhāntakaumudī is an essential introductory primer of Pāṇinian Sanskrit grammar composed by Varadarāja in the seventeenth century. It condenses the comprehensive Siddhāntakaumudī of his teacher Bhaṭṭoji Dīkṣita into 1,279 select sūtras from Pāṇini's Aṣṭādhyāyī, reorganized according to a topical, derivation-focused order (prakriyā) rather than the sequential order of the eight adhyāyas. Accompanied by Varadarāja's concise explanatory commentary (vṛtti) and standard grammatical derivations, the work has served for centuries as the primary pedagogical manual in traditional pāṭhaśālās and modern academic institutions.

summary: The Abhidharmakośakārikā consists of verses in eight chapters composed by Vasubandhu, synthesizing the doctrinal system of the Sarvāstivāda-Vaibhāṣika school of Abhidharma. The text classifies all conditioned and unconditioned phenomena across eight subjects: ultimate constituents (dhātu), sensory and psychological faculties (indriya), cosmological realms (loka), intentional action (karma), underlying afflictions (anuśaya), noble spiritual paths and attainers (mārgapudgala), transcendent cognitions (jñāna), and meditative absorptions (samāpatti). Designed for memorization, it served as the baseline verse manual upon which Vasubandhu constructed his famous auto-commentary (Abhidharmakośabhāṣya), and it remains a fundamental Abhidharma textbook.

summary: The Abhidharmakośabhāṣya is Vasubandhu's prose auto-commentary on his metrical Abhidharmakośakārikā, standing as the foundational masterwork of Buddhist Abhidharma scholasticism. Across eight chapters, the work details the constituents of reality (dhātu), sensory and spiritual faculties (indriya), cosmology and rebirth (loka), action and its fruits (karma), latent defilements (anuśaya), the path and spiritual attainments (mārga and pudgala), direct knowledges (jñāna), and meditative absorptions (samāpatti). Vasubandhu articulates the Sarvāstivāda-Vaibhāṣika system while frequently subjecting it to trenchant Sautrāntika critiques, concluding with an appended ninth chapter that refutes both the Buddhist Pudgalavādin thesis of an inexpressible person and Brahmanical theories of a permanent self (ātman).

summary: Vasubandhu's Triṃśikāvijñaptikārikā ('Thirty Verses on Representation-Only') is a foundational work of Yogācāra/Vijñānavāda Buddhist philosophy outlining the three transformations of consciousness (ālayavijñāna, kliṣṭamanas, and pravṛttivijñāna), the three intrinsic natures (trisvabhāva), and the realization of cognition-only (vijñaptimātratā). Sthiramati's Triṃśikāvijñaptibhāṣya is the sole surviving Sanskrit commentary on the text preserved in the original language. It systematically expounds Yogācāra psychology, the nature of mental factors (caitta), the role of metaphorical designation (upacāra) in establishing consciousness-only without external objects, and the soteriological progression toward fundamental transformation (āśrayaparāvṛtti).

summary: The Triṃśikāvijñaptikārikā (Thirty Verses on Representation-Only) by Vasubandhu is a foundational treatise of Yogācāra Buddhism. In thirty concise kārikās, it expounds the threefold transformation of consciousness (vijñānapariṇāma)—the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna), the afflicted mentation (manas), and the six object-cognizing consciousnesses (pravṛttivijñāna)—alongside the doctrine of the three natures (trisvabhāva). The work outlines the path to realizing mere representation (vijñaptimātratā), culminating in the transformation of the psycho-physical base (āśrayaparāvṛtti) and liberation.

summary: The Trisvabhāvanirdeśa ('Exposition of the Three Natures') is a concise verse work of 38 kārikās by Vasubandhu presenting the classical Yogācāra doctrine of the three natures: the imagined (parikalpita), dependent (paratantra), and consummate (pariniṣpanna). Using the simile of a magician conjuring an elephant from a piece of wood, Vasubandhu demonstrates how subject-object duality is an unreal mental construction upon causally dependent mental processes, and how liberation entails the cessation of this duality and the realization of non-dual reality (dharmadhātu).

summary: The Viṃśatikāvijñaptimātratāsiddhi with its autocommentary (Viṃśatikāvṛtti) is Vasubandhu's foundational defense of the Yogācāra doctrine that reality is cognition-only (vijñaptimātra) and devoid of external, mind-independent physical objects. The text systematically counters realist objections regarding spatiotemporal coordination, collective experience, and causal efficacy through analogies to dreams, collective torment in hell, and shared karmic fruition. It is especially famous for stanzas 11–15, which formulate a decisive refutation of atomism by demonstrating that physical atoms can neither possess parts nor be partless without rendering composite macroscopic extension conceptually impossible.

summary: The Vasudhārādhāraṇī is a widely recited Mahāyāna Buddhist dhāraṇī-sūtra centered on Vasudhārā, the goddess of wealth and grain. In the Kauśāmbī setting, the Buddha instructs the impoverished householder Sucandra on the protective incantation and ritual practices revealed by the ancient tathāgata Vajradharasāgaranirghoṣa to overcome poverty and dispel harm. This e-text preserves a unique recension copied in 1638 CE (Vikrama Saṃvat 1695) in Gujarat, documenting the cross-sectarian adoption and ritual use of the Buddhist prosperity spell by Jaina communities.

summary: The Vasudhārādhāraṇī is a Mahāyāna dhāraṇī scripture framed by a narrative setting in Kauśāmbī. The impoverished householder Sucandra approaches the Buddha to ask how one may obtain abundant wealth, grain, and prosperity in order to provide for a large family and sustain extensive charitable offerings. In reply, the Buddha imparts the Vasudhārā dhāraṇī received from the past Tathāgata Vajradharasāgaranirghoṣa, detailing its ritual practice, protective benefits, and power to produce torrential rains of grain and precious treasures.

summary: The Spandakārikā is a seminal verse treatise of the Spanda school of non-dual Kashmir Śaivism, expounding spanda—the dynamic, unceasing pulsation of supreme consciousness (Śiva/Śakti) that underlies all cosmic manifestation, maintenance, and dissolution. Composed across four sections (niḥṣyandas), the verses present a contemplative methodology for yogic practitioners to recognize this vibrating consciousness within all sensory, cognitive, and affective states, leading to liberation in this life (jīvanmukti). This e-text provides the complete text of the kārikās together with the Spandanirṇaya, the influential eleventh-century commentary by Abhinavagupta's disciple Kṣemarāja, which systematically interprets the work through the synthetic theological framework of Trika and Pratyabhijñā.

summary: The Spandakārikā is the primary doctrinal and meditative manual of the Spanda branch of non-dual Kashmir Śaivism, composed in the 9th century CE and attributed either to the sage Vasugupta or his disciple Bhaṭṭa Kallaṭa. Across approximately 53 verses, the text expounds the principle of spanda—the dynamic, unceasing pulse and creative vibration of absolute Consciousness (Śiva-Śakti) that constitutes the true nature of both macrocosmic manifestation and microcosmic cognitive awareness. Rather than prescribing the complete suppression of mental and sensory operations, the text teaches that by sustained introspective mindfulness of the subtle throb underlying emotions, sense-perceptions, and transitions between mental states, the practitioner attains direct recognition of their essential divine autonomy (svātantrya) and mastery over the psychic energies (cakreśvaratva).

summary: The Viṃśatikākārikā ('Twenty Verses on Representation-Only') is a foundational Yogācāra-Vijñānavāda polemical treatise composed by Vasubandhu. The text refutes the reality of mind-independent external physical objects (bāhyārtha) through a rigorous critique of atomism (paramāṇuvāda), demonstrating that atomic partlessness and spatial extension are mutually incompatible. Vasubandhu defends the thesis that all experiential phenomena are appearances only (vijñaptimātra), answering realist objections by showing that spatial-temporal determination, intersubjective consistency, and practical efficacy can function without external objects, as seen in dreams, collective karmic hallucinations, and demonic mental projections.

summary: The Viṃśatikāvijñaptimātratāsiddhi ('Proof of Mere Representation in Twenty Verses') is a foundational treatise of Yogācāra-Vijñānavāda philosophy composed by Vasubandhu in the 4th to 5th century CE. In twenty-two concise kārikās, Vasubandhu defends the thesis that external objects do not exist independently of cognition (vijñaptimātra), refuting realist objections regarding spatiotemporal determinacy, intersubjective consensus, and causal efficacy through comparisons with dreams and hell visions. The work also articulates a famous critique of atomism (paramāṇuvāda), arguing that indivisible partless atoms cannot coalesce into composite extended bodies without logical contradiction.

summary: The Viṣṇudharma is an early Vaiṣṇava devotional and ritual handbook of approximately 4,200 verses in 105 chapters, generally dated to the 3rd–5th century CE. Framed as an exposition given by the sage Śaunaka to King Śatānīka, it instructs householders and lay devotees on the worship, liturgy, mental contemplation, vrata observances, and festivals dedicated to Viṣṇu. It represents one of the foundational texts of early non-sectarian Vaiṣṇavism, serving as a direct predecessor to the larger encyclopedic Viṣṇudharmottarapurāṇa and functioning alongside the roughly contemporary Śivadharmaśāstra as a crucial witness to early medieval devotional religion.

Comprising six books (aṃśas) arranged as a dialogue between Parāśara and Maitreya, it treats cosmology, geography, varṇāśramadharma, and devotes book five to an extensive early biography of Kṛṣṇa. Frequently dated in its core to the Gupta period (c. 4th–5th century CE), it is a foundational scripture for classical Vaiṣṇava theology and Vedāntic exegesis.

Arranged into 50 thematic sections (vrajyās) encompassing 1,738 stanzas, it collects works from over two hundred poets, opening with Buddhist and Hindu devotional hymns and progressing through the seasons, love, social types, nature, gnomic sayings, and praise of poets. summary: The Pratāparudrīya (or Pratāparudrayaśobhūṣaṇa) by Vidyānātha is a manual of Sanskrit poetics and dramaturgy. Across nine chapters (prakaraṇas), it covers the hero (nāyaka), the nature of kāvya, dramaturgy (nāṭaka), rasa, poetic flaws (doṣa), poetic excellences (guṇa), and verbal and semantic ornaments (śabdālaṅkāra, arthālaṅkāra, miśrālaṅkāra). Its third chapter incorporates a play, the Pratāparudrakalyāṇa, designed as a model drama.

summary: The Vidyāsthānopamasūtra is a short canonical Buddhist discourse contrasting mundane crafts and occult sciences (śilpa-, karmasthāna, incantations, herbal drugs, sorcery, medicine, clairvoyance, and supernatural powers) with the liberative doctrine of the Buddhas. While mundane branches of learning emerge during the evolution of the world, they cannot eliminate suffering; only the Buddhas disclose the supreme science—the Four Noble Truths and the Noble Eightfold Path leading to nirvāṇa.

summary: The Vijñānabhairava is an influential scripture of the Trika and Kaula non-dual Śaiva traditions of Kashmir, presented as an esoteric dialogue between Bhairava and the goddess Bhairavī. Transcending external rituals and formal visualizations, Bhairava imparts 112 contemplative practices (dhāraṇās) intended to lead to direct experiential realization of non-dual consciousness. These techniques utilize breath movement, sensory and perceptual gateways, intervals between mental states, aesthetic absorption, and heightened affective experiences to induce spontaneous immersion (samāveśa) into the reality of Śiva.

summary: The Sāṅkhyasāra is an independent philosophical manual (prakaraṇa) of the Sāṅkhya system composed by the 16th-century synthesizer Vijñānabhikṣu. Structured into two parts—a Pūrvabhāga of four paricchedas and an Uttarabhāga of seven paricchedas—it sets out the nature of liberation (puruṣārtha), discriminative insight (vivekakhyāti), the material evolutes (prakṛti and tattvas), puruṣa, and the essential distinctions between self and non-self. The work encapsulates the core positions elaborated in his larger Sāṅkhyapravacanabhāṣya, harmonizing classic Sāṅkhya dualism with theistic elements and Pātañjala Yoga.

summary: The Mitākṣarā by the twelfth-century Sanskrit author Vijñāneśvara is a commentary on the Yājñavalkyasmṛti (Yājñavalkya-dharmaśāstra). Its subject is dharma, legal and religious duty, encompassing ācāra, vyavahāra, and prāyaścitta. Along with the Mānava-dharmaśāstra, it is one of the most influential works of classical Hindu law, forming the foundation of the Mitākṣarā legal school.

summary: The Vimalakīrtinirdeśa is an influential Mahāyāna sūtra set in Vaiśālī, centered on the lay bodhisattva Vimalakīrti, who feigns illness to receive visitors and instruct them. In a series of witty dialogues with major arhat disciples and bodhisattvas, Vimalakīrti dismantles dualistic attachments regarding renunciation, purity, and emptiness (śūnyatā), culminating in his famous silence to signify direct entry into non-duality (advayadharmamukha-praveśa). Long celebrated in East Asian Buddhism and Tibet via early translations, the complete Indic Sanskrit text was identified in a palm-leaf manuscript preserved at the Potala Palace in Lhasa.

summary: Guṇaprabha's Vinayasūtra is the definitive scholastic digest of the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya, condensing canonical narrative and disciplinary legal codes into concise aphorisms. This first chapter, the Pravrajyāvastu, sets forth monastic regulations and formal legal acts (karmavācanā) regarding novice reception (śrāmaṇeratvopanayana) and full ordination (upasaṃpad). Accompanied here by Guṇaprabha's auto-commentary (Vinayasūtravṛtti or Svavyākhyāna), it served as an authoritative reference work for Buddhist monastic jurisprudence in late Indian and Tibetan Buddhism.

summary: A Mahāyāna sūtra transmitted within the Ratnakūṭa collection that contrasts the monastic prātimokṣa rules of śrāvakas with the ethical conduct of bodhisattvas. The Buddha explains that while the śrāvaka discipline centers on strict detachment to avoid any rebirth in saṃsāra, bodhisattva discipline is guided by skillful means (upāyakauśalya) and intention, prioritizing the welfare and gathering of beings. Consequently, offenses rooted in aversion or hatred are considered severe for a bodhisattva because they cause abandonment of beings, whereas infractions rooted in desire can serve to gather beings and are deemed comparatively less obstructive. The sūtra concludes with an exposition by Mañjuśrī on the unconditioned, inherently pure nature of all dharmas.

summary: The Saṃvitsiddhi is the third treatise of Yāmunācārya's celebrated Siddhitraya ('Triad of Demonstrations'), a foundational work of Viśiṣṭādvaita Vedānta. Written primarily in verse with argumentative prose transitions, the work offers an extensive critique of Advaita Vedānta epistemology and ontology, refuting the concept of contentless, undifferentiated consciousness (nirviśeṣa-cinmātra), the unreality of difference, and the doctrine of anirvacanīyatva. Instead, Yāmuna demonstrates that consciousness (saṃvit) is inherently qualified, intentional, and the attribute of an enduring knowing self (jñātṛ). This text directly influenced Rāmānuja's Mahāsiddhānta in the Śrībhāṣya. The digital file presents the surviving portions of the Saṃvitsiddhi accompanied by the Siddhāñjana commentary by P. B. Aṇṇaṅgarācārya.

summary: The Rasaprakāśasudhākara is a major 13-chapter Sanskrit treatise on alchemy and iatrochemistry (rasaśāstra), composed by Yaśodhara Bhaṭṭa in Saurashtra (Gujarat). It describes the origins, grades, and eighteen purification and transmutational processes (aṣṭādaśa-saṃskāra) of mercury, followed by treatments of primary and secondary minerals (mahārasas and uparasas), metals, gemstones, and apparatus (yantras, crucibles). The text holds an important position in the history of Indian chemistry for offering one of the earliest explicit accounts of zinc (yaśada/rasaka-sattva) distillation extraction and for key iatrochemical formulations such as Somanāthī tāmrabhasma and calomel (karpūrarasa).

summary: The Yogaśataka ('Century of Formulations') is an influential early Āyurvedic formulary compiling approximately one hundred standard therapeutic recipes (yogas). Arranged largely according to the classical eight branches (aṣṭāṅga) of Indian medicine, it provides practical remedies for fevers, gastrointestinal and urinary disorders, respiratory complaints, poisoning, pediatrics, and eye conditions, concluding with general principles of humoral pathology and regimen. Its popularity across Buddhist Asia is attested by early translations into Tibetan and Tocharian B.

summary: The Śāṅkhāyanagṛhyasūtra is the domestic ritual manual (gṛhyasūtra) of the Śāṅkhāyana branch of the Ṛgveda. Across six adhyāyas, it sets out the rules for household sacraments (saṃskāra) such as upanayana and vivāha, daily morning and evening oblations, seasonal rites, ancestor worship (śrāddha), and expiations. The final two chapters contain supplementary rites and mantras. Closely related to the Kauṣītaki-Gṛhyasūtra, it forms one of the principal domestic authorities of the Ṛgvedic tradition.

It details the ritual roles, duties, and recitations of the hotṛ priest and his assistants (Maitrāvaruṇa, Acchāvāka, and Grāvastut) across the full spectrum of Vedic sacrifices, including the agnihotra, darśapūrṇamāsa, cāturmāsya, paśubandha, and extensive soma rituals (Agniṣṭoma, Ahīna, and Sattra). The text comprises 18 adhyāyas, of which chapters 1–16 form the primary sūtra core and chapters 17–18 constitute later supplementary sections (pariśiṣṭa).

summary: The Bodhicaryāvatāra ('Entering the Way of Awakening') is an influential Mahāyāna verse manual and classic of Buddhist devotional-philosophical literature composed in ten chapters by Śāntideva. It outlines the spiritual cultivation of the bodhisattva, tracing the generation and stabilization of the awakening mind (bodhicitta), ritual confession, vigilance (apramāda), guard over awareness (saṃprajanya), and the perfections of patience (kṣānti), vigor (vīrya), meditative absorption (dhyāna), and dedication of merit (pariṇāmanā). The ninth chapter develops a Madhyamaka dialectical critique of intrinsic nature (svabhāva), refuting rival Buddhist and non-Buddhist philosophical systems.

summary: The Bodhicaryāvatāra ('Entering the Bodhisattva Path') is an 8th-century Sanskrit didactic and philosophical poem by the Madhyamaka master Śāntideva. Arranged in ten chapters, it serves as a practical manual for generating and sustaining the awakening mind (bodhicitta) and cultivating the six bodhisattva perfections (pāramitās). The work is celebrated for its ethical power—notably the exchange of self and other (parātmaparivartana) in chapter 8—and its rigorous philosophical exposition in chapter 9 (Prajñāpariccheda), which defends Madhyamaka emptiness (śūnyatā) against rival Buddhist and non-Buddhist metaphysical positions.

summary: The Śārdūlakarṇāvadāna (Divyāvadāna Chapter 33) narrates how the low-caste Mātaṅga (Caṇḍāla) maiden Prakṛti falls in love with the Buddha's disciple Ānanda and attempts to entrap him with love sorcery, but is rescued by the Buddha, ordained as a bhikṣuṇī, and attains arhatship. In explaining this event, the Buddha recounts the past-life debate between Triśaṅku, the chieftain of the Caṇḍālas, and the learned Brahmin Puṣkarasārin, providing a vigorous critique of the Brahmanical hereditary caste hierarchy by arguing that the four varṇas are mere nominal conventions rather than innate biological categories. Within this dialogue, the text incorporates an encyclopedic treatise on pre-Hellenistic Indian divination, palmistry, and nakṣatra astronomy and astrology.

summary: The Kaṭhopaniṣad is a classical Vedic Upaniṣad framed as a dialogue between the young seeker Naciketas and Yama, the lord of death. Yama instructs Naciketas on the distinction between the pleasant (preyas) and the truly beneficial (śreyas), the famous chariot allegory illustrating the relationship between the self, intellect, mind, and senses, and the transcendent, immortal nature of the ātman. In his Kaṭhopaniṣadbhāṣya, Śaṅkara offers a rigorous Advaita Vedānta exposition, establishing that liberation (mokṣa) is achieved exclusively through the non-dual intuitive realization of the individual self's identity with Brahman rather than through ritual action or meditation.

summary: The Upadeśasāhasrī ('Thousand Teachings') is a treatise (prakaraṇagrantha) attributed to Śaṅkara. Consisting of a metrical section (Padyabandha, 19 chapters) and a prose section (Gadyabandha, 3 chapters), it presents a concise exposition of Advaita Vedānta focusing on the identity of the individual self (ātman) with absolute reality (Brahman). The text emphasizes the complete renunciation of ritual action (karma) in favor of knowledge (jñāna), explicates Upaniṣadic mahāvākyas (especially 'tat tvam asi'), and demonstrates the pedagogical dialogue through which an enlightened teacher dismantles superimposition (adhyāsa) in a qualified pupil.

summary: The Vivekacūḍāmaṇi ('Crest-Jewel of Discrimination') is one of the most widely read verse manuals (prakaraṇa-grantha) of Advaita Vedānta, composed in 580 verses. Set as a pedagogical dialogue between a spiritual teacher and a qualified disciple, it outlines the fourfold qualifications of an aspirant (sādhana-catuṣṭaya), analyzes the three bodies and five sheaths (pañca-kośa), elucidates the nature of māyā and ignorance, and demonstrates the fundamental discrimination (viveka) between the eternal Self (ātman) and the non-Self (anātman). The work culminates in the direct realization of non-duality and the characteristics of the liberated sage (jīvanmukta).

It lays out the foundational epistemology of the Pūrva Mīmāṃsā school: the investigation of dharma (dharmajijñāsā), Vedic injunction (codanā) as the sole epistemic means for suprasensory dharma, the definition of perception (pratyakṣa), and the innate, beginningless relationship between linguistic expressions and their meanings (autpattikaḥ śabdārthasaṃbandhaḥ). summary: The Atharvaśiropaniṣad ('Head of the Atharvaveda') is an early Śaiva and Pāśupata Upaniṣad traditionally attached to the Atharvaveda. It begins with the gods questioning Rudra about his identity, to which Rudra responds with a grandiose self-proclamation asserting that he is the sole eternal reality, transcendent and immanent in all deities, natural phenomena, and meters. The text expounds esoteric meditations on the sacred syllable Om (praṇava) and prescribes the observance of the Pāśupata vow (pāśupatavrata), including the application of sacred ashes (bhasmasnāna) for severance of worldly bondage (paśupāśa). Already cited in ancient Dharmasūtras (e.g. Gautama and Baudhāyana), it constitutes one of the foundational scriptural texts of early Śaivism.

summary: The Śivasūtra is the foundational revealed text of the non-dual Kashmiri Trika school, outlining the nature of supreme consciousness and the three successive means (upāyas)—śāmbhava, śākta, and āṇava—by which the bound soul realizes its inherent identity with Śiva. This e-text pairs the root sūtras with the Śivasūtravārttika of Varadarāja (alias Kṛṣṇadāsa), a verse exposition that versifies and condenses the classic prose interpretation provided in Kṣemarāja's Śivasūtravimarśinī. Through accessible anuṣṭubh verses, Varadarāja systematically elucidates the metaphysical definitions of bondage, the dynamics of divine energy (spanda/mātṛkā), and yogic integration.

summary: The Śrāvakabhūmi ('Stage of the Disciple') is a major treatise within the Maulī Bhūmi of the Yogācārabhūmi corpus, structured across four yogasthānas. This e-text contains Yogasthānas 1 and 2, which systematically treat the spiritual requisites of practice, the classification of disciples, qualified spiritual masters, ālambana (meditative objects), and initial tranquilization and insight. In addition, the file incorporates three other independent bhūmis from the Yogācārabhūmi edited as appendices in the 2007 Taisho publication: the Asamāhitā bhūmi, the Śrutamayī bhūmi, and the Cintāmayī bhūmi (concluding with the Ābhiprāyikārthagāthānirdeśa).

summary: The Śrīghanācārasaṃgraha ('Compendium of Conduct according to the Buddha') is a Buddhist Vinaya manual in verse outlining monastic discipline and deportment for novices (śrāmaṇera). Affiliated with the Mahāsāṃghika (or Lokottaravādin) disciplinary lineage, the work is organized into four adhyāyas treating the three refuges, the ten novice precepts (śikṣāpada), and supplementary rules of conduct. Because no separate manuscript of the root verses survives, the e-text presents the modern philological reconstruction by Sanghasen Singh extracted from the lemmata and glosses of Jayarakṣita's Sphuṭārthā commentary.

summary: The Ratnatrayaparīkṣā ('Examination of the Three Jewels') is an influential 10th–11th-century Sanskrit doctrinal treatise in 322 verses by the Kashmirian Śaiva Siddhānta scholar Śrīkaṇṭhasūri. Instead of examining the school's general ontological triad (pati, paśu, and pāśa), the work focuses specifically on the 'three jewels' defined as bindu (the material cause of pure sound, language, and the pure universe), śakti (the conscious power of the Lord), and śiva (the supreme agent and consciousness). Drawing heavily on earlier Kashmirian exegesis (especially Bhaṭṭa Rāmakaṇṭha), it provides a detailed metaphysical exposition of the pure path (śuddhādhvan), phonematic cosmogony, and soteriological initiation.

summary: The Śukasaptati ('Seventy Tales of the Parrot') is a popular Sanskrit frame-tale narrative (kathā). When the young merchant Madanavinoda embarks on a lengthy commercial journey abroad, his wife Prabhāvatī is tempted by dissolute companions to pursue illicit liaisons; her wise parrot keeps her at home each night by narrating an ingenious story of wit, trickery, or adulterous escape, cunningly breaking off the tale until dawn. Over the course of seventy consecutive nights, the parrot deters her from infidelity until the merchant returns. Renowned for its realistic depiction of rogue life and practical cleverness, the collection enjoyed immense popularity throughout Asia and formed the direct basis for the Persian Ṭūṭī-nāma.

summary: The Śvetāśvataropaniṣad is a classical metrical Upaniṣad belonging to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda tradition, dating approximately to the late centuries BCE. Comprising six chapters, it synthesizes older Upaniṣadic non-dualism with an explicitly theistic framework, identifying the supreme transcendent Brahman with the personal deity Rudra-Śiva (also addressed as Hara, Īśa, and Maheśvara). The text incorporates concepts that later became central to classical Sāṃkhya and Yoga—such as pradhāna/prakṛti, puruṣa, the guṇas, and physical postures and breath control for meditation—and concludes with an influential early articulation of personal devotion (bhakti) toward God and the guru.

summary: The Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad is a classical metrical Upaniṣad associated with the Black Yajurveda tradition, dating to approximately the late centuries BCE. It synthesizes Vedāntic non-dualism with early Sāṃkhya-Yoga categories, yogic contemplation and posture (adhyāya 2), and personal theism centered on Rudra-Śiva. The text outlines a threefold reality comprising the individual soul (bhoktṛ), the objective world (bhogya), and the supreme lord (preritṛ / īśa), and provides one of the earliest occurrences of the concept of bhakti in classical Sanskrit literature (6.23).

summary: The Perumāḷ Tirumoḻi is an anthology of 105 Tamil devotional verses by Kulacēkara Āḻvār forming part of the canonical Nālāyira Divya Prabandham. The collection comprises ten decades dedicated to Viṣṇu in various manifestations and shrines (such as Śrīraṅgam, Veṅkaṭam, and Tillai Cittirakūṭam), exploring diverse devotional stances (bhāvas) including bridal devotion, maternal tenderness as Kauśalyā and Yaśodā, and devotion to Rāma. Periyavāccāṉ Piḷḷai's 13th-century Maṇipravāḷam commentary provides a line-by-line grammatical, theological, and devotional exposition reflecting classical Viśiṣṭādvaita doctrine.

summary: The Vajrāvalī (or Vajrāvalīnāmamaṇḍalopāyikā) by Abhayākaragupta is a comprehensive ritual compendium of late Indian tantric Buddhism. Structured around sequential rites (vidhi), it details the selection and purification of the ritual ground, maṇḍala construction and coloration, installation and consecration of images and monastic dwellings (pratiṣṭhā), the progression of tantric initiations (abhiṣeka), post-initiatory observances (vrata), fire rituals (homa), and maṇḍala dissolution. Providing the liturgical framework for maṇḍalas also described in Abhayākaragupta's Niṣpannayogāvalī, the work became a foundational ritual authority in Tibetan Buddhist traditions.

summary: The Krīḍākhaṇḍa ('Book of Divine Play') is the second and concluding part of the Gaṇeśapurāṇa, an Upapurāṇa central to the Gāṇapatya tradition. In 155 chapters, it narrates the cosmic deeds and avataras of Gaṇeśa across the four yugas: Mahotkaṭa in the Kṛtayuga, Mayūreśvara in the Tretāyuga, Gajānana in the Dvāparayuga, and Dhūmraketu in the Kaliyuga. Chapters 138–148 form the celebrated Gaṇeśagītā, wherein Gaṇeśa expounds yoga and non-dualist devotion to King Vareṇya, modeling its philosophy and verse forms directly on the Bhagavadgītā.

Composed in elaborate classical metres, it commemorates the installation of Śiva-liṅgas (including Rājendrabhadreśvara) and various deities by King Rājendravarman II. The composition details royal genealogy, mythical lineages, religious foundations, and royal decrees with exceptional grammatical and literary sophistication.

summary: A 15-canto Sanskrit mahākāvya composed in the 13th century CE by Someśvaradeva, court priest to the Caulukya rulers of Gujarat. Elaborating on the foundational framing story of the Devīmāhātmya from the Mārkaṇḍeyapurāṇa, the epic narrates the life of King Suratha: his loss of sovereignty, forest retreat, devotion and rigorous penance to the Goddess, her destruction of the demon army, and Suratha's restoration to power. summary: The Suśrutasaṃhitā is one of the three foundational classics of classical Āyurveda (the Bṛhat-trayī) and ancient India's premier authority on surgery (śalyatantra). Framed as instructions delivered by Divodāsa Dhanvantari, king of Kāśī, to his student Suśruta, it describes surgical instruments, practical anatomy through human cadaveric dissection, and operative procedures such as rhinoplasty, couching of cataracts, lithotomy, and abdominal suture. The treatise comprises 186 chapters divided across the five sthānas of the Pūrvatantra (Sūtra-, Nidāna-, Śārīra-, Cikitsā-, and Kalpasthāna) and the supplementary Uttaratantra, which treats ophthalmology and ENT (śālākya), pediatrics (kaumārabhṛtya), toxicology/psychiatry (bhūtavidyā), and general medicine (kāyacikitsā).

summary: The Īśvarasaṃhitā is a prominent canonical text of the Pāñcarātra Vaiṣṇava Āgama, traditionally treated as an elaboration of the foundational Sāttvatasaṃhitā. Spanning 25 chapters, it systematically sets forth temple rituals, daily worship (nityapūjā), the fivefold division of time (pañcakāla), temple layout, iconography, image consecration (pratiṣṭhā), initiation (dīkṣā), and expiation (prāyaścitta). It is historically significant in the South Indian Śrīvaiṣṇava tradition, notably informing ritual practice at Melkote (Yadugiri).

summary: The Kātantra (also known as Kalāpa or Kaumāra), attributed to Śarvavarman, is the foundational work of the earliest post-Pāṇinian Sanskrit grammatical school. Designed as an accessible alternative to Pāṇini's Aṣṭādhyāyī without employing the complex Śivasūtra pratyāhāra apparatus, it systematically treats phonology and sandhi, nominal morphology and compounds, verbal conjugation, and primary derivatives across four books. Durgasiṃha's Kātantravṛtti is the canonical commentary elucidating the sūtras, which established the school's doctrinal authority and ensured its widespread transmission throughout Kashmir, eastern India, Central Asia, and Tibet.

summary: The Anuttaraprakāśapañcāśikā is a concise philosophical work in 51 anuṣṭubh verses belonging to the non-dual Śaiva (Trika/Spanda) tradition of Kashmir. It expounds the nature of ultimate reality (anuttara) as autonomous pure consciousness (cit, prakāśa) inherently endowed with dynamic self-awareness (vimarśa, svātantrya, spanda). The work systematically maps the manifestation and reabsorption of the thirty-six cosmic principles (ṣaṭtriṃśat-tattva) back into undivided supreme subjective awareness (aham).

This second volume (chapters 23–47) details ritual procedures including mantroddhāra (extraction of mantras), extensive mudrāvidhi (hand gestures and seals), maṇḍala construction, and karmavidhi rites associated with Mañjuśrī and retinue. summary: The Mantrakoṣa of Āśāditya Tripāṭhin is a tantric ritual compendium (mantranibandha) organized into sixteen chapters (paricchedas). It outlines procedures and mantras for pūjā, dīkṣā, guru-śiṣya qualification, bhūtaśuddhi, mātṛkānyāsa, yantras, and mudrās, drawing upon authorities such as the Prapañcasāratantra. The deity sections encompass pañcāyatana worship (Sūrya, Gaṇapati, Śiva, Viṣṇu/Nṛsiṃha, Sarasvatī/Śrī) along with protective and astrā mantras.

The Sanskrit kārikās are accompanied by an explanatory Maṇipravāḷa commentary in Tamil and Sanskrit discussing day-to-day exceptions, commensality, and purificatory rites.

summary: The Īśānaśivagurudevapaddhati is an encyclopedic manual of ritual, temple consecration, and mantra-śāstra composed by the Kerala Śaiva authority Īśānaśivagurudeva (c. 11th–12th century CE). This opening division, the Sāmānyapāda (paṭalas 1–14), provides the common preliminary framework for ritual activity, including the classifications and recitation of mantras, the nature of letters (mātṛkā), the dimensions and preparation of sacrificial pits (kuṇḍa) and diagrams (maṇḍala), morning ablutions, and the rites of the sacred fire (agnikalpa). Synthesizing Śaivasiddhānta tenets with regional Kerala tantric traditions, it serves as a key witness to medieval South Indian ritual literature.

summary: The Mantrapāda forms the second division of Īśānaśivagurudeva's paddhati, completing its first half (Pūrvārdha). It provides an exhaustive treatment of mantravāda, including meditation verses (dhyāna), nyāsa, and japa for Gaṇapati, Sarasvatī, Viṣṇu, Śiva, Mṛtyuñjaya, and numerous forms of the Goddess. It also incorporates extensive sections on toxicology (viṣacikitsā), spirit exorcism (bhūtavidyā), magical protection (rakṣā), and martial sorcery (yuddhajaitrakarman).

summary: The Īśānaśivagurudevapaddhati (also titled Siddhāntasāra) is an encyclopedic Śaivasiddhānta ritual compendium composed by Īśānaśivagurudeva. This volume preserves the first half of the Kriyāpāda (paṭalas 1–30), covering the theological foundations of Śaivism, daily liturgy (nityapūjā), the tiered structure of Śaiva initiation (dīkṣā), and extensive treatises on temple architecture, vāstu, and iconography (vimāna, upapīṭha, adhiṣṭhāna).

summary: The Ṣaḍāmnāyapūjāvidhi is an anonymous Śākta ritual manual (paddhati) detailing daily worship rituals focused on Mahātripurasundarī structured by the six regional traditions (ṣaḍāmnāya) of Kaulism and Śrīvidyā. It prescribes the preliminary rites including morning ablutions, guru contemplation, bodily purification (bhūtaśuddhi), extensive nyāsa sequences (such as mātṛkā- and śrīkaṇṭhanyāsa), and the worship of surrounding retinue goddesses and cakras. The surviving manuscript witness was transcribed in Nepal in 1922 CE by Śāradāvilāsa Śarman for Nepalese Royal Preceptor Hemarāja Śarman from an older palm-leaf codex.

summary: An anonymous Kaula/Tantric yoga treatise on subtle-body physiology centered on the standard schema of the six cakras (ṣaṭcakra), sixteen bodily supports (ṣoḍaśādhāra), three gazing targets (trilakṣya), and five internal spaces (vyomapañcaka). The work combines kārikā verses with prose explanation and comparative citations ('anyaśāstrābhiprāyaḥ'), concluding with a stuti section. It is distinct from Pūrṇānanda's well-known Ṣaṭcakranirūpaṇa.

Kālottara section (pp. 2–36, vv. 1–495): opens without title in a passage on maṇḍala and exegesis (vv. 1–2 repeated as 20–21), then chapters with Ṣaṭsahasrikālottara colophons: gaṇapatipūjā, aghorakalpa, rudraśānti, āśrama, gocara (paṭala 14), samayācāra, guruvicāra (16) and aṃśakatālakṣaṇa (17); paṭala numbering is irregular and many chapters of a 6,000-verse work are absent. From v. 496 (p. 36) the text is a compilation on worship, homa, kuṇḍas, iconography, pratiṣṭhā, festivals and Śivarātri, with source rubrics such as 'iti kāraṇe', 'iti bhīmakāraṇe pratiṣṭhātantre vināyakavratavidhipaṭalaḥ', 'sūkṣmatantre', 'dīptatantre', 'iti vijayākhya mahātantre śivarātrividhiḥ'; it ends abruptly at v. 2343 (flower/leaf substitutes in worship) with no colophon.

Most of the transcript, however, is a South Indian temple-ritual compilation quoting the Kāraṇa, Sūkṣma, Dīpta, Vijaya and other Āgamas on homa and kuṇḍas, images, liṅgas, installation, festivals and Śivarātri.

summary: The Aṃśumatkāśyapāgama is an authoritative Śaiva Siddhānta Āgamic treatise centered on temple architecture (vāstu), sacred iconography (mūrtilakṣaṇa / citra), and ritual consecration. Framed as an exposition delivered by Śiva to the sage Kāśyapa summarizing the ancient Aṃśumān tantra, it details temple layout, ground examination, foundation deposits, and structural elements of vimānas, maṇḍapas, and prākāras, followed by extensive rules on iconometric proportions (tālamāna) and iconographic forms of Śiva, Devī, and associated divinities.

summary: This text comprises Volume 1 of Abhinavagupta's Īśvarapratyabhijñāvivṛtivimarśinī, his extensive philosophical commentary on Utpaladeva's Vivṛti/Ṭīkā to the Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā. It encompasses the first three chapters (āhnikas) of the Jñānādhikāra, establishing the purpose of the treatise (Upodghātāhnika), refuting the Buddhist argument regarding the non-apprehension (anupalabdhi) of the Self, and critiquing externalist and reductionist rival schools (paradarśana). The work serves as a foundational text for non-dual Kashmir Śaiva epistemology and remains the primary witness for reconstructing Utpaladeva's lost Vivṛti.

summary: The Īśvarapratyabhijñāvivṛtivimarśinī (also known as the Bṛhatī Vimarśinī) is Abhinavagupta's monumental philosophical commentary on Utpaladeva's auto-commentary (Vivṛti) to the Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā. This third volume covers the Kriyādhikāra (examining divine agency, temporal and spatial succession, causality, and relations), the Āgamādhikāra (integrating philosophical analysis with scriptural revelation and the 36 tattvas), and the concluding Tattvasaṅgrahādhikāra (summarizing the ontology and soteriology of recognizing oneself as Śiva). It represents one of the most sophisticated masterworks of classical non-dual Kashmir Śaivism.

summary: The Mālinīvijayavārttika (also known as the Mālinīślokavārttika) is a major verse commentary composed by Abhinavagupta interpreting the opening sentence of the Mālinīvijayottaratantra, the foundational scriptural authority of the Trika Śaiva lineage. Arranged in two books (kāṇḍas), the text formulates a comprehensive theology of revelation (āgama), hermeneutics, and nondual metaphysics while mounting extensive polemics against Buddhist epistemologists, Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika, and Mīmāṃsā.

summary: The Paramārthasāra ('Essence of the Supreme Truth') is a concise manual of nondual Kashmir Śaivism in 105 verses by Abhinavagupta. It surveys the nondual nature of absolute consciousness, cosmic manifestation across the thirty-six categories (tattvas), the mechanisms of contraction and ignorance, and liberation. Yogarāja's Vivṛti, composed by a direct student of Kṣemarāja at Vitastāpurī, offers an indispensable running prose commentary elucidating Abhinavagupta's verses in light of Trika and Pratyabhijñā doctrine.

summary: Āhnikas 15 through 37 form the extensive ritual, yogic, and canon-defining second half of Abhinavagupta's Tantrāloka, accompanied by Jayaratha's Viveka commentary. The text systematically expounds daily and occasional Trika worship, multiple grades and variations of initiation (dīkṣā), post-initiatory practice, construction of maṇḍalas, funerary and ancestral rites (antyeṣṭi, śrāddha), and esoteric Kaula ritual (āhnika 29). The work concludes in āhnika 37 with an evaluation of the Śaiva scriptural hierarchy, the transmission of the teaching, and Abhinavagupta's personal lineage.

summary: The Tantrāloka ('Light on the Tantras') is Abhinavagupta's monumental encyclopedic synthesis of nondual Kashmir Śaivism (Trika and Kaula), presenting a comprehensive exposition of Śaiva metaphysics, yoga, and ritual based primarily upon the Mālinīvijayottaratantra. Accompanied by Jayaratha's indispensable Viveka commentary, āhnikas 1–14 set forth the philosophical and soteriological core of the system. This includes the four means to liberation (anupāya, śāmbhavopāya, śāktopāya, and āṇavopāya), the cosmology of the six paths (ṣaḍadhvan), the doctrine of time (kāla), and the preliminary requirements for initiation (dīkṣā).

summary: The Tantrasāra ('Essence of Tantra') is an influential prose compendium composed by the Kashmiri polymath Abhinavagupta as an accessible digest of his monumental encyclopedic treatise, the Tantrāloka. Arranged into 22 āhnikas ('daily lessons'), the work systematically expounds the metaphysics, ritual, yoga, and soteriology of the non-dual Trika and Pratyabhijñā traditions. It is centrally structured around the hierarchy of means to spiritual liberation—anupāya, śāmbhavopāya, śāktopāya, and āṇavopāya—alongside an extensive treatment of the descent of divine grace (śaktipāta) and initiation rituals (dīkṣā).

summary: The Advayatārakopaniṣad is a short Yoga Upaniṣad reckoning as the 53rd text in the Muktikā canon and traditionally belonging to the Śuklayajurveda. It expounds Tārakayoga ('the deliverer yoga'), detailing the meditative absorption in internal and external light signs (antarlakṣya, bahirlakṣya, and madhyamalakṣya), the practice of the śāmbhavī mudrā, and the crossing over of saṃsāra into nondual Brahman. Upaniṣadbrahmayogin's Vivaraṇa interprets the yogic physiology and photic visions in terms of Advaita Vedānta metaphysics.
