summary: This text contains two major ritual sections from Aghoraśiva's Śaivasiddhānta paddhati, the Kriyākramadyotikā: the Mahotsavavidhi and the Prāyaścittavidhi. The Mahotsavavidhi provides exhaustive prescriptions for the temple's annual festival (mahotsava), including flag raising (dhvajārohaṇa), yāgaśālā ceremonies, processional rites, and sacred immersion. The Prāyaścittavidhi outlines expiatory rituals, homas, and rededications for ritual flaws, impurities, and structural disruptions in the Śiva temple.

summary: An anonymous Kashmiri ritual manual (paddhati) for the fire ritual (agnikārya/homa) in a Bhairava/Kaula-oriented Śaiva setting. It begins with worship of Pustakavāgīśvarī (Sarasvatī) and Gaṇapati, kalaśa worship, purification of the subtle body, and preparation and consecration of the kuṇḍa and fire. It then gives oblation and tarpaṇa sequences for many deities, including Durgā, the Lokeśas and the planets, and ends with an incomplete section on animal sacrifice. The Muktabodha description stresses its incidental information on Kashmiri cults, e.g. the goddess Siddhalakṣmī.

summary: The Ahirbudhnyasaṃhitā is an important theological and ritual text of the Vaiṣṇava Pāñcarātra tradition, presented as a revelatory discourse taught by Ahirbudhnya (Śiva) to Nārada. This first volume (adhyāyas 1–36) details the cosmogony and metaphysics of the school, emphasizing the six divine attributes (ṣaḍguṇa), the emanations of Viṣṇu (vyūhas), and the cosmogenetic activity of his śakti embodied in the Sudarśana cakra. It also includes comprehensive treatises on mantravidyā, yoga, royal apotropaic rituals, and military/weapon sorcery (astramantra).

summary: The Ahirbudhnyasaṃhitā is a foundational scripture of the Vaiṣṇava Pāñcarātra tradition, presented as an exposition given by Ahirbudhnya (Śiva as an enlightened devotee and manifestation of Saṃkarṣaṇa) to the sage Nārada. This second volume covers chapters 37 through 60, focusing on the esoteric iconography and worship of the sixteen-armed Sudarśana, mantra diagrams (yantras), royal protection rituals, the philosophy and six limbs of self-surrender (nyāsa/prapatti), and a significant survey of classical philosophical systems (including the Ṣaṣṭitantra tradition of Sāṃkhya and Yoga). The volume concludes with an appendix containing the Śrīsudarśanasahasranāmastotra.

summary: The Amṛtabindūpaniṣad is a concise Yoga Upaniṣad in 22 verses expounding the nature and control of the mind as the prime cause of bondage and liberation (bandhāya viṣayāsaktaṃ muktyai nirviṣayaṃ smṛtam). It distinguishes the mind attached to objects from the unattached mind, teaching the dissolution of thought into Brahman. In this e-text, the root text is accompanied verse-by-verse by the complete Vivaraṇa commentary of Upaniṣadbrahmayogin, who concludes by identifying the transcendental Brahman with Vāsudeva.

summary: The Amṛtanādopaniṣad is a classical Yoga Upaniṣad that outlines a sixfold yoga (ṣaḍaṅgayoga: pratyāhāra, dhyāna, prāṇāyāma, dhāraṇā, tarka, and samādhi). It uses the allegory of ascending the chariot of Oṃkāra to transcend worldly existence, details breath retention measured by specific mātrā counts, and describes the ascent of prāṇa through the crown of the head as the path to immortality. Upaniṣadbrahmayogin's commentary (Vivaraṇa) integrates these yogic techniques into an Advaita Vedāntic framework culminating in non-dual Self-realization.

summary: The Bṛhannīlatantra ('Great Nīla Tantra') is an important Kaula Śākta ritual work in 24 chapters (paṭalas) framed as an esoteric dialogue between Mahākālabhairava and the Goddess. Centered on the worship of the Mahāvidyās Tārā (specifically Nīlasarasvatī / Ugratārā) and Kālī, the text details mantras, yantras, dīkṣā procedures, puraścaryā, kavacas, and sahasranāmas. It also contains significant material on the Mahācīnācāra path, vīrasādhana, alchemical transmutation (rasaśāstra / dhātuvāda), and the worship of Annapūrṇā.

summary: The Mātṛkārṇanighaṇṭu (or Mātṛkāvarṇasaṃgraha) is a short tantric glossary in 87 verses composed by Bhānudīkṣita, son of Nārāyaṇa Dīkṣita. It systematically catalogues the esoteric names, deities, bodily locations, and symbolic code-words associated with each syllable of the Sanskrit alphabet (mātṛkā)—from oṃkāra and a to kṣa—serving as a key for mantroddhāra (the deciphering and construction of secret mantras encoded in tantric treatises).

Kṣemarāja's Vivṛti provides an extensive philosophical commentary elucidating the verses in terms of Trika and Spanda doctrines.

summary: The Gītārthasaṃgraha is Abhinavagupta's philosophical commentary on the Bhagavadgītā written from the perspective of non-dual Kashmir Śaivism (Pratyabhijñā). It interprets Kṛṣṇa's instruction to Arjuna as a revelation of supreme non-dual consciousness (anuttara-saṃvid), synthesizing action (karma), knowledge (jñāna), and devotion (bhakti) as integrated expressions of divine sovereignty and self-awareness (svātantrya). The work reflects the Kashmirian recension of the Bhagavadgītā, containing distinct textual variants and additional verses.

summary: The Spandapradīpikā is an exegetical commentary on the Spandakārikā composed by Bhagavatutpala (Utpala Vaiṣṇava) of Kashmir, probably active around the tenth century. The commentary is notable for its syncretic perspective, interpreting non-dual Śaiva Spanda concepts through the lens of Pāñcarātra Vaiṣṇava theology and citing early canonical saṃhitās such as the Jayākhya, Sātvata, Pauṣkara, and Ahirbudhnya.

summary: The Varivasyārahasya ('Secret of Worship') is an influential manual of Śrīvidyā theology, mantra-śāstra, and internal contemplative worship composed by the polymath Bhāskararāya Makhin, accompanied by his autocommentary, the Prakāśa. The text provides an esoteric analysis of the fifteen-syllable Śrīvidyā mantra (pañcadaśākṣarī), demonstrating how each letter and component encodes cosmological principles, subtle yogic centers, deities, and philosophical correspondences across multiple hermeneutical registers. Synthesizing Śākta ritual theology with Advaita Vedānta, Bhāskararāya argues that the culmination of mantra worship is the non-dual realization of identity between the practitioner, the mantra, and the supreme Goddess as pure consciousness.

summary: The Tattvaprakāśa ('Illumination of the Principles') is a canonical verse primer of Śaiva Siddhānta metaphysics traditionally attributed to King Bhojadeva of Dhārā (early 11th c.). The work systematically sets forth the dualist Siddhānta system structured by the three categories of Pati (Śiva), Paśu (individual souls), and Pāśa (bonds), mapping the unfolding of the 36 tattvas across the pure and impure realms. This digital text pairs the kārikās with two principal commentaries: Aghoraśivācārya's 12th-century Vṛtti, which rigorously defends classical dualist Siddhānta against monistic readings, and Śrīkumāra's Tātparyadīpikā, which seeks to harmonize Siddhānta philosophy with orthodox Vaidika and Mīmāṃsaka tenets.

summary: The Tārārahasya ('Secret of Tārā') by Brahmānandagiri is a fundamental ritual manual (nibandha) dedicated to the worship, mantras, and meditative forms (dhyāna) of the Mahāvidyā Tārā and her manifestations (such as Ugratārā, Nīlasarasvatī, and Ekajaṭā). Divided into four chapters (paṭalas), it incorporates both normative tantric ritual procedures and the esoteric Mahācīnakrama. Synthesizing citations from older authorities such as the Nīlatantra, Mahācīnatantra, and Rudrayāmala, it served as one of the primary handbooks of the Tārā cult across Bengal and Assam.

summary: An anonymous Śaiva yoga text in which Śiva instructs Skanda. It covers the subtle body (the nine doors, nāḍīs such as piṅgalā and suṣumṇā, the vital winds), the 'joining to brahman' (brahmasandhāna) through the brahmadvāra, and yogic exit at death (utkrānti). It also treats the cosmogony from cicchakti, the composition of the human body, the nāda as brahman, and a purely mental worship (mānasayāga) with bathing at the inner Śivatīrtha. It closes with an internal fire worship (agnipūjā), in which the five breaths are offered into the fire in the heart.

summary: The Candrāvalokana is a short Haṭhayogic tract framed as a dialogue between Maheśvara (Śiva) and Matsyendranātha. It is best known in yoga historiography as a key early source for the definition of śāmbhavīmudrā and the absorption (laya) of mind and breath, famously cited in chapter 4 of the Haṭhapradīpikā. It interprets esoteric yogic gazes through lunar allegories (amāvāsyā, pratipad, and paurṇamāsī).

summary: The Candrajñānāgama (or Candrajñāna) is a Śaiva revealed text framed as a teaching imparted on Mount Kailāsa by Śiva (Bhairava) to Candra. Distressed by the transient and illusory nature of worldly phenomena (māyā, indrajāla) and questioning the efficacy of conventional ritual and verbalized mantras, Candra receives esoteric instruction resolving these doubts into transcendent non-dual awareness. This digital text represents a diplomatic transcription of Banaras Hindu University MS C4243 (fols. 55a–67b).

It defends the Vedic status and spiritual supremacy of Vīraśaiva philosophy and practice, drawing upon Upaniṣadic, Purāṇic, and Śaivāgama authorities to elucidate key tenets such as the ṣaṭsthala, aṣṭāvaraṇa, pañcācāra, and atyāśrama. summary: The Cinmayadīkṣāvidhāna is an anonymous Śaiva ritual manual (paddhati / vidhāna), closely aligned with the Vīraśaiva tradition, detailing the rite of consciousness-pervaded initiation (cinmayadīkṣā) and the accompanying worship and wearing of the liṅga (liṅgadhāraṇa). summary: The Yantracintāmaṇi is a widely cited medieval Sanskrit tantric treatise on yantras composed by Dāmodara, son of Gaṅgādhara. Structured as a dialogue between Umā and Maheśvara upon Mount Kailāsa, the work provides detailed instructions for constructing, inscribing, and ritually activating yantras across eight principal sections corresponding to the ṣaṭkarman (vaśya, ākarṣaṇa, stambhana, vidveṣaṇa, māraṇa, uccāṭana) as well as rites for pacification (śānti), protection (rakṣā), and liberation from physical confinement (bandhamokṣa).

summary: An anonymous Kashmiri manual for Śaiva (Bhairava-oriented) initiation, which Muktabodha describes as showing an intensely tantric local pantheon like Nepal's. The surviving part covers the preparatory days in detail: purification of the officiant, kalaśa installation, fire consecration, caru, and preparation of the disciple. It also maps the six paths (kalās, tattvas, bhuvanas) onto the disciple's body and gives the dream rite of the adhivāsa night. It then begins the third day (interpretation of dreams, drawing of the maṇḍala) before breaking off. Extensive marginal glosses in the manuscript are transcribed in round brackets.

summary: The Dīkṣottaraprakaraṇa constitutes the concluding nineteen-chapter section of the Niśvāsakārikā, an early metrical scripture of the Niśvāsa corpus of the Mantramārga. It systematically covers the rites and theology of tantric initiation (dīkṣā), the purification of the six cosmic pathways (ṣaḍadhvan), and interiorized yogic absorptions (lakṣya). The work represents an indispensable transitional witness for the development of classical Śaivasiddhānta ritual liturgy.

summary: The Darśanopaniṣad is one of the twenty minor Yoga Upaniṣads in the Muktikā canon, affiliated with the Sāmaveda. Framed as an instructional dialogue between Dattātreya and Sāṃkṛti, it details an eightfold yoga (aṣṭāṅga-yoga) integrated with Advaita Vedānta, covering the ten yamas and niyamas, āsanas, the subtle anatomy of fourteen principal nāḍīs and ten prāṇas, prāṇāyāma, pratyāhāra, dhāraṇā, dhyāna, and samādhi. This e-text presents the root Upaniṣad along with the Vivaraṇa of Upaniṣadbrahmayogin.

summary: The Devīrahasya is a Śākta tantric digest and ritual compilation framed as part of the Rudrayāmala, composed in Kashmir. It is structured into a Pūrvārdha of 25 paṭalas dealing with initiation, mantra vitalization and unlocking, puraścaraṇa, yantras, and ritual ingredients, followed by an Uttarārdha of 35 paṭalas providing pañcāṅgas (paṭala, kavaca, paddhati, sahasranāma, and stotra) for various deities. The appended text is the Uddhārakośa of Dakṣiṇāmūrtimuni, a 7-kalpa lexicon defining and deciphering tantric mantras.

It includes Śaiva forms (Sadāśiva, Dakṣiṇāmūrti), forms of the Goddess (Durgā, the Lakṣmīs), Vaiṣṇava deities and the nine planets with their gotras and directions. summary: The Dhyānabindūpaniṣad is one of the classical Yoga Upaniṣads, focusing on the practice and philosophy of dhyāna (meditation) and nada-yoga. It expounds meditation on the sacred syllable Om (praṇava) along with its constituent mātrās, bindu, and nāda, the sixfold yoga (ṣaḍaṅgayoga), the nature of the jīva, and the awakening of Kuṇḍalinī to achieve non-dual liberation. The Vivaraṇa commentary by Upaniṣadbrahmayogin interprets the yogic terminology and practices from an Advaita Vedānta perspective of pure consciousness (brahmamātra).

summary: The Gautamatantra (also known as Gautamīyatantra) is a prominent Vaiṣṇava (Kṛṣṇaite) tantric text framed as a dialogue between Gautama and Nārada. The text treats initiation (dīkṣā), nyāsa, dhyāna, yantras, and ritual attainment (siddhi).

summary: The Gorakṣayogaśāstra (also called Mūlasāra) is a short Nātha yoga text of 65 verses framed in the style of a stotra/saṃvāda opened by Īśvara. summary: The Gorakṣaguṭikā ('Pill/Amulet of Gorakṣa') is a late Nātha liturgical and mythological text framed as a Tantric Haragaurīsaṃvāda (dialogue between Śiva and Gaurī), claiming affiliation to the Kalpadrumavivekinī. Unlike standard Haṭha Yoga treatises, it centers on devotional ritual and Guru worship, recounting the miraculous birth and deeds of Gorakṣanātha in its opening chapter, followed by protective kavacas, mantras, and stotras (including his dvādaśanāma, aṣṭottaraśatanāma, and sahasranāma) across nine chapters (taraṅgas).

summary: The Guhyasamājatantra is the foundational scripture of the Buddhist Mahāyoga / Anuttarayoga tantric class, centered on Akṣobhya and the fivefold Buddha family maṇḍala. Structured in eighteen chapters, it details deity visualization, mantras, ritual enactments, and subtle-body meditation forming the basis of generation (utpattikrama) and completion (niṣpannakrama) stage yogas. Celebrated for its paradoxical, antinomian imagery representing non-dual gnosis, it gave rise to two prominent Indian exegetical schools: the Jñānapāda school and the Ārya school.

summary: The Tripurārahasya (Jñānakhaṇḍa) is a Śākta non-dualist philosophical text framed as a discourse between Dattātreya and Paraśurāma, recited by the sage Sumedhas Hāritāyana to Nārada. It blends Advaita Vedānta, Pratyabhijñā Śaivism, and Śrīvidyā tantric metaphysics, demonstrating through dialogues and narrative parables that supreme reality is unconditioned pure Consciousness (Cit / Tripurā). The e-text contains all 22 chapters of the Jñānakhaṇḍa along with Śrīnivāsa Bhaṭṭa's classic commentary, the Tātparyadīpikā.

summary: The Haṃsopaniṣad is a minor Yoga Upaniṣad framed as an esoteric dialogue between Gautama and Sanatkumāra. It elaborates on the ajapā-mantra ('haṃsa'/'so'ham') in relation to breath, the petals of the heart lotus, and internal meditative absorption through the manifestation of ten internal sounds (nāda). Upaniṣadbrahmayogin's Vivaraṇa commentary interprets these disciplines from an Advaita Vedānta perspective.

summary: The Hariharatāratamya is a Śaiva stotra and polemical work in 94 verses comparing the mythological deeds, forms, and attributes of Viṣṇu (Hari) and Śiva (Hara). The stanzas rhetorical frame poses the constant refrain asking wise elders to judge who is greater ('ko vānayor adhika ityanucintya vṛddhāḥ satyaṃ vadantu tam imaṃ vayam āśrayāmaḥ'), consistently resolving in favor of Śiva's transcendence and non-dual supreme reality.

summary: The Jñānārṇavatantra ('Ocean of Knowledge') is an authoritative scripture of the Śākta Tantric tradition and one of the principal scriptural sources for the Kādi division of Śrīvidyā. Cast in 26 paṭalas as a revelation by Īśvara to Devī, the work begins with esoteric expositions of the sacred alphabet (akṣamālā / mātṛkā), the phonematic matrix, and the threefold bindu. The remaining chapters detail the internal and ritual pūjā of Mahātripurasundarī and her attendants, yantra meditations, mantra recitation, and seasonal observances, culminating in the damanāropaṇa rite.

summary: A brief anonymous Śaiva Siddhānta tract on jñānadīkṣā, initiation through knowledge. It sets out the categories of Pati, Paśu and Pāśa (mala, māyā, karma), citing Siddhāntāgamas such as the Mataṅgapārameśvara and Kiraṇa, and treats the awakening of the soul by Śiva's power, including the role of kuṇḍalinī-śakti (as noted in the Muktabodha description). summary: The Jñānasaṅkalinītantra ('Tantra of the Collection of Gnosis') is a concise Śākta-Śaiva tantric treatise framed as a dialogue on Mount Kailāsa between Śiva and the Devī. It subordinates external ritualism, caste prescriptions, and scholastic learning to internal non-dual knowledge (brahmajñāna) and subtle yogic contemplation. The text expounds the esoteric anatomy of the body (piṇḍa) as identical to the cosmos (brahmāṇḍa), identifying the internal channels iḍā, piṅgalā, and suṣumnā with sacred rivers (Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Sarasvatī), and explains the symbolic significance of the Praṇava (Oṃ) alongside inner mudrās such as khecarī and śāmbhavī.

summary: The Mokṣasopāna ('Staircase to Liberation') is a Śākta-Śaiva treatise on esoteric yoga, cakra meditation, and internal worship affiliated with the Kubjikā tradition. summary: The Kākacaṇḍeśvarīmata is an early Śākta-Śaiva alchemical (rasaśāstra) and iatrochemical tantra presented as a dialogue on Mount Kailāsa between Bhairava and the goddess Kākacaṇḍeśvarī (a form of Kālī/Cāmuṇḍā). The text details mercurial processing, calcination, mineral operations, and herbal recipes (kalpas) for rejuvenation (rasāyana) and therapeutic medicine. Preserved in Nepalese manuscripts, it represents an important early stratum in medieval Indian tantric alchemy.

summary: The Kālottaratantra (or Kālottara) is one of the earliest and most influential scriptural authorities of the Śaiva Siddhānta Mantramārga. Transmitted in multiple recensions of differing lengths, its texts provided the foundational mantric, ritual, and yogic framework for medieval Saiddhāntika liturgies and paddhatis. This digital text is a diplomatic transcription of a composite Nepalese manuscript preserving seven recensions: the Jñānapañcāśikā, Śatikakālottara (Kālajñāna), Sārdhaśatikakālottara, Dviśatikakālottara, Adhyuṣṭaśatikakālottara (Sārdhatriśatika), Saptaśatikakālottara, and Trayodaśaśatikakālottara.

summary: The Kāmadhenutantra is a Śākta Tantra in twenty-four paṭalas structured as an esoteric dialogue between Śiva and Pārvatī. It focuses primarily on phonematic mysticism (mātṛkā- and varṇa-vidyā), treating the fifty letters of the Sanskrit alphabet as vibrational sound-manifestations of Kālī and Vāc/Sarasvatī. The work details the esoteric values, bodily correlation (nyāsa), cakra centers, and meditative visualisations (dhyāna) for individual letters and key bījamantras.

summary: The Śrītattvanidhi ('Treasure of Realities') is an encyclopedic Sanskrit compendium attributed to Maharaja Kṛṣṇarāja of Mysore. Organized into nine thematic 'nidhis' (treasures), it compiles iconographic descriptions, dhyāna verses, astronomical lore, temple practices, and esoteric lore culled from Purāṇas, Āgamas, and Tantras. The final section (Kautukanidhi) contains descriptions of traditional games and yoga postures.

summary: The Parāprāveśikā is a short prose primer of nondual Kashmir Śaivism (Trika/Pratyabhijñā) composed by the 11th-century master Kṣemarāja. It expounds the nature of Parameśvara as pure light (prakāśa) and reflective awareness (vimarśa), details the thirty-six principles of cosmic manifestation (tattvas) from Śiva down to earth (pṛthivī), and introduces the supreme Śakti (Parā) and the esoteric significance of the mantra aham.

summary: The Kṣurikopaniṣad is an early Yoga Upaniṣad affiliated with the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda, counted as the 31st Upaniṣad in the Muktikā canon. It expounds yogic practice through the metaphor of a razor-sharp instrument of dhāraṇā and discriminative knowledge that cuts through karmic bonds, bodily attachment, and the knot of the heart (hṛdayagranthi). The text details steady posture, breath control coordinated with the twelve-mātrā praṇava, sense withdrawal, and subtle meditative ascension along the nāḍīs up to liberation. The e-text contains the entire mūla along with the vivaraṇa of Upaniṣadbrahmayogin.

Framed as a dialogue between Bhairava and Bhairavī, it expounds the esoteric correspondence between the fifty phonemes of the Sanskrit alphabet (mātṛkā) and Śiva-Śakti, followed by yogic teachings on the six cakras, yonimudrā, and the ascent and descent of Kuṇḍalinī. It further prescribes the worship of the Goddess and her attendant ḍākinīs, along with instructions on puraścaraṇa and devotion to the guru.

summary: The Kaivalyasāra is a foundational Sanskrit Vīraśaiva theological and philosophical treatise composed by Maritoṃṭadārya. Structured around the system of 101 progressive spiritual stations (ekottaraśatasthala) divided across six major prakaraṇas, the treatise correlates Upaniṣadic śruti passages with Śaivāgamic doctrines to articulate the Śivādvaita philosophy. It systematically expounds the metaphysical non-dual union (aṅgaliṅgasāmarasya) between the individual practitioner (aṅga) and transcendent-immanent Śiva (liṅga).

summary: The Kāraṇāgama is traditionally ranked fourth among the twenty-eight canonical Siddhāntāgamas; this e-text contains the ten-chapter Kriyāpāda section of its Uttarabhāga preserved in the Vīraśaiva (Liṅgāyata) tradition. Structured as a divine discourse between Pārvatī and Śiva, the text establishes the supremacy of Vīraśaiva dharma, the observance of the śāmbhavavrata, and the transmission of the threefold initiation (vedhā-, mantra-, and kriyādīkṣā). It provides extensive ritual prescriptions for the worship, wearing, and maintenance of the personal liṅga (iṣṭaliṅga), culminating in expiatory rites (prāyaścitta) to be performed in the event of ritual errors or the loss of the liṅga (naṣṭaliṅga).

summary: The Karpūrādistotra (or Dakṣiṇakālikāsvarūpastotra) is an influential Śākta hymn celebrating Dakṣiṇakālikā, traditionally attributed to Mahākāla. summary: The Kubjikāguhyeśvarīpūjāpaddhati is a Nepalese Tantric ritual manual dedicated to Goddess Guhyeśvarī venerated in her Kubjikā aspect. Written in Sanskrit with Newari liturgical directions and ritual glosses, it outlines standard liturgical procedures including bhūtaśuddhi, nyāsa, pātrapūjā, gurumaṇḍala worship, kramārcana, offerings (bali), and animal sacrifice (paśujāga). The surviving witness was written by King Sumati Jayajitāmitramallavarman.

summary: The Kulārṇavatantra ('Ocean of the Kula') is one of the foundational scriptural texts of the Kaula tradition within Śākta Tantrism, framed as an esoteric dialogue between Śiva and the Goddess. Comprising seventeen ullāsas (chapters) and more than two thousand verses, the text presents the doctrine and ritual praxis of the Ūrdhvāmnāya (upper transmission). It systematically expounds the necessity of human embodiment for liberation, guru-śiṣya relations, dīkṣā, mantra-sādhana, and the sacramental integration of enjoyment (bhukti) with liberation (mukti) through the esoteric rites of the pañcamakāras.

summary: The Kulacūḍāmaṇitantra is an important Śākta Kaula scripture comprising seven chapters (paṭalas). Unusually structured as a nigama—wherein Śiva (Bhairava) serves as the questioner while the Goddess (Bhairavī/Kālī) reveals teachings—the text expounds the inner and outer rites of Kula worship, including mantra-sādhana, nyāsa, kulācāra practices, and philosophical discussions on Śiva and Śakti.

summary: The Kulasāra is an early Kaula Śaiva scripture surviving in archaic Nepalese manuscripts and cited by non-dual Kashmiri Śaiva authors prior to the eleventh century. It expounds Kaula metaphysics—including the categories of piṇḍa, pada, rūpa, and rūpātīta, as well as Akula and Kula—combined with yogic practices for bodily internalization, mantra protection, visualization of Bhairava and yoginīs, non-dual ritual purity, and internal pilgrimage (caryā). This e-text preserves an unedited diplomatic transcript of chapters 4 (fragment) and 8–17 (incomplete).

summary: The Lakṣmītantra is an influential Pāñcarātra Vaiṣṇava Āgama in 57 chapters, notable for elevating Lakṣmī, the dynamic Śakti of Viṣṇu-Nārāyaṇa, to the primary cosmological and soteriological agent. This e-text provides the complete scripture together with Pandit V. Krishnamacharya's Sanskrit gloss.

In this e-text, the root verses are accompanied by a Sanskrit commentary gloss by Pandit V. Krishnamacharya.

summary: The Lalleśvarīvākyāni ('Sayings of Lalleśvarī') comprises 60 mystical Kashmiri quatrains (vākhs) by the 14th-century poet-saint Lallā (Lal Dĕd), accompanied verse-for-verse by Sanskrit metrical translations (arthacchāyāpadya) composed by the 18th-century Kashmiri Śaiva scholar Rājānaka Bhāskarakaṇṭha. Rooted in nondual Trika and Pratyabhijñā Śaivism, the verses convey internal yogic absorption, prāṇāyāma, mind control, critique of ritualism and external caste distinctions, and the nondual realization of the Self as Śiva. As the earliest attested literary compositions in the Kashmiri language, Lallā's verses hold foundational importance in Kashmiri literary and religious culture, while Bhāskarakaṇṭha's translation represents their earliest formal reception in classical Sanskrit scholarship.

The text concludes with a devotional appendix comprising stotras attributed to Kālidāsa, Kulaśekhara, Śaṅkarācārya, and Abhinavagupta (Śivastuti).

summary: The Mṛgendrāgama (or Mṛgendratantra) is an authoritative scripture of dualistic Śaiva Siddhānta, traditionally regarded as an upāgama of the Kāmikāgama. This e-text contains its philosophical Vidyāpāda and practical Yogapāda, which formulate core Siddhānta ontology across the categories of pati (the Lord), paśu (the bound individual), and pāśa (fetters/bonds), followed by an exposition of tantric yoga. The root text is accompanied by the commentary (Mṛgendravṛtti) of Bhaṭṭa Nārāyaṇakaṇṭha and the sub-commentary (Dīpikā) of Aghoraśiva.

summary: The Mṛtitattvānusmaraṇa is an eschatological and ritual text framed as a dialogue between Śrībhairava and Bhairavī, traditionally transmitted as a section of the Kashmiri Śaiva Bhṛṅgīśasaṃhitā. It provides a detailed account of the post-mortem journey of the soul, the geography and punishments of Yamaloka, the accounting of deeds by Citragupta, and the specific duties of relatives during dying, cremation (śāvasnāna, antyeṣṭi), the ten-day period (daśāha), and the performance of dīpaśrāddha to dispel the darkness of the pretamārga.

summary: The Maṇḍalabrāhmaṇopaniṣad is a minor Yoga Upaniṣad affiliated with the Śukla Yajurveda, framed as a dialogue between the sage Yājñavalkya and the deity residing in the solar disc (ādityamaṇḍala, identified with Nārāyaṇa). In five brāhmaṇas, it synthesizes Haṭhayogic bodily techniques with Rājayoga and Advaita Vedāntic metaphysics, detailing a redefined eight-limbed yoga (aṣṭāṅgayoga), contemplation of internal and external luminosity (tārakayoga), the five voids (vyomapañcaka), and the trans-mental absorption of amanaskayoga leading to manonāśa and jīvanmukti. In this file, the root text is accompanied by the complete Vivaraṇa commentary of the 18th-century Advaitin Upaniṣadbrahmayogin.

summary: The Mahānirvāṇatantra is an influential Śākta work structured as a discourse between Sadāśiva and the Goddess (Ādyā Śakti) on ritual and moral duty in the degraded Kali Yuga. It combines monotheistic Advaita Vedānta and the meditation on formless Brahman with devotional worship of Ādyā Kālī, while reforming traditional Kaula rituals such as the pañcatattva. Unusually among Tantras, it devotes extensive sections to social ethics, duties of the householder, sacramental ceremonies (saṃskāras), and civil law regarding marriage, property, and inheritance.

summary: The Mahāvākyopaniṣad is a short minor Upaniṣad belonging to the Atharvavedic tradition and counted as the 92nd text in the Muktikā canon of 108 Upaniṣads, classified as one of the twenty Yoga Upaniṣads. This e-text provides the complete root text accompanied by the Advaitic Vivaraṇa commentary of Upaniṣadbrahmayogin.

summary: The Akulavīratantra is an early Kaula / Yoginī Kaula scriptural text transmitted within the corpus ascribed to Matsyendranātha. It expounds an uncompromising non-dual realization of ultimate reality designated as the Akulavīra ('Hero of the Transcendent'), identified with innate bliss (sahajānanda) and the all-pervading divine nature within the practitioner's own body. Rejecting the doctrines of scholastic systems (Nyāya, Vaiśeṣika, Bauddha, Jaina, Somasiddhānta, Mīmāṃsā) as well as outward ritual and haṭhayogic technicalities, it teaches immediate liberation through effortless dwelling in the transcendent state.

summary: The Kaulajñānanirṇaya is a foundational Śaiva-Śākta scripture of the Yoginī Kaula (Matsyendramata) lineage, traditionally held to have been transmitted by the mahāsiddha Matsyendranātha in Candradvīpa. In 24 chapters (paṭalas), it expounds esoteric Kaula teachings, including the nonduality of Śiva and Śakti, the metaphysics of kula and akula, subtle yogic physiology (bindu, nāda, cakras), siddhi acquisition, and antinomian yoginī rituals.

summary: The Merutantra is an encyclopedic Śaiva-Śākta tantric manual comprising 35 chapters (prakāśas), framed as a revelation given by Sadāśiva on Mount Meru to the gods after their distress under the demon Jalandhara. Functioning much like a nibandha (digest) of mantra-śāstra and ritual practice, it details initiation (dīkṣā), preliminary discipline (puraścaraṇa), nyāsa, and rituals for numerous deities, including Mahākāla, Devī, Sūrya, Viṣṇu, Gaṇeśa, and Kārtavīryārjuna. Containing notable historical anachronisms, such as predictions naming London, Christianity, and the British (chapter 35), the text in its present form dates to the early modern period (ca. 16th–18th century CE).

summary: The Mohacūḍottara is an early Śaiva scriptural manual on installation (pratiṣṭhā-tantra) framed as a dialogue between Skanda and Śakra (Indra). It focuses on the ritual selection and testing of materials (stone, wood, metals), iconometry, the architecture of temples (prāsāda) and ritual halls (maṇḍapa), and the rites of consecration for liṅgas and deities. Preserved primarily in early Nepalese manuscripts, it forms an important witness to early medieval Śaiva architectural and ritual doctrine.

summary: The Muṇḍamālātantra is a late Śākta Kaula scripture in ten chapters (paṭalas). The work also details mantroddhāra, stotras, kavacas, and esoteric ritual practices including śavasādhanā.

summary: The Nāṭyaśāstra is the foundational Sanskrit treatise on dramaturgy, performance, dance, music, and aesthetic theory, ascribed to the mythic sage Bharata Muni. This volume comprises chapters 1 through 7 accompanied by the Abhinavabhāratī commentary of Abhinavagupta. These chapters cover the mythological origins of drama, stagecraft and playhouse architecture (prekṣāgṛha), stage rituals (pūrvaraṅga), classical dance movements (karaṇas and aṅgahāras), and the foundational exposition of rasa (aesthetic relish) and bhāva (affective states).

summary: A short Haṭha- and Layayoga tract in 67 verses framed as an instruction delivered by Śiva to Pārvatī. It outlines the practice of absorption in the ten inner unstruck sounds (anāhatanāda)—beginning with ciṇi, ciñciṇī, and bell/conch sounds up to thunder and kettle-drums—along with elemental tattva-dissolution, bodily signs, and mind absorption leading to liberation.

summary: The Nādabindūpaniṣad is one of the classical Yoga Upaniṣads belonging to the Muktikā canon. It opens by mapping the cosmic Praṇava (Oṃkāra) and its twelve constituent mātrās onto the sacred Haṃsa bird, delineating the respective planes attained through contemplation of each measure. It then expounds Nādānusandhāna (meditation on the inner mystic sound) seated in the Siddha posture, detailing the progression from coarse internal sounds to increasingly subtle vibrations, leading to dissolution of the mind (manolaya) into the supreme soundless Absolute. Upaniṣadbrahmayogin's Vivaraṇa interprets the entire yogic progression through the lens of non-dual Advaita Vedānta culminating in videhamukti.

summary: The Āścaryayogamālā ('Rosary of Wondrous Recipes/Applications'), also known as Yogaratnamālā or Yogaratnāvalī, is a medieval manual of magic and occult recipes (ṣaṭkarman) attributed to Nāgārjuna. It details preparations and spells for subjugation (vaśīkaraṇa), immobilization (stambhana), and other powers. It is accompanied by the concise commentary (Laghuvṛtti) of the Śvetāmbara Jaina scholar Guṇākara.

summary: The Tripurāsārasamuccaya of Nāgabhaṭṭa is an important compendium of the Śākta Śrīvidyā tradition in ten chapters (paṭalas). It details the daily and special ritual worship, mantra extraction and repetition, yantra diagrams, nyāsa procedures, mudrās, and homa (fire offerings) associated with Goddess Tripurasundarī. Govindācārya's commentary Padārthādarśa clarifies technical mantric code-words, ritual injunctions, and traditional Śākta interpretations.

summary: The Mantravyākhyāprakāśikā (also designated Kātyāyanītantraṭīkā) is a tantric commentary by Nīlakaṇṭha Śaiva on the 23rd chapter (paṭala) of the Kātyāyanītantra. This chapter establishes the authoritative 700-mantra breakdown (saptaśatīmantrasaṅkhyāvibhāga) of the Devīmāhātmya / Durgāsaptaśatī necessary for ritual applications such as homa, japa, and saṃpuṭīkaraṇa. The commentary meticulously accounts for each chapter's verse segments, half-verses, and uvāca-lines to verify the exact tally of seven hundred mantras.

summary: The Kriyāsāra ('Essence of Practice') by Nīlakaṇṭha Śivācārya (c. 14th–15th century CE) is a major Vīraśaiva metrical treatise harmonizing Śaiva ritual, ethical conduct, and devotional observance with the philosophical framework of the Brahmasūtras. Structured into thirty-one chapters (upadeśas), the text systematically expounds the doctrine of the 101 stages (ekottaraśatasthala) and daily religious duties. This portion comprises Upadeśas 5 through 14, focusing on regular and occasional duties (ācāra), the theological symbolism and rites of holy ash (bhasma) and rudrākṣa, ablutions, sandhyā, and the liturgical manual of Śiva worship (śivapūjā).

summary: The Liṅgadhāraṇacandrikā is a Vīraśaiva apologetic and theological treatise composed by Nandikeśvara. Applying Mīmāṃsā hermeneutical principles to Vedic, Upaniṣadic, Āgamic, and Smṛti citations, the work establishes the scriptural validity, necessity, and orthodoxy of constantly bearing the personal liṅga on the body (iṣṭaliṅgadhāraṇa) and examines associated funerary practices. The accompanying Sanskrit commentary, written by Mahāmahopādhyāya Śivakumāra Śāstrī in 1903, provides glosses and defends the dialectical arguments against rival philosophical schools.

summary: The Tārābhaktisudhārṇava ('Ocean of the Nectar of Devotion to Tārā') is an extensive Śākta ritual digest (nibandha) dedicated to the worship of the Mahāvidyā Tārā in her various forms (including Ugratārā, Ekajaṭā, and Nīlasarasvatī). Divided into eleven taraṅgas ('waves'), it provides comprehensive ritual guidance on guru-disciple requirements, initiation (dīkṣā), daily worship, mantra recitation (japa), yantra designs, nyāsa, puraścaraṇa, and esoteric rites such as śavasādhana, compiling canonical passages from scriptures such as the Rudrayāmala, Brahmayāmala, and Tārātantra.

summary: The Tantracintāmaṇi is an extensive Śākta Tantric digest (nibandha) composed in the late seventeenth century by Navamīsiṃha (Ādyānanda), a minister in the Newar Malla kingdom of Kathmandu. Organized in forty prakāśas, it compiles citations from numerous Āgamic and Tantric authorities to delineate cosmology, mantra lore, the worship of the Daśamahāvidyās (focusing particularly on Dakṣiṇakālikā/Śyāmā), Kulācāra rites, and dīkṣā ceremonies. This digital transcription covers chapters 1 through 30 with its autocommentary (Pañjikā).

summary: A Newar tantric ritual manual (paddhati) composed in mixed Sanskrit and Newari for the propitiation of the nine sacred seats (navapīṭha) and eight mother goddesses (aṣṭamātṛkā), primarily in the context of the Kubjikā and Śākta traditions (invoking Kubjikā, Siddhilakṣmī, and Ucchiṣṭhanātha). It was commissioned for King Bhūpatīndra Malla for a Durgā temple consecration (durgāprāsādapratiṣṭhā), and contains liturgical instructions, mantras, nyāsas, bali rituals, and embedded devotional hymns including the Mālinīdaṇḍaka and Pīṭhāvatārastotra.

summary: The Varuṇapaddhati is a South Indian Śaiva Siddhānta ritual manual (paddhati) composed by Varuṇaśiva. This e-text provides the root text along with the Vilocana commentary by Nigamajñānadeva, a Śaiva scholar of Vyāghrapura (Chidambaram). The manual expounds two fundamental aspects ('bījadvaya') of Śaiva ritual practice: initiation (dīkṣā) and consecration or temple installation (pratiṣṭhā).

summary: A short Śaiva yoga text of 90 anuṣṭubh verses structured as an instruction delivered by Bhagavān to Guha. summary: The Nirvāṇatantra is a Śākta scripture framed as an esoteric dialogue between Śiva and Caṇḍikā. In this 14-chapter recension, the text expounds cosmogony, identifying Kālī with supreme Brahman and prime source of the universe, along with the significance of the Gāyatrī mantra, spiritual lineage and devotion to the guru, and rituals of the five makāras. The concluding paṭalas delineate the duties of the four varṇas and āśramas, culminating in an exposition of the avadhūta ascetic path.

The first sets out the outer worship of Tripurasundarī and the sixteen Nityās: mantras, the Śrīcakra, mudrās and ritual applications. The second treats the inner meaning of cakra, mantra and pūjā. This e-text gives both with the Setubandha, the extensive commentary by the 18th-century scholar Bhāskararāya, which uses Mīmāṃsā methods to treat the two parts as one tantra in eight viśrāmas.

summary: The Nityādisaṅgraha is an extensive Kashmiri Śaiva ritual manual (paddhati) composed by Rājānaka Takṣakavarta. Synthesizing liturgical and mantric traditions from the Bhairavatantras and Śaiva Siddhānta (relying heavily on the Svacchandatantra), it details daily worship (nityapūjā), oblations, initiation obligations, ritual procedures for linga and sthaṇḍila worship, and occasion-specific rites such as the Śivarātri observance.

summary: The Pāśupatabrahmopaniṣad is a Yoga Upaniṣad structured around a dialogue between the creator Brahmā and his son Vaiśravaṇa (Vālakhilya). Across two sections (Pūrvakāṇḍa and Uttarakāṇḍa), the text internalizes Vedic sacrificial concepts, reinterpreting the sacrificial thread (yajñasūtra) and external ritual offerings as internal spiritual awareness, the Haṃsa mantra, and continuous contemplation of the Paramātman. It fuses Pāśupata Śaiva imagery with non-dual Vedāntic metaphysics. Upaniṣadbrahmayogin's commentary (Vivaraṇa) interprets the text from an Advaita Vedānta perspective, emphasizing the realization of unconditioned Brahman (niṣpratiyogika-brahman).

summary: The Pārānandasūtra (also called Pārānandamīmāṃsā) is an anonymous Śākta-Kaula ritual code written in sūtras, in two adhyāyas of seven āhnikas each, modelled on the Vedic and Mīmāṃsā sūtra style. It teaches one supreme Self, the Īśvaras and the countless souls. It describes the three paths of practice (dakṣiṇa, vāma and uttara), the qualifications of guru and disciple, initiation and order of precedence, daily and special worship, sacrificial sessions (satra) with offerings of wine and animals, expiations, and rules of conduct, and it often cites the differing opinions of named authorities.

summary: The Parātantra is a Śākta-Kaula scripture framing its revelation within the Śiraścheda tradition. It systematically harmonizes the six transmissions (ṣaḍāmnāya) by assigning major Śākta lineages and deities—including Kubjikā (Western), Tripurasundarī (Southern), Guhyakālī and Siddhilakṣmī (Northern), and Vajrayoginī (Lower)—to six thrones, synthesizing them as manifestations of the singular supreme Goddess Parā.

summary: The Parameśvarīmatatantra is a scripture of the Western Transmission (Paścimāmnāya) of Kaula Śaivism, intimately connected with the Kubjikā cycle. Set as a dialogue between Mahābhairava and the Devī, the text treats the esoteric symbolism of Mount Meru (Meruddhāra), the sixfold lineage (ṣaḍvidha kulāmnāya), mantras, mudrās, and yantras. In this manuscript transcription, paṭala 24 marks the conclusion of the 24-chapter Meruddhāra of the Pārameśvarīmata, while the remainder continues through to chapter 56, ending with a colophon to the Kubjikāmata.

summary: The Paraśurāmakalpasūtra is a foundational manual of Śākta ritual worship in the Śrīvidyā (Kaula) tradition, composed in ten khaṇḍas of concise aphorisms. Traditionally attributed to Paraśurāma, it codifies ritual procedures, mantra transmission, dīkṣā, and Śrīcakra worship for Lalitā Mahātripurasundarī and affiliated deities such as Bālā, Mātaṅgī, and Vārāhī. This e-text presents the sūtras together with the commentary Saubhāgyodaya by Rāmeśvara.

summary: The Pauṣkarasaṃhitā is one of the principal canonical scriptures of the Vaiṣṇava Pāñcarātra tradition, revered alongside the Sāttvatasaṃhitā and Jayākhyasaṃhitā as one of the 'Three Gems' (ratnatraya). Across 43 chapters, it provides detailed instructions on ritual diagrams (maṇḍala), initiatory grades (samayī, putraka, sādhaka), installation (pratiṣṭhā), iconography, temple architecture, and caturvyūha theology. It is a major classical source for Śrīvaiṣṇava temple liturgy and ritual philosophy.

summary: This is a Newar ritual manual (paddhati) of the Kubjikā cult (Paścimāmnāya, the 'Western Transmission'), mixing Sanskrit mantras with Newari ritual instructions. It sets out the worship of the goddess Kubjikā and her retinue in 28 sequences (aṣṭāviṃśatikrama): guru veneration, purification of the hands and of the vessels for water and arghya, bhūtaśuddhi, extensive nyāsas, meditation on the kramas, and worship of the lineages of Siddhas/Nāthas (navanātha, the 'ānanda' teachers). The manuscript then gives supplementary rites, chiefly bali offerings to Vaṭuka, the 64 yoginīs and other deities, and closing formulas for dakṣiṇā and gifts.

summary: The Piṅgalāmata (also titled Jayadrathādhikāra) is an early Śaiva pratiṣṭhātantra associated with the Brahmayāmala and Jayadrathayāmala. Practically all early surviving Pratiṣṭhātantras are Saiddhāntika, but the Piṅgalāmata incorporates ritual procedures and iconographic details of the Vāma, Yāmala, and Trika traditions alongside pratiṣṭhā rites (consecration and installation of deities, temples, monasteries, palaces, and towns).

summary: A short anonymous Śaiva text in verse and prose on the 'agnihotra in the breath' (prāṇāgnihotra), taught by Śiva to Ṣaṇmukha for people who cannot afford the Vedic fire ritual. It maps the elements of the sacrifice onto the body, its faculties and the cosmos. It then describes the vital breaths and their deities, and the eating of food as an inner fire offering. The surviving text breaks off in this section.

summary: An anonymous commentary (vyākhyā) on the Prāsādaṣaṭślokī, a Śaiva Siddhānta text consisting of six verses analyzing the Prāsādamantra (hauṃ). summary: The Prāsādaṣaṭślokī is a six-verse Śaiva esoteric text detailing the phonic, spatial, and yogic ascent of the Prāsādamantra (the bījamantra of Paramaśiva, hauṃ) from the mūlādhāra through bodily and cranial centers up to unmanā. The accompanying anonymous prose Vyākhyā explicates the twelvefold and sixteenfold divisions (kalā) of the mantra, its anatomical measurements (aṅgula), phonic stages, and internal absorption (laya). The transcript concludes with supplementary passages detailing the Kalāprāsāda and the yogic viṣuvats.

summary: The Prāyaścittasamuccaya of Hṛdayaśiva is an early Śaiva Siddhānta digest on expiatory rites (prāyaścitta). summary: The Prabhuliṅgalīlā is a Sanskrit Vīraśaiva hagiographical text presented as part of the Bhaviṣyatpurāṇa, narrating the life, deeds, and teachings of the 12th-century saint Allama Prabhu. Closely related to Cāmarasa's Kannada work Prabhuliṅgalīle, it depicts Allama Prabhu's conquest of Māyā and his spiritual dialogues with prominent Vīraśaiva figures such as Gorakṣanātha, Muktāyakkā, and Basava, elucidating Vīraśaiva philosophical principles including the Ṣaṭsthala system.

summary: The Kāmakalāvilāsa is a Śrīvidyā treatise by Puṇyānanda expounding the non-dual cosmogonic and metaphysical doctrine of the Supreme Goddess Tripurasundarī. It details the emanation of the universe from the primordial union of illumination (prakāśa) and reflexive awareness (vimarśa) via the kāmakalā—the creative principle embodied in the three primal bindus. The text articulates the manifestation of sacred speech through the four levels of sound and maps this cosmogony onto the geometry and presiding deities of the Śrīcakra. The accompanying Cidvallī commentary by Naṭanānanda provides essential elucidation of the esoteric terminology and ritual correlations.

summary: The Kāmakalāvilāsa is a foundational doctrinal treatise of the Śrīvidyā tradition of Śākta Tantra, attributed to Puṇyānandanātha. In 55 verses, it sets forth the non-dual metaphysics of Kāmakalā—the creative pulsation and self-manifestation of pure consciousness (Prakāśa-Vimarśa / Śiva-Śakti)—and elaborates the esoteric emergence and symbolic structure of the Śrīcakra and the fifteen-syllabled mantra (Kādimata / Hādimata). The text is accompanied by the Cidvallī, the classic Sanskrit commentary by Naṭanānanda, which elucidates its dense philosophical vocabulary and meditative correspondences.

summary: The Puraścaryārṇava is a Śākta-Tāntrika ritual compendium (nibandha) compiled under the patronage of King Pratāpasiṃha Śāha of Nepal. Organized into taraṅgas ('waves'), it synthesizes scriptural injunctions from numerous Tantras and Purāṇas on the requirements and performance of puraścaryā (preparatory mantra realization) and ritual worship. This first volume encompasses taraṅgas 1 to 4, concluding with kriyāvatī dīkṣā.

summary: The Puraścaryārṇava ('Ocean of Preliminary Ritual Practice') is an encyclopedic Śākta and Tāntrika ritual digest (nibandha) compiled under the auspices of King Pratāpasiṃha Śāha of Nepal (r. 1775–1777). This third volume contains taraṅgas 9 through 12, completing the twelve-chapter digest. It covers the mantras and puraścaraṇa rituals of the Daśamahāvidyās (taraṅga 9), other deities including Sarasvatī alongside Vaidika mantras like the Gāyatrī (taraṅga 10), the worship of Durgā with an extensive manual for the autumnal Durgotsava / Navarātri (taraṅga 11), and the mantras, yantras, stotras, and kavacas of Brāhmī and various other deities (taraṅga 12). Citing scores of canonical tantras, Purāṇas, and earlier ritual paddhatis, it is an essential reference for northern Indian and Nepalese tantric liturgy.

summary: The Parātrīśikā is a scripture of Kashmir Śaivism's Trika lineage, traditionally received as an extract from the Rudrayāmalatantra. In 35 verses, Śiva (Bhairava) expounds to the Goddess the mystery of the supreme reality (anuttara), the Goddess Parā as non-dual awareness, and the esoteric phonemic emanations (mātṛkā) through which cosmos and mantra manifest. In this vivṛti, Rājānaka Lakṣmīrāma provides an exposition of the text in light of Abhinavagupta's earlier work.

summary: The Nādakārikā (also known as Nādasiddhi) is a 26-verse treatise by the Kashmirian master Bhaṭṭa Rāmakaṇṭha establishing the dualist Śaiva Siddhānta metaphysics and epistemology of sound. The text is accompanied by the vyākhyā of Aghoraśiva, which unpacks the polemical nuances and technical vocabulary.

This section focuses on kāmya rituals (optional rites directed at specific worldly and spiritual fruits), detailing mantra practice, puraścaraṇa, rosary rites (mālāprakaraṇa), pilgrimage/pīṭha rules, prayogas for deities such as Kārtavīrya, Dhūmāvatī, and Ucchiṣṭacaṇḍālinī, as well as an exhaustive treatment of the autumn Durgotsava. summary: The Prāṇatoṣiṇī is an extensive Śākta tantric digest (nibandha) compiled in 1820 CE by Rāmatoṣaṇa Vidyālaṅkāra. Bringing together citations from scores of Tantras, Purāṇas, and ritual compendia, it forms an encyclopedic reference work of the late traditional Bengali Śākta school. summary: The Rudrayāmala is traditionally celebrated as one of the major early Śaiva-Śākta Yāmala tantras, although the ancient scripture cited by non-dual Kashmirian Śaiva authors survives only in fragmentary quotations. The extant Uttaratantra (presented here in its extensive 90-paṭala recension) is a later Kaula-Śākta compilation devoted to esoteric yoga, ritual, and mantra practice. It provides detailed expositions of Kuṇḍalinī yoga, subtle bodily physiology, the cakras along with their presiding Śaktis (Ḍākinī, Rākinī, Lākinī, Kākinī, Śākinī, and Hākinī), guru-sevā, and the worship of goddesses such as Kumārī, Tripurasundarī, and Mahākālī.

summary: The Bhogakārikā ('Verses on Worldly Experience') by Sadyojyoti is a foundational philosophical treatise of the dualist Śaiva Siddhānta tradition and one of the eight canonical primers known collectively as the Aṣṭaprakaraṇa. In 146 verses, Sadyojyoti investigates the nature of bhoga (embodied experience of pleasure and pain), explaining how the bound individual soul (paśu)—whose innate powers of consciousness and action are obscured by beginningless primordial impurity (mala)—is endowed by Śiva with bodies, faculties, and worlds evolved out of māyā to experience karmic fruit and mature its impurity. Aghoraśiva's vṛtti elucidates Sadyojyoti's concise verses line by line, rigorously defending the realist ontology of pati (Lord), paśu (soul), and pāśa (bond) against rival arguments from Sāṅkhya, Nyāya, and Buddhist philosophy.

summary: The Mokṣakārikā is an authoritative doctrinal treatise of Śaiva Siddhānta composed by Sadyojyoti, traditionally included as one of the Aṣṭaprakaraṇa. Across 157 verses, it expounds the nature of liberation (mokṣa), rejecting non-dualist and nihilistic theories to argue that liberation consists in the eradication of innate impurity (mala) and karma, whereby the liberated soul realizes innate omniscience and omnipotence equal to Śiva (śivasāmya). It is accompanied by the commentary (vṛtti) of Bhaṭṭa Rāmakaṇṭha, who elaborates the epistemological and ontological arguments against rival positions.

summary: The Paramokṣanirāsakārikā is an early Śaiva Siddhānta polemical and doxographical treatise by Sadyojyoti, accompanied here by the comprehensive commentary (vṛtti) of Bhaṭṭa Rāmakaṇṭha. Across 59 kārikās expounding a passage of the Rauravasūtra, the work systematically refutes twenty non-Śaiva and heterodox soteriological viewpoints—including Sāṅkhya, Yoga, Vedānta, Pāñcarātra, Nyāya, Vaiśeṣika, Buddhist, Jaina, and non-Siddhānta Śaiva models—showing that liberation cannot consist in mere isolation, dissolution, cessation of consciousness, or acquisition of mundane qualities. In their place, Sadyojyoti and Rāmakaṇṭha defend the orthodox Siddhānta doctrine that liberation is the manifestation of the soul's innate, co-equal Śiva-nature (śivatvavyakti), consisting in unobstructed omniscience and omnipotence, actualized through initiation (dīkṣā).

Across 32 kārikās condensing doctrines from the Svāyambhuvasūtrasaṅgraha, it establishes the three eternal realities: the Lord (Śiva / pati), bound souls (puruṣa / paśu), and the primordial material cause (māyā / pāśa), alongside the innate beginningless impurity (mala). Aghoraśiva's vṛtti provides an authoritative commentary on the treatise.

summary: The Nareśvaraparīkṣā ('Examination of the Soul and the Lord') by Sadyojyoti is an early systematic treatise of dualistic Śaiva Siddhānta. It opens with the Sarasvatīstotra, a hymn attributed to the sage Āśvalāyana invoking Sarasvatī as the supreme Brahman and power of speech, complete with nyāsa/viniyoga formulas. summary: The Pārāyaṇavidhi section of the Saubhāgyatantra is a Śākta tantric manual detailing the astronomical, calendrical, and liturgical calculations (ahargaṇa) necessary for the systematic continuous recitation (pārāyaṇa) of Śrīvidyā mantras. summary: An anonymous Śaiva Siddhānta doctrinal compendium in mixed prose and verse that synthesizes tenets of the Śaivāgama tradition. It quotes foundational scriptures and commentaries including the Svāyambhuvasūtrasaṃgraha, Kiraṇatantra, Mālinīvijayottara, Rauravatantra, and Mataṅgapārameśvara, as well as Rāmakaṇṭha. summary: The Suprabhedāgama is one of the twenty-eight canonical Mūlāgamas of dualist Śaiva Siddhānta, traditionally categorized among the five Śivabhedas emanating from the Vāmadeva face of Śiva. It is one of the relatively few Āgamas preserved across all four classical divisions (pādas): Kriyāpāda (temple layout, iconography, installation of liṅgas, and daily/occasional worship rituals), Caryāpāda (initiation, duties of devotees, royal rites, and expiation), Yogapāda (subtle anatomy, prāṇāyāma, and meditation), and Jñānapāda (cosmogony, thirty-six tattvas, and the adhvans). It has long served as a prominent ritual authority for South Indian temple architecture and liturgical performance.

summary: The Haṭhayogapradīpikā is the principal medieval manual of Haṭhayoga, composed by Svātmārāma. summary: The Tārātantra is a short Śākta scripture in six paṭalas formatted as a dialogue between Bhairava and Bhairavī, devoted to the worship of the Mahāvidyā goddess Tārā (in forms such as Ugratārā and Ekajaṭā). It details her five-syllable root mantra, visualizations (dhyāna), daily liturgy (prātaḥkṛtya, guru-pūjā), and magical rites (ṣaṭkarman). The text is especially renowned for its integration of the Mahācīnakrama ('Chinese/Tibetan rite'), recounting how both the sage Vasiṣṭha and the Buddha attained spiritual perfection (siddhi) through this esoteric discipline.

summary: The Tantrarājatantra is one of the primary canonical scriptures of the Kādimata lineage within the Śākta Śrīvidyā tradition, structured in 36 chapters as an esoteric dialogue between Śiva and the Devī. It presents comprehensive instruction on the worship of Lalitā Mahā-Tripurasundarī and the fifteen Nityā goddesses, detailing mantra formulas, yantra geometry, the nyāsa rites of the Śrīcakra, and non-dual Śākta metaphysics. In this edition, the scripture is accompanied by the running Manoramā commentary, written up through chapter 22 by Subhagānandanātha and finished for chapters 23–36 by his disciple Prakāśānandanātha.

summary: The Troṭalātantra (or Troṭalamahātantra) is an early medieval Śaiva/Śākta tantric scripture framed as an exposition delivered by Śiva to Garuḍa (Tārkṣya). It centers on the goddess Troṭalā—identified with Tvaritā and linked with the Kubjikā tradition—so named because she shatters (troṭana) worldly bonds. The work covers her visual iconography, mantra formulas, internal yogic ascent through the centers to union with Bhairava, and rites for protection against poison and the subjugation of spirits.

summary: The Parārthapūjāvidhi (also titled Nityapūjāvidhi on fol. 1a) is a Śaivasiddhānta ritual manual (paddhati) specifying daily communal temple worship (parārthapūjā). summary: The Uḍḍāmareśvaratantra (also styled Uḍḍāmareśvaramahātantra) is a 15-chapter applied Tantric manual dedicated primarily to pragmatic magic and ritual pharmacology (ṣaṭkarman rites such as vaśīkaraṇa, uccāṭana, stambhana, and māraṇa). It details incantations, herbal and mineral recipes (auṣadhi), and counter-sorcery remedies for curing fevers, expelling demonic and planetary possession (bhūtas, grahas, brahmarākṣasas), counteracting poisons, and evoking yakṣiṇīs and related semi-divine entities for material acquisition. The work is structured as an instruction delivered by Śiva to Gaurī and belongs to the wider milieu of practical medieval grimoire literature closely allied with the Uḍḍīśa/Uḍḍāmara traditions.

summary: The Mahānayaprakāśa ('Illumination of the Great Way') is an anonymous Sanskrit verse treatise belonging to the esoteric Krama (Mahānaya/Mahārtha) school of non-dual Kashmir Śaivism. Divided into nine ullāsas, it systematically presents the sequential and non-sequential cycles of divine manifestation and reabsorption, focusing on the wheels of deities (cakras), the pīṭhas, and the twelve forms of Kālī. It emphasizes the direct transmission of non-dual realization through the grace and penetrating glance of the guru (gurudṛkpāta) as superior to external ritual practices.

summary: The Ajaḍapramātṛsiddhi ('Proof of a Conscious Knower') is one of three short treatises comprising Utpaladeva's Siddhitrayī, written to establish the foundational tenets of non-dual Pratyabhijñā philosophy. In 27 kārikās, Utpaladeva argues against Buddhist momentariness and static Vedāntic consciousness, maintaining that both cognition and practical causal efficacy (arthakriyā) require an active, self-reflective subject (vimarśa, ahaṃbhāva) rather than an insentient (jaḍa) continuum. In this edition, the lost original auto-commentary is replaced by a concise Sanskrit Vṛtti composed in Śāka 1841 by Kashmiri scholar Harabhaṭṭa Śāstrī.

summary: The Īśvarasiddhi ('Establishment of the Lord') is one of the three monographs comprising the Siddhitrayī by Utpaladeva, a master of the Pratyabhijñā school of Kashmir Shaivism. Consisting of 56 kārikās and the author's own prose vṛtti, the work defends the necessity of an intelligent conscious agent (Īśvara) behind the cosmos. It critically examines rival models—particularly the Sāṅkhya theory of insentient material transformation (pariṇāmavāda) and the Nyāya inferential proof—before resolving divine agency into recognition (pratyabhijñā).

summary: The Sambandhasiddhi ('Establishment of Relation') is one of the three foundational polemical monographs constituting Utpaladeva's Siddhitrayī. Composed in verse with an integral prose autocommentary (vṛtti), the text defends the ontological and linguistic reality of relations (sambandha) against Buddhist nominalist critiques, particularly Dharmakīrti's Sambandhaparīkṣā. Integrating Bhartṛhari's grammatical philosophy with non-dual Pratyabhijñā metaphysics, Utpaladeva argues that relation as identity-in-difference cannot subsist purely among insentient entities, but necessarily depends on the synthesizing, reflective awareness (vimarśa, anusaṃdhāna) of universal consciousness (Śiva).

summary: The Vāmakeśvarīmata (more commonly known as the Nityāṣoḍaśikārṇava) is a foundational scriptural tantra of the Kaula Śrīvidyā tradition dedicated to the goddess Tripurasundarī. It details the geometry and esoteric worship of the Śrīcakra, the mantras and iconography of the fifteen Nityā goddesses, ritual hand gestures (mudrās), and mantric practices. In this commentary (Vivaraṇa), the Kashmiri master Rājānaka Jayaratha interprets the Śākta liturgy through the non-dualistic philosophical lens of the Kashmir Śaiva Trika and Pratyabhijñā traditions.

summary: An extensive Śākta Kaula Tantra belonging to the Dakṣiṇāmnāya (Southern transmission) and associated in its opening verses with the Kāmarūpa pīṭha. It centers on the worship of the goddess Vārāhī along with Sundarī and Kālikā, serving as a comprehensive manual of ritual procedures, mantras, yantras, nyāsa, and yogic practices. The text is cited in several major Tantric digests, providing a terminus ante quem prior to the late 18th-century Puraścaryārṇava.

summary: The Varāhopaniṣad is a minor Yoga Upaniṣad (reckoned as the 98th in the Muktikā canon) attached to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda, framed as an instruction imparted by Viṣṇu in his boar form (Varāha) to the sage Ṛbhu. Across five adhyāyas, it enumerates the 24, 36, and 96 tattvas, details subtle yogic physiology (cakras, nāḍīs, and kuṇḍalinī), outlines prāṇāyāma and haṭhayogic disciplines, and elucidates the seven stages of spiritual knowledge (jñānabhūmikās) culminating in jīvanmukti. Upaniṣadbrahmayogin's commentary (Vivaraṇa) interprets the yogic practices in the light of Advaita Vedāntic non-dualism.

summary: A late Vīraśaiva theological and polemical treatise composed in mixed verse and prose by Vīracannabasava of Sudhāpurī, writing within the lineage of the 15th–16th century saint Tōṭada Siddhēśvara and Murigā Śāntavīra. The work expounds classical Vīraśaiva doctrine, focusing on the eight protective shields (aṣṭāvaraṇa), five conducts (pañcācāra), six stages (ṣaṭsthala), and the superiority of personal liṅga worship (iṣṭaliṅga) over temple idols (sthiraliṅga). It supports its positions by citing extensive passages from Purāṇic and Tantric/Āgamic texts such as the Śāṅkarasaṃhitā, Pārameśvara, Kūrmapurāṇa, and Sūtasaṃhitā.

summary: An anonymous Vīraśaiva scripture cast as a dialogue between Devī and Śiva, whose colophons assign it to a 'Sahasrakoṭisaṃhitā'. It opens with a classification of Śaiva and other sectarian traditions and declares Vīraśaivism superior to them. Its chapters set out the stages (sthala) of Vīraśaiva devotion and the doctrine and worship of the prāṇaliṅga and its six petals (ṣaḍdala). The surviving part of the last chapter deals with the preparation and wearing of sacred ash (bhasma).

summary: The first book (Vairāgyaprakaraṇa, 33 sargas) of the Yogavāsiṣṭha describes the profound disillusionment and existential grief of the young prince Rāma after his pilgrimage across the country. Confronting the transience of life, wealth, youth, and the physical body, Rāma articulates his despair before king Daśaratha and the royal assembly, creating the need for sage Vasiṣṭha's extensive exposition of non-dual liberation. Ānandabodhendra Sarasvatī's accompanying commentary Tātparyaprakāśa provides word-by-word glosses and an orthodox Advaita Vedānta framing.

summary: The Mumukṣuvyavahāraprakaraṇa is the second book of the Yogavāsiṣṭha (or Mokṣopāya), consisting of twenty chapters. Addressing Rāma's spiritual disaffection introduced in the opening book (Vairāgyaprakaraṇa), this section analyzes the nature of human striving (pauruṣa) versus fate (daiva), details the narrative of Śuka's attainment of peace through King Janaka, and introduces the four 'gatekeepers of liberation' (dvārapālas: śama, vicāra, santoṣa, and sādhasaṅgama). The root text is accompanied throughout by the Advaita Vedāntic commentary Tātparyaprakāśa of Ānandabodhendra Sarasvatī.

summary: The Utpattiprakaraṇa ('Section on Origin/Creation') is the third book of the Yogavāsiṣṭha (traditionally ascribed to Vālmīki), an extensive philosophical poem expounding non-dualism through dialogues between the sage Vasiṣṭha and Prince Rāma. This section demonstrates how the external universe arises as a mental illusion or conceptual vibration (saṃkalpa/cittaspanda) within unconditioned consciousness (cit/Brahman), using extended allegories such as the story of Queen Līlā and the story of Karkaṭī. The root verses are accompanied by Ānandabodhendrasarasvatī's classic Advaita Vedānta commentary, the Tātparyaprakāśa.

summary: The Sthitiprakaraṇa constitutes the fourth book of the Yogavāsiṣṭha (consisting of 62 sargas), elucidating the apparent preservation and sustenance (sthiti) of the manifest phenomenal cosmos from the perspective of radical non-dualism. Sage Vasiṣṭha instructs Prince Rāma through philosophical discourse and pedagogical narratives—such as the allegorical tales of Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa, and the story of the ascetic Dāśūra—demonstrating that the universe possesses no independent reality and is merely an ungrounded vibration of consciousness (cittaspanda) sustained by delusion. The accompanying commentary, the Tātparyaprakāśa by Ānandabodhendra Sarasvatī, elucidates the text in terms of classical Advaita Vedānta epistemology and metaphysics.

summary: The Upaśamaprakaraṇa is the fifth prakaraṇa of the Yogavāsiṣṭha (or Vāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa), an encyclopedic philosophical text framed as instruction given by the sage Vasiṣṭha to Prince Rāma. It focuses on the calming or pacification (upaśama) of mental fabrications and the dissolution of worldly bondage through philosophical discourses and narrative parables (including the stories of Janaka, Bali, Prahlāda, and Uddālaka). The text is accompanied by the extensive commentary Tātparyaprakāśa of Ānandabodhendra Sarasvatī.

summary: The Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa is the sixth book of the Yogavāsiṣṭha, divided into two halves (Pūrvārdha and Uttarārdha). It brings the philosophical instructions of sage Vasiṣṭha to Prince Rāma to their culmination, expounding the nature of ultimate liberation (nirvāṇa), the total dissolution of the conceptual mind and world-appearance into pure non-dual consciousness, and the state of the living-liberated sage (jīvanmukta). This volume preserves the text according to the vulgate tradition along with the Advaita commentary Tātparyaprakāśa by Ānandabodhendrasarasvatī.

summary: The foundational scripture of Kashmir Shaivism, the Śivasūtra, expounds non-dual Śaiva metaphysics and yogic realization across three sections corresponding to the divine (śāmbhava), cognitive (śākta), and individual (āṇava) means. The Śivasūtravārttika by Bhaṭṭa Bhāskara is an early metrical commentary representing the direct lineage of Vasugupta and Kallaṭa. It provides an important alternative exegetical perspective to Kṣemarāja's later prose Śivasūtravimarśinī.

summary: The Vātūlanāthasūtra is a short Kashmiri Krama/Kaula text of thirteen aphorisms traditionally regarded as an oral revelation from the Yoginīs to the master Vātūlanātha. Accompanied by the commentary (vṛtti) of Anantaśaktipāda, the work articulates the Sāhasa ('sudden leap') transmission of nondual Śaivism, expounding the immediate entry (mahāsāhasa-vṛtti) into transcendent Śiva-consciousness that bypasses gradual contemplative disciplines. It constitutes an essential witness to the non-systematic, esoteric lineage of the Mahārtha school.

summary: The Virūpākṣapañcāśikā is a concise South Indian non-dual Śaiva treatise attributed to Virūpākṣanātha, deeply rooted in Pratyabhijñā and Trika philosophy. This e-text features the root verses embedded within the authoritative Vivṛti commentary composed by Vidyācakravartin.

summary: The Āgamaprāmāṇya is a foundational philosophical and polemical treatise by the Śrīvaiṣṇava master Yāmunācārya. The text defends the scriptural authority (prāmāṇya) and orthodox Vedic status of the Pāñcarātra Āgamas against charges of heterodoxy, invalidity, or non-Vedic origin raised primarily by Mīmāṃsakas and Advaitins. Yāmunācārya argues for the intrinsic validity and divine authorship of the Āgamas by Nārāyaṇa and defends the orthodox caste status and temple-worship rituals of the Bhāgavatas, laying the foundation for Rāmānuja's Viśiṣṭādvaita Vedānta.

summary: The Yogajāgama is traditionally enumerated as the second of the twenty-eight Mūlāgamas of the Śaivasiddhānta canon, categorized as one of the ten Śivabhedas. The text deals primarily with kriyā and caryā aspects of Śaiva temple ritual and architecture, including temple planning (prāsādalakṣaṇa), iconometry (pratimālakṣaṇa), the installation of attendant deities (parivārasthāpana), liṅga installation (liṅgasthāpana), fire rituals (agnikārya), and initiation rites (dīkṣā). This e-text is an unpublished diplomatic transcription of an incomplete palm-leaf manuscript preserved at the French Institute of Pondicherry (IFP MS 39691).

summary: The Yogakuṇḍalyupaniṣad is one of the twenty Yoga Upaniṣads belonging to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda. This e-text includes both the root Upaniṣad and the running Vivaraṇa commentary by Upaniṣadbrahmayogin.

summary: The Yogaśikhopaniṣad is a classical Yoga Upaniṣad traditionally grouped under the Kṛṣṇayajurveda and counted as the 63rd text in the Muktikā list. This e-text preserves the entire scripture alongside the Advaita commentary (vivaraṇa) composed by Upaniṣadbrahmayogin.

summary: The Yoginīhṛdaya ('Heart of the Yoginī') is a canonical scripture of the Śrīvidyā Kaula lineage, regarded as the Uttaracatuḥśatī (second part of 400 verses) of the Vāmakeśvaratantra. Across three chapters—Cakrasaṃketa, Mantrasaṃketa, and Pūjāsaṃketa—it presents the cosmogenetic and subtle-body symbolism of the Śrīcakra, the phonic emanation of Tripurasundarī's fifteen-syllable Vidyā, and esoteric internal ritual meditation. The accompanying Dīpikā by Amṛtānanda is the earliest extant commentary on the treatise, systematically interpreting its Śākta ritual liturgy through non-dual Pratyabhijñā and Trika philosophy.

summary: The Śāṇḍilyopaniṣad is a classical Yoga Upaniṣad framed as an instruction given by Atharvan to the sage Śāṇḍilya. Its first and longest chapter details an eight-limbed yoga (aṣṭāṅga-yoga) incorporating Haṭha-yogic practices, including ten yamas, ten niyamas, eight āsanas, detailed instructions on nāḍī-purification, prāṇāyāma, pratyāhāra, dhāraṇā, dhyāna, and samādhi. The second and third chapters expound the non-dual nature of Brahman in both saguṇa/sakala and nirguṇa/niṣkala aspects, integrating bodily yoga into Advaita Vedānta. In this edition, the text is accompanied by the complete Advaitic commentary (vivaraṇa) of Upaniṣadbrahmayogin.

summary: An anonymous South Indian ritual manual of the late Śaiva Siddhānta for worship of the Goddess in the sacrificial pavilion (śaktimaṇṭapa / śaktiyāga). Appended are several nyāsa procedures: Dūtikānyāsa, Devīśrīkaṇṭhanyāsa, Devīṣaḍadhvanyāsa, kalānyāsa and Śrīkaṇṭhamātṛkānyāsa.

summary: The Sundarīkhaṇḍa is the third section of the extensive Śākta compendium Śaktisaṅgamatantra, framed as a dialogue between Akṣobhya and Mahogratārā. In 21 chapters (paṭalas), it expounds rituals, mantras, and esoteric doctrines centering on the goddess Tripurasundarī (Lalitā) and the Śrīvidyā tradition, detailing initiation (dīkṣā), nyāsas, Śrīcakra worship, and related Mahāvidyās such as Dhūmāvatī. The section is also well known in South Asian historiography for its seventh paṭala (the Deśavyavasthāniyama / Ṣaṭpañcāśaddeśavibhāga), which provides a valuable late-medieval geographical gazetteer dividing the subcontinent into fifty-six regions.

summary: The Śambhunirṇaya (also known as the Śambhunirṇayatantra) is an influential Śāmbhava Kaula tantric ritual work divided into 26 avacchedas. It expounds initiation, maṇḍala layout, mantra pīṭhas, and the ritual framework of the Śāmbhava tradition, mentioning lineages and teachers such as Lakuleśin and Kroḍamuni. It circulated widely in South India, inspiring commentaries such as Śivānandamuni's Śambhunirṇayadīpikā.

summary: A composite e-text containing two Vīraśaiva/Śaiva philosophical treatises. The first, Svaprabhānanda's Śivādvaitamañjarī, defends Vīraśaiva Śivādvaita against Kevalādvaita Vedānta, opening with an examination and refutation of Śaṅkara's Adhyāsabhāṣya. The second, Śaṃbhudeva's Śaivasiddhāntadīpikā (also designated Pāśupatamataprakaraṇa), provides an exposition of Śaiva and Pāśupata doctrine, explaining the five bonds (pāśapañcaka), the attributes of released souls, and Śiva's fivefold cosmic activity (pañcakṛtya).

summary: The Śaivaparibhāṣā is a Sanskrit manual of Śaiva Siddhānta philosophy composed by Śivāgrayogin, patterned after dialectical manuals such as the Vedāntaparibhāṣā. In five chapters, the work methodically details the epistemology (pramāṇa) and the three central ontological categories—the Lord (pati), the bound soul (paśu), and the fetters of bondage (pāśa)—before concluding with the path of initiation and liberation (mukti). Drawing heavily on the Saiddhāntika Āgamas (particularly the Pauṣkarāgama), it represents a major milestone in the late Sanskrit scholasticism of the school.

summary: The Kulapradīpa ('Lamp of the Kula') is a Sanskrit Śākta-Kaula compendium (nibandha) in seven chapters (prakāśa) composed in verse by Śivānandācārya. Drawing heavily upon authoritative Āgamic sources such as the Kulārṇavatantra, it provides an exposition of the doctrines and ritual practices of the Kaula path, including the distinction between dakṣiṇa and vāma conduct, the purification and use of the five substances (pañcamakāra), dūtīyāga, and cakra worship.

summary: The Śivarahasya is a massive Śaiva compendium structured as an itihāsa in twelve books (aṃśas), expounding the supremacy of Śiva, mythological narratives, and ritual and devotional observances. summary: The Śivasūtra is the foundational scriptural text of non-dual Kashmir Shaivism (Trika/Pratyabhijñā), traditionally revealed to Vasugupta on Mount Mahādeva. It expounds the nature of ultimate consciousness and liberation through three sequential stages: Śāmbhavopāya, Śāktopāya, and Āṇavopāya. The Śivasūtravṛtti is a concise anonymous commentary explicating each sūtra with glosses and scriptural citations from texts such as the Mālinīvijayottaratantra and Ucchuṣmabhairava.

summary: The Sanskrit Basavapurāṇa (Basaveśvarapurāṇa) is a Vīraśaiva (Liṅgāyat) purāṇa in 43 adhyāyas, framed as a dialogue in which Skanda answers Agastya's questions. It narrates the birth of Basava (Basaveśvara) as a partial incarnation of Nandin, his marriage, his service at the court of Bijjala and his miracles. It also tells the legends of many Śaiva and Vīraśaiva devotees (e.g. Kannappa, Dīpada Kaliya, Moligemāra, Śivanāgadeva) and argues for Vīraśaiva doctrine and practice against Vedic ritualism and rival sects. It closes with a scene in which Viśvakarman weighs the work against Vyāsa's other compositions and finds it the best of all purāṇas.

summary: The Ratnatrayaparīkṣā ('Examination of the Three Jewels') is one of the eight classical treatises (Aṣṭaprakaraṇa) of the dualist Sanskrit Śaiva Siddhānta tradition. Unlike the tripartite categorization of souls, bonds, and the Lord (paśu, pāśa, pati), the 'three jewels' investigated here are Śiva (the conscious efficient cause), Śakti (Śiva's innate conscious energy), and Bindu (the pure material cause / mahāmāyā). The accompanying commentary, the Ratnatrayollekhinī by Aghoraśivācārya, offers comprehensive ontological and exegetical analysis according to the dualist Śaiva Siddhānta school.

summary: The Śrīkarabhāṣya is the primary Vīraśaiva (Liṅgāyat) bhāṣya on Bādarāyaṇa's Brahmasūtras, expounding the doctrine designated as Viśeṣādvaita or Bhedābhedātmaka-Śaktiviśiṣṭādvaita. Śrīpati establishes Paraśiva as the supreme non-dual Brahman, arguing for a relation of natural difference during bondage and non-difference upon liberation (bhedābheda) between the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman. The text also integrates and validates distinctive Vīraśaiva socio-religious practices such as liṅgadhāraṇa, bhasma, and rudrākṣa on Vedic and Upaniṣadic authorities.

summary: The Śukavākya is a didactic dialogue in Purāṇic verse recounting an exchange between the sage Vyāsa and his son Śuka. summary: The Adhikaraṇasārāvalī is a philosophical poem in Sragdharā metre composed by the Viśiṣṭādvaita master Veṅkaṭanātha (Vedānta Deśika). summary: The Advaitamakaranda is a celebrated short Advaita Vedānta prakaraṇa in 28 anuṣṭubh verses by Lakṣmīdhara Kavi. summary: The Advaitasiddhi is a monumental 16th-century polemical treatise of Advaita Vedānta by Madhusūdanasarasvatī, composed primarily in response to Vyāsatīrtha's Dvaita masterwork Nyāyāmṛta. Formulated using the rigorous technical terminology of Navya-Nyāya, the work systematically refutes Dvaita critiques across four paricchedas. It is celebrated for its intricate dialectical defense of the five classical definitions of the world's falsity (mithyātva), non-dual scriptural hermeneutics, and the Advaitic conception of mokṣa.

summary: Advaitānubhūti is a short Advaita Vedānta prakaraṇa in 84 anuṣṭubh verses expounding non-dualism. summary: The Anātmaśrīvigarhaṇaprakaraṇa is an 18-verse Advaita Vedānta didactic poem traditionally attributed to Śaṅkarācārya. Through the recurring question and refrain 'tataḥ kiṃ ... yena svātmā naiva sākṣātkṛto 'bhūt' ('what then of it, if one has not directly realized one's own Self?'), the text systematically dismisses secular learning, wealth, physical pleasures, social honors, austerities, yogic powers, and celestial realms as worthless in the absence of direct Self-realization (ātmasākṣātkāra).

summary: The Bhagavadbhaktirasāyana is a prominent 16th-century treatise by the Advaita master Madhusūdana Sarasvatī synthesizing Advaita Vedānta philosophy with devotional aesthetics (rasaśāstra). Over three ullāsas, the work formulates bhakti (devotion to Kṛṣṇa) as an autonomous aesthetic rasa and the ultimate puruṣārtha, adapting classical Nāṭyaśāstra categories (vibhāva, anubhāva, vyabhicāribhāva, sthāyibhāva) into a theological framework. An extensive autocommentary (ṭīkāmatallikā) accompanies the first ullāsa.

summary: The Bhāṭṭarahasya (also called Bhāṭṭatantrarahasya) is a treatise by Khaṇḍadeva on the semantics of verbal cognition (śābdabodha) according to the Bhāṭṭa Mīmāṃsā school. Formulated in the precise terminology of Navya-Nyāya, it examines the definitions of dharma and adharma, the semantic import of injunctive endings (vidhi) and productive agency (bhāvanā), verbal roots (dhātu), verbal suffixes (ākhyāta), and case terminations (vibhakti). This incomplete e-text ends with the discussion of the nominative case.

summary: The Karmanirṇaya ('Determination of Ritual Action') is one of the ten philosophical treatises (Daśaprakaraṇa) composed by Madhva (Ānandatīrtha), the founder of Dvaita Vedānta. summary: The Naiṣkarmyasiddhi ('Establishment of Actionlessness') is an independent prakaraṇa work in four adhyāyas composed in mixed verse and prose by Sureśvara, a direct disciple of Śaṅkarācārya. The text provides a systematic philosophical defense of Advaita Vedānta soteriology, arguing that liberation (mokṣa) is achieved solely through knowledge (jñāna) of the non-dual Self and rejecting the necessity of ritual action (karma) or the combination of knowledge and action (jñānakarmasamuccaya). summary: The Kārikāvalī (also known as Bhāṣāpariccheda) together with its auto-commentary, the Nyāyasiddhāntamuktāvalī, is a standard 17th-century manual of the syncretic Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika system composed by Viśvanātha Pañcānana Bhaṭṭācārya. Spanning 168 metric kārikās and accompanying prose, the work systematically explains the seven ontological categories (dravya, guṇa, karma, sāmānya, viśeṣa, samavāya, and abhāva) alongside the four Nyāya means of valid cognition (pratyakṣa, anumāna, upamāna, and śabda). Due to its precision and accessible pedagogical organization, it became one of the standard foundational textbooks of Navya-Nyāya philosophy across traditional pandit schools.
