summary: The Pañcadaśī ('Fifteen Chapters') is an influential 14th-century manual of Advaita Vedānta traditionally attributed to Vidyāraṇya (and in part to Bhāratītīrtha). It is divided into three pentads corresponding to the tripartite nature of Brahman: Viveka-pañcaka (discrimination of existence, sat), Dīpa-pañcaka (illumination of consciousness, cit), and Ānanda-pañcaka (nature of bliss, ānanda). Through pedagogical metaphors—such as the picture-canvas (citradīpa) and the stage lamp (nāṭakadīpa)—the work systematically expounds non-dual ontology, epistemology, and liberation (jīvanmukti).

summary: The Pramāṇalakṣaṇa is one of the ten short philosophical treatises (Daśaprakaraṇa) authored by Madhva (Ānandatīrtha, 13th c.), the founder of Dvaita Vedānta. The treatise systematically analyzes definitions, scopes, and fallacies, defending Dvaita realism against Advaita and other rivals.

summary: The Pramāṇapaddhati is an influential primer of Dvaita epistemology and logic composed by Jayatīrtha. Systematizing the epistemological doctrine set forth in Madhvācārya's Pramāṇalakṣaṇa, the treatise is divided into three sections corresponding to the three valid means of knowledge accepted in Dvaita: perception (pratyakṣa), inference (anumāna), and verbal testimony (āgama). It provides clear definitions of pramāṇa, discusses truth and error, expounds syllogistic reasoning and fallacies (hetvābhāsas), and defends the authoritativeness and intrinsic validity (svataḥprāmāṇya) of Vedic scripture.

summary: The Praśnottararatnamālikā ('Garland of Jewels of Questions and Answers') is a didactic gnomic poem of 67 verses in āryā metre structured as a series of moral and philosophical catechisms. It addresses virtues such as truthfulness, discernment (viveka), charity, guru devotion, and liberation from worldly suffering. Widely esteemed for its concise practical wisdom, it was preserved in distinct versions across Hindu, Jain, and Buddhist lineages.

summary: The Ratnamālāvadāna ('Garland of Jewels of Edifying Deeds') is a late Sanskrit Buddhist metrical collection of thirty-eight avadāna tales framed as instruction given by the arhat Upagupta to Emperor Aśoka. It versifies and expands narratives familiar from older collections such as the Avadānaśataka, illustrating the inexorable results of karma, devotion to the Three Jewels, and the cultivation of the Mahāyāna pāramitās. Preserved in Nepalese Sanskrit manuscripts, it was critically edited in full by Kanga Takahata in 1954.

summary: The Sarvavedāntasiddhāntasārasaṃgraha is a comprehensive verse manual (prakaraṇa) of 1006 kārikās presenting an accessible overview of classical Advaita Vedānta philosophy. Structured largely as an instructional dialogue between guru and disciple, it systematically treats the four qualifications for study (anubandhacatuṣṭaya), discrimination of real and unreal (nityānityavastuviveka), renunciation, the nature of avidyā and superimposition (adhyāropa/apavāda), the interpretation of the Upaniṣadic mahāvākyas, and the attainment of jīvanmukti.

summary: The Siddhāntaleśasaṅgraha is an influential doxographical compendium of Advaita Vedānta by Appayyadīkṣita. Organized into four paricchedas, the work systematically presents and reconciles the divergent doctrines, sub-schools, and interpretations developed by post-Śaṅkara Advaitins (including the Bhāmatī and Vivaraṇa traditions). It analyzes key topics such as the nature and locus of avidyā, the ontological status of jīva and īśvara, the theory of error (adhyāsa), and the direct means of release.

summary: The Svayambhūpurāṇa is the foundational mythic chronicle and pilgrimage guide (sthala-māhātmya) of Newar Buddhism in the Kathmandu Valley. It recounts the myth of the primordial lake (Nāgadaha) drained through the Chobhar gorge by the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, followed by the appearance of the primordial lotus and the self-existent flame (svayambhūjyotis) of the Dharmadhātu enshrined within the Svayambhū Mahācaitya (Swayambhunath). The work incorporates visits of the previous Buddhas of antiquity, legends of local tīrthas, deities, and nāgas, and the transformation of the valley into a Buddhist kingdom. summary: The Tattvabodha is a concise introductory catechism (prakaraṇa) of Advaita Vedānta traditionally attributed to Śaṅkara. Written primarily in simple didactic prose, it defines fundamental concepts and technical terms, including the fourfold preliminary qualifications (sādhanacatuṣṭaya), the three bodies (śarīratraya), the five sheaths (pañcakośa), the three states of experience (avasthātraya), and the manifestation of the twenty-four cosmic principles. It culminates in an exposition of the non-difference between the individual soul and the supreme reality (jīveśvaraikya) and describes the nature and state of the liberated being (jīvanmukta).

summary: The Tattvopadeśa is an Advaita Vedānta prakaraṇa text of 87 verses traditionally attributed to Śaṅkara. Structured as pedagogical instructions from a preceptor to a disciple, the treatise analyzes the Upaniṣadic mahāvākya 'tat tvam asi' ('Thou art that'). It systematically isolates the conscious witness (ātman) from bodily, sensory, and mental superimpositions, elucidates the role of secondary indication (lakṣaṇā) in understanding non-difference, and emphasizes steady devotion and non-duality toward the guru.

summary: The Tithinirṇaya is a short astronomical and calendrical treatise of 29 verses composed by Madhva (Ānandatīrtha) as part of his Sarvamūlagrantha corpus. It sets forth mathematical procedures, sine tables (jyāvākya), and correctional calculations (saṃskāra) for establishing the exact duration of lunar days (tithi). The text is intended to settle the proper timing for ritual fasts (upoṣaṇa), particularly Ekādaśī and Dvādaśī, in accordance with Dvaita tradition.

summary: The Vaiśeṣikasūtra attributed to Kaṇāda is the foundational text of the Vaiśeṣika school, establishing its realist ontological ontology around six ontological categories (padārthas): dravya, guṇa, karma, sāmānya, viśeṣa, and samavāya (with non-existence, abhāva, treated subsequently). The Upaskāra ('Supplement' / 'Exposition') by the philosopher Śaṅkaramiśra served historically as the primary transmitted commentary on the sūtras, elucidating the aphorisms through a lens influenced by classical and early Navya-Nyāya debate.

summary: The Vedāntaparibhāṣā is a classic manual of Advaita Vedānta epistemology and ontology by Dharmarājādhvarīndra. Formulating Advaita concepts in technical philosophical style, the work defines and defends six pramāṇas (pratyakṣa, anumāna, upamāna, āgama, arthāpatti, and anupalabdhi). Its final chapters delineate the central subject matter (viṣaya) as the identity of jīva and Brahman, and the ultimate aim (prayojana) as liberation (mokṣa).

summary: The Viṣṇutattvavinirṇaya is the longest and doctrinally central treatise among the ten philosophical monographs (Daśaprakaraṇa) of Madhva (13th c. CE), the founder of Dvaita Vedānta. In three chapters (paricchedas), it establishes the intrinsic validity of knowledge (svataḥprāmāṇya), the authorlessness (apauruṣeyatva) and primary authority of the Vedas, and the ontological reality of difference (bheda) against Advaita non-dualism and the doctrine of māyā. The second and third chapters demonstrate that the supreme deity Viṣṇu (Nārāyaṇa) is entirely free from imperfections (nirdoṣa) and possessed of infinite auspicious attributes (aśeṣasadguṇapūrṇa).

summary: The Vyomavatī by the Śaiva-Vaiśeṣika master Vyomaśiva (10th century CE) is the earliest surviving commentary on Praśastapāda's Padārthadharmasaṅgraha, pre-dating the commentaries of Śrīdhara (Nyāyakandalī) and Udayana (Kiraṇāvalī). It provides an extensive defense and elaboration of the classical Vaiśeṣika categories (substance, quality, motion, universal, particularity, and inherence), addressing epistemology, ontology, and the Vaiśeṣika doctrine of liberation. The work is noted for its rigorous polemical engagements with Buddhist (especially Dharmakīrtian), Jaina, and Mīmāṃsaka positions, as well as its integration of Śaiva theological perspectives.

summary: The Yogatārāvalī is a short Sanskrit treatise in 29 verses bridging Haṭhayoga physical practices with Rājayoga meditation. It describes the practice of the three bandhas (mūla, uḍḍīyana, jālandhara), kevalakumbhaka, and absorption in inner sound (nādānusandhāna) as the means to dissolve mental fluctuations into amanaska (the transcendent mindless state) and yoganidrā. While traditionally ascribed to Ādi Śaṅkara, it is characteristic of the late medieval syncretism between Haṭhayogic methods and non-dual Advaita metaphysics.

summary: The Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā along with its auto-commentary (vṛtti) by Utpaladeva constitutes the foundational philosophical treatise of the Pratyabhijñā ('Recognition') system of non-dual Kashmir Śaivism. summary: The Īśāvāsyopaniṣad (or Īśopaniṣad) forms the 40th and final chapter of the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā of the Śukla Yajurveda, preserved here in its 18-mantra Kāṇva recension. It synthesizes the contemplation of the cosmos as pervaded by the Lord (īśa) with teachings on renunciation, the dual functions of action (avidyā/karman) and knowledge (vidyā), and final release. Śaṅkara's commentary (bhāṣya) interprets the work within classical Advaita Vedānta, arguing that ritual works pertain solely to worldly and heavenly ends while direct, non-dual knowledge of the self (ātman) alone eliminates ignorance and secures liberation.

summary: The Śarīravāda is a Viśiṣṭādvaita polemical treatise (vāda) by Anantārya of Yādavādri (Melkote) on the defining property (pravṛttinimitta) of the word 'body' (śarīra). It argues that 'bodyhood' is not a jāti and examines the Śrībhāṣya definition: a substance that a conscious being can wholly control and support for its own purposes, and that is entirely subsidiary (śeṣa) to it. It does so with reference to the Śrutaprakāśikā and the Nyāyasiddhāñjana, in Navya-Nyāya style. It also discusses related questions such as the inner self's entering (anupraveśa) and the soul's departure and movement.

summary: The Śataślokī is an Advaita Vedānta verse compendium composed in sragdharā metre and traditionally attributed to Śaṅkarācārya. Across 101 verses, it systematically expounds key Advaitic teachings, including the role of the guru, the illusion of the empirical world, self-realization through discrimination between ātman and anātman, the interpretation of Upaniṣadic Mahāvākyas, and the nature of jīvanmukti. While firmly integrated into the Advaita curriculum, modern philology regards the work as an unauthentic composition of the later Śaṅkara tradition.

Texts of this genre served as reference tools for poets (especially for citrakāvya), scribes, and practitioners interpreting tantric bījamantras.

summary: The Saṅgītaratnākara is a foundational medieval treatise on Indian music and performing arts. Arranged into seven chapters (saptādhyāyī), it provides an exhaustive analysis of notes and intervals (svara), melodic modes (rāga), miscellaneous musicological concepts (prakīrṇa), song and meter forms (prabandha), rhythm and metrics (tāla), musical instruments (vādya), and dance (nartana). The treatise forms an essential transition between ancient dramatic musical theory (gāndharva/mārga) and regional performance traditions (deśī).

Framed as a discourse recited by the wind god Vāyu to the sages in Naimiṣāraṇya, it preserves an archaic core adhering faithfully to the classical pañcalakṣaṇa topics: cosmogony, recreation, genealogies of gods and kings, manvantaras, and dynastic history. Arranged into four distinct sections—Prabhāsakṣetramāhātmya, Vastrāpathakṣetramāhātmya, Arbudakhaṇḍa, and Dvārakāmāhātmya—it forms a massive compendium of sacred geography and pilgrimage lore (tīrthamāhātmya) centered on western India, notably the Somanātha jyotirliṅga, Mount Girnar, Mount Abu, and Dwarka. summary: The Advaitaśataka ('Centuria on Non-Duality') is a 100-verse didactic Vedantic tract (prakaraṇa) summarizing fundamental teachings of Advaita ('sarvavedāntasaṃgraha'). It expounds the nature of the four bodies (sthūla, sūkṣma, kāraṇa, and the transcendent sāmānya/turīya deha), the jīva's bondage through ignorance (ajñāna) and identification with the bodily apparatus, the operation of prārabdha karma, and final emancipation through recognition of one's intrinsic identity with Śiva as unconditioned consciousness (jñaptimātra).

It integrates poetic theory with theatrical rules, discussing auspicious syllabic patterns (varṇagaṇa), word and meaning (śabdārtha), aesthetic sentiment (rasa), heroes and heroines (netṛbheda), figures of speech (alaṅkāra), poetic faults and virtues (doṣa and guṇa), dramatic junctures and plots (sandhyaṅga), major dramatic genres (rūpaka), theatrical embellishments (nāṭyālaṅkāra), and court panegyric compositions (cāṭuprabandha).

summary: The Ardhanārīnaṭeśvarastotra (or Ardhanārīnaṭeśvarāṣṭaka) is an eight-verse hymn dedicated to the androgynous composite form of Śiva and Pārvatī (Ardhanārīśvara). In each stanza, the poet pairs and contrasts the feminine half (Pārvatī) and the masculine half (Śiva) in appearance, ornaments, and cosmic roles (such as creation through lāsya and cosmic dissolution through tāṇḍava), closing each verse with the dual refrain 'namaḥ śivāyai ca namaḥ śivāya'. Traditionally ascribed to Śaṅkarācārya, the poem concludes with a phalaśruti verse promising auspiciousness and longevity.

summary: The Aucityavicāracarcā is an 11th-century treatise on poetic theory by the Kashmiri polymath Kṣemendra. Formulating the Aucitya doctrine of alaṅkāraśāstra, Kṣemendra establishes appropriateness or propriety (aucitya) as the vital essence (jīvita) of poetic art, arguing that poetic ornaments (alaṅkāra) and qualities (guṇa) fail without it. The treatise defines and analyzes distinct loci of propriety, examining each through classical quotations illustrative of poetic excellence or flaw.

summary: Avimāraka is a six-act Sanskrit drama traditionally attributed to Bhāsa, dramatizing a romantic tale likely drawn from the Bṛhatkathā cycle. summary: A collection of three 'centuries' (śataka) of gnomic and lyric epigrams traditionally attributed to Bhartṛhari: the Nītiśataka on worldly prudence, ethics, and civic conduct; the Śṛṅgāraśataka on the pleasures, moods, and pitfalls of erotic desire; and the Vairāgyaśataka on renunciation, transience, and ascetic withdrawal. The triad moves across the classic aims of life (dharma, artha, kāma) toward ultimate spiritual dispassion (vairāgya). Widely anthologized, memorized, and translated, it remains among the most influential works in the Sanskrit subhāṣita tradition.

summary: The Bālacarita ('The Deeds of the Boy') is a five-act Sanskrit drama dramatizing the early life of Kṛṣṇa. The narrative follows his birth in Mathurā, his transfer to Gokula, the subduing of the serpent Kāliya, the slaying of various demons (such as Dhenuka, Ariṣṭa, and Keśin), and his eventual overthrow of King Kaṃsa in the wrestling arena. A distinctive dramaturgical feature of the play is the stage personification of Viṣṇu's divine weapons and an appearance by the goddess Kātyāyanī.

summary: Cārudatta (also known as Daridracārudatta) is a classical Sanskrit-Prakrit play in four acts attributed to Bhāsa. It relates the romance between Cārudatta, an impoverished and noble merchant of Ujjayinī, and the wealthy courtesan Vasantasenā, intertwined with scenes involving the thief Sajjalaka (Śarvilaka) and the thief's burglary of Cārudatta's house. The surviving text breaks off at the end of the fourth act without a formal conclusion or bharatavākya, paralleling the first four acts of Śūdraka's ten-act Mṛcchakaṭikā.

summary: The Gorakṣaśataka ('Hundred Verses of Gorakṣa') is a manual of haṭhayoga traditionally attributed to Gorakṣanātha. The work expounds a six-limbed (ṣaḍaṅga) yoga system comprising posture (āsana), breath control (prāṇāyāma), sense-withdrawal (pratyāhāra), concentration (dhāraṇā), meditation (dhyāna), and absorption (samādhi). It describes esoteric anatomy—including cakras and nāḍīs—alongside mudrās and breath practices aimed at liberation.

summary: The Hammīramahākāvya is a 15th-century historical Sanskrit epic (mahākāvya) composed by the Jain monk Nayacandrasūri. It celebrates the lineage and heroic reign of the Cāhamāna (Chauhan) ruler Hammīradeva of Raṇastambhapura (Ranthambore), culminating in his celebrated defence and ultimate fall against the Delhi Sultan Alauddin Khalji in 1301 CE. The work combines classical court-poetic conventions with historical and regional bardic narratives.

summary: The Madhyamavyāyoga ('The Middle One') is a one-act Sanskrit drama belonging to the vyāyoga genre, traditionally attributed to Bhāsa. Drawing on characters from the Mahābhārata, the play depicts Ghaṭotkaca demanding the sacrifice of the middle son of a wandering Brahmin family as food for his mother Hiḍimbā. summary: The Mānasollāsa is an influential metrical exposition (vārttika) in ten chapters (ullāsas) expounding Śaṅkara's celebrated ten-verse hymn, the Dakṣiṇāmūrtistotra. Traditionally ascribed to Sureśvara, the text systematically develops the hymn's pithy Advaita Vedānta doctrines, treating themes such as the illusory nature of phenomenal diversity (māyā/vivarta), the mirror-like reflection of the world in pure consciousness, the critiques of rival philosophical views (including Buddhist Śūnyavāda and Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika), and the ultimate identity of the individual soul (jīva) with Parameśvara (Śiva-Dakṣiṇāmūrti).

summary: The Naiṣadhīyacarita (or Naiṣadha) by the philosopher-poet Śrīharṣa (12th century CE) is one of the five celebrated mahākāvyas ('great court epics') of classical Sanskrit literature. Across 22 cantos, it narrates the story of King Nala and Princess Damayantī up to their wedding and honeymoon, elaborating on the Nalopākhyāna from the Mahābhārata. Famed for its intricate linguistic craftsmanship, double entendres (śleṣa), and profound philosophical references, the work is traditionally regarded as the ultimate test of scholarship ('naiṣadhaṃ vidvad-auṣadham').

summary: The Ujjvalanīlamaṇi ('The Blazing Sapphire') is an influential treatise on devotional aesthetics and theology by Rūpa Gosvāmin. Written as a continuation of the madhura-rasa section of his Bhaktirasāmṛtasindhu, the work presents an analysis of madhura-rasa (the erotic-devotional sentiment) in relation to Kṛṣṇa. Rūpa treats classifications of hero and heroine (nāyaka- and nāyikā-bheda), supporting characters, excitant factors (vibhāva), involuntary physical responses (anubhāva), and permanent emotions (sthāyibhāva) to explain loving relations between Kṛṣṇa and the gopīs of Vraja, culminating in the preeminence of Rādhā.

summary: A modern liturgical compilation for the worship of the eight forms of Lakṣmī (Aṣṭalakṣmī). summary: The Rāmagītā is an Advaita Vedānta philosophical dialogue forming the fifth chapter of the Uttarakāṇḍa of the Adhyātmarāmāyaṇa. In response to questions posed by Lakṣmaṇa, Rāma teaches that release from saṃsāra is attained not by ritual works (karma) or a combination of knowledge and action (jñānakarmasamuccaya), but solely through direct knowledge (jñāna) of the non-dual Self (ātman). The work systematically synthesizes classical Upaniṣadic Advaita epistemology with devotion to Rāma.

Narrated by Śiva, it gives Rāma's instruction to Hanumān on the self, the non-self and the supreme self. summary: The Śṛṅgāraprakāśa is an encyclopedic masterwork of Sanskrit poetics (alaṅkāraśāstra) and dramaturgy (nāṭyaśāstra) in 36 chapters (prakāśas) composed by King Bhoja of Dhārā (11th century). Chapters 1 to 12 form the foundational half of the work, treating grammatical and semantic theory (śabdārtha, padārtha, vākyārtha, vṛtti), literary flaws (doṣa), excellences (guṇa), ornamentation (alaṅkāra), and dramatic and poetic genres (prabandha). The remainder of the work (chapters 13–36, omitted here) develops Bhoja's famous aesthetic theory that śṛṅgāra (identified with ego/self-awareness, ahaṃkāra/abhimāna) is the single supreme and all-encompassing rasa.

summary: The Muktikopaniṣad is a late Vedāntic text framed as a dialogue between Śrī Rāma and Hanūmān in Ayodhyā. It is famous for formulating the canonical catalog of 108 Upaniṣads mapped to the four Vedic Saṃhitās and describing four graduated forms of liberation (sālokya, sāmīpya, sārūpya, sāyujya) leading to kaivalya. The second adhyāya draws heavily on philosophical formulations related to the Mokṣopāya/Yogavāsiṣṭha tradition, focusing on the destruction of latent impressions (vāsanākṣaya), the dissolution of the mind (manonāśa), and the attainment of jīvanmukti and videhamukti.

summary: The Muṇḍakopaniṣad is a classical verse Upaniṣad affiliated with the Atharvaveda tradition. Divided into three muṇḍakas, each comprising two khaṇḍas, it structures its philosophical instruction as a dialogue between the sage Aṅgiras and the householder Śaunaka. The text is renowned for distinguishing lower ritual and empirical knowledge (aparā vidyā) from higher liberating knowledge of the imperishable Brahman (parā vidyā), and it contains foundational Upaniṣadic allegories including the two birds on the same tree, the bow and arrow aimed at Brahman, and the national motto of India ('satyam eva jayate').

summary: The Nirālambopaniṣad ('Upaniṣad of the Supportless') is a minor Upaniṣad arranged as an Advaita catechism, posing and systematically defining over thirty core ontological, cosmological, and soteriological terms—including Brahman, Īśvara, Jīva, Prakṛti, Karma, Jñāna, Ajñāna, Bandha, Mokṣa, and Saṃnyāsa. It concludes that ultimate reality is non-dual consciousness devoid of worldly support (nirālamba), accessible through experiential realization of the mahāvākyas.

summary: The Nārāyaṇapūrvatāpinīyopaniṣad is a late Vaiṣṇava Upaniṣad framed within the Ātharvaṇarahasya. Topics treated include the correlation of the mantra's syllables with cosmic elements (aṣṭamūrti), the veneration of Mahālakṣmī as supreme Prakṛti, and the design and deity layout (āvaraṇadevatā) of the Nārāyaṇa-yantra.

It synthesizes Śaiva and Vaiṣṇava devotional motifs into Advaita Vedānta, concluding with the Vedic refrain 'tad viṣṇoḥ paramaṃ padam'.

It also elaborates subtle heart anatomy, the nature of the inner ruler (antaryāmin), and conditions for liberation.

summary: The Vajrasūcyupaniṣad examines the defining criteria of a Brāhmaṇa. Through sequential refutations, it denies that brāhmaṇahood consists in the individual self (jīva), the physical body (deha), caste or lineage by birth (jāti), scriptural learning (jñāna), ritual action (karma), or religious merit (dhārmika). It concludes that a true Brāhmaṇa is defined by realization of the non-dual Brahman (sat-cit-ānanda) coupled with self-mastery and absence of egotism.

It details the five gross elements (mahābhūtas) and their bodily constituents, the sensory and motor faculties (indriyas), the fourfold internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), the three guṇas, and the four states of consciousness (jāgrat, svapna, suṣupti, turīya), concluding with the identification of the seventeenfold subtle body (liṅgaśarīra) and the supreme Self transcending the embodied soul (jīva/kṣetrajña).

summary: The Śāṇḍilyopaniṣad is a classical Yoga Upaniṣad framed as an instruction given by Atharvan to the sage Śāṇḍilya. Its first and longest chapter details an eight-limbed yoga (aṣṭāṅga-yoga) incorporating Haṭha-yogic practices, including ten yamas, ten niyamas, eight āsanas, detailed instructions on nāḍī-purification, prāṇāyāma, pratyāhāra, dhāraṇā, dhyāna, and samādhi. The second and third chapters expound the non-dual nature of Brahman in both saguṇa/sakala and nirguṇa/niṣkala aspects, integrating bodily yoga into Advaita Vedānta. In this edition, the text is accompanied by the complete Advaitic commentary (vivaraṇa) of Upaniṣadbrahmayogin.

It compiles liturgical verses and formulas for domestic (gṛhya) ceremonies, including marriage, garbhādhāna, upanayana, and funeral rites, functioning as the mantra collection corresponding to the Gobhilagṛhyasūtra. In four adhyāyas it gives esoteric interpretations of the sāman chant (especially the gāyatra-sāman and the udgītha), the syllable om, prāṇa and the correspondences between ritual, cosmos and person. The fourth adhyāya contains the Kena Upaniṣad (4.18–21), and the text ends with an exposition of the Sāvitrī verse (4.27–28).

summary: The Suśrutasaṃhitā is one of the three foundational classics of classical Āyurveda (the Bṛhat-trayī) and ancient India's premier authority on surgery (śalyatantra). Framed as instructions delivered by Divodāsa Dhanvantari, king of Kāśī, to his student Suśruta, it describes surgical instruments, practical anatomy through human cadaveric dissection, and operative procedures such as rhinoplasty, couching of cataracts, lithotomy, and abdominal suture. The treatise comprises 186 chapters divided across the five sthānas of the Pūrvatantra (Sūtra-, Nidāna-, Śārīra-, Cikitsā-, and Kalpasthāna) and the supplementary Uttaratantra, which treats ophthalmology and ENT (śālākya), pediatrics (kaumārabhṛtya), toxicology/psychiatry (bhūtavidyā), and general medicine (kāyacikitsā).

summary: The Vājasaneyisaṃhitā (Mādhyandina recension) is the foundational mantra collection of the White (Śukla) Yajurveda, preserving the formulas and verses recited by the adhvaryu priest during śrauta sacrificial rites. Unlike the Black (Kṛṣṇa) Yajurvedic saṃhitās, which intermingle liturgical formulas with brāhmaṇa prose exposition, the White Yajurveda separates the liturgical mantras into this collection, relegating exegesis to the Śatapatha-Brāhmaṇa. In 40 adhyāyas, it covers ceremonies including the New and Full Moon sacrifices (Darśapūrṇamāsa), the Soma ritual (Agniṣṭoma), the piling of the fire altar (Agnicayana), and major royal offerings (Vājapeya, Rājasūya, Aśvamedha, Puruṣamedha), concluding in its final chapter with the Īśāvāsyopaniṣad.

summary: The Ṛgvedaprātiśākhya is the oldest surviving phonological and metric treatise (prātiśākhya) of the Vedic literature, affiliated with the Śākala recension of the Ṛgveda and traditionally attributed to Śaunaka. Organized into three adhyāyas comprising eighteen paṭalas, it systematically describes Vedic phonetics, sandhi rules, accentuation (svara), syllable length, meter (chandas), and the phonetic modifications required to derive the continuous saṃhitāpāṭha from the word-by-word padapāṭha. It forms an indispensable source for the history of Vedic phonology and early Indian grammatical thought.

summary: The Dhātupāṭha is the canonical verbal inventory of the Pāṇinian grammatical tradition (Vyākaraṇa), serving as the foundational auxiliary text to the Aṣṭādhyāyī. It arranges approximately two thousand verbal roots into ten conjugation classes (gaṇas), starting from bhvādi and ending with curādi. Each entry provides the root's base form with diacritical markers (anubandhas) denoting accent, voice (parasmaipada, ātmanepada, or ubhayapada), and morphophonological traits, alongside traditional semantic glosses.

summary: The Bṛhaddevatā ('Great [Index of] Deities') is an extensive metrical treatise in eight adhyāyas belonging to the Vedāṅga and Anukramaṇī literature of the Ṛgveda, traditionally attributed to Śaunaka. Composed predominantly in anuṣṭubh verses, it systematically catalogs the deities presiding over every hymn, verse, hemistich, and quarter-verse of the Ṛgveda Saṃhitā in sequential order. In addition to ritual classification and etymological remarks reflecting Nirukta traditions, the work is especially renowned for preserving early narrative legends (ākhyānas) explaining the mythical contexts of the hymns.

summary: The Dhātukārikā (subtitled Bālarañjanī) by Śrīkaṇṭha is a versified grammatical mnemonic handbook on Sanskrit verbal roots according to the Pāṇinian system. summary: The Karaṇapaddhati is an astronomical and mathematical manual (karaṇa) composed around 1730 CE by Putumana Somayājin of the Kerala school. summary: The Khādiragṛhyasūtra (also known as the Drāhyāyaṇagṛhyasūtra) is an aphoristic Kalpasūtra manual of domestic ritual belonging to the Sāmaveda, closely related to the Gobhilagṛhyasūtra of which it represents an abridged and systematized recension. summary: The Nighaṇṭu is the oldest surviving Vedic word-list. It has three parts: synonym lists (naighaṇṭuka-kāṇḍa, adhyāyas 1–3), difficult and homonymous words (naigama, 4) and names of deities (daivata, 5). Yāska's Nirukta is the Vedāṅga treatise on etymology and Vedic exegesis and is built as a commentary on the Nighaṇṭu. It sets out the four word classes (nāman, ākhyāta, upasarga, nipāta), defends the derivation of nouns from verbal roots, and explains the Vedic words and deities with citations of the mantras. The e-text adds the later Pariśiṣṭa (adhyāyas 13–14).

summary: A short Vedic lakṣaṇa (śikṣā) tract from the Taittirīya tradition. It explains the Nāradabaiṭ, a mnemonic syllable code ascribed to Nārada that encodes the counts of anuvākas and vākyas in the Taittirīyasaṃhitā. Seven paribhāṣā verses set out the rules (which vowels count, how conjunct consonants count in kaṭapayādi fashion, and the bindu-marked syllables ma, da, ga, ta, sa standing for tens). The author's prose commentary, Bhāvaprakāśikā, follows, and then the code strings for all seven kāṇḍas.

summary: The Chandaḥsūtra of Piṅgala is the foundational classical treatise on Sanskrit metrics (chandas), traditionally classified as the primary surviving manual of the Chandas Vedāṅga. Spanning eight adhyāyas, it systematically treats both Vedic meters (chapters 1–4) and classical meters (laukika chandas, chapters 4–8), covering both syllabic (varṇa) and moraic (mātrā) structures. The concluding section of the eighth adhyāya is renowned for introducing early combinatorial algorithms, binary representation, and prastāra methods.

summary: The Piṇḍalakṣaṇa is a short Vedic phonetic treatise (Lakṣaṇa/Śikṣā) examining the pronunciation and tightness of cohesion in consonant clusters (varṇapiṇḍa). It classifies clusters into analogical categories such as ayaḥpiṇḍa (compact like an iron ball), dārupiṇḍa (moderately bound like wood), and tūlapiṇḍa (loosely bound like cotton), depending on whether stops, semivowels, sibilants, or nasals are conjoined. It also details the articulation of clusters containing hakāra, citing traditional Śikṣā rules on chest (urasya) versus guttural (kaṇṭhya) voicing.

summary: The Pāraskaragṛhyasūtra is the sole surviving domestic ritual manual (gṛhyasūtra) of the White Yajurveda school. Arranged in three kāṇḍas, it prescribes the full cycle of domestic rites and life-cycle sacraments (saṃskāras)—such as marriage, pregnancy rites, tonsure, upanayana, and samāvartana—as well as domestic daily and seasonal oblations (pākayajñas, śrāddha, and seasonal offerings). The text forms an essential witness to late Vedic domestic ritual and social life.

summary: The Pāṇinīyaśikṣā is the principal Vedāṅga treatise on phonetics and pronunciation associated with the Pāṇinian grammatical tradition. It systematically describes the inventory of 63 or 64 speech sounds (varṇa), the physiology of speech production, places of articulation (sthāna), internal and external effort (prayatna), pitch accents (udātta, anudātta, svarita) and their correlation with musical notes, as well as rules and faults in Vedic recitation. This e-text contains the widely cited vulgate metrical recension in 61 verses.

summary: The Svaraśikṣā is a short Vedic phonetic treatise (śikṣā) in 35 verses dedicated to accentuation (svara). summary: The Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇasāra is Kauṇḍabhaṭṭa's (17th c.) auto-abridgment and concise commentary on the 74 verses (Vaiyākaraṇasiddhāntakārikā) of his uncle Bhaṭṭoji Dīkṣita. This e-text also contains the Kāśikā sub-commentary composed by Harirāma Kāla in 1797 CE.

summary: The Vaiyākaraṇasiddhāntamañjūṣā (commonly referred to as Bṛhanmañjūṣā to distinguish it from the Laghu- and Paramalaghu-mañjūṣā) is Nāgeśabhaṭṭa's masterwork on the philosophy of language and semantic theory in the Pāṇinian tradition. It systematically investigates word meaning, communicative functions (śakti, lakṣaṇā, vyañjanā), verbal roots, morphemes, case relations, and sentential comprehension, critically engaging the positions of Nyāya and Mīmāṃsā. The treatise concludes with a rigorous exposition of the sphoṭa doctrine as the ontological core of meaningful language.

summary: The Varṇaśikṣā is a short Sanskrit treatise of 48 verses cataloguing the esoteric and symbolic dimensions of the Sanskrit alphabet (varṇas). summary: The Vākyapadīya by Bhartṛhari is the foundational treatise of the philosophy of grammar (Vyākaraṇadarśana) and classical Indian semantic theory. Comprising three books—Brahmakāṇḍa (on Śabdabrahman and the metaphysics of language), Vākyakāṇḍa (on sentence-meaning wholism and the sphoṭa doctrine), and Padakāṇḍa or Prakīrṇaka (fourteen specialized treatises exploring universals, particulars, relations, time, action, and case-roles)—it articulates a non-dualist linguistic philosophy that shaped subsequent debates across Buddhist, Mīmāṃsā, and Nyāya traditions. This e-text contains the complete kārikās across all three books together with their principal classical Sanskrit commentaries.

In sixteen chapters, it covers units of measurement, requirements for craftsmen and architects (sthapati, sūtragrāhin, takṣaka, vardhakin), site selection and soil examination (bhūmiparīkṣā), the vāstupuruṣamaṇḍala, orientation of residences, layout of hall houses (śālā), joinery and timber examination, and the fabrication and firing of roofing tiles and clay elements (mṛlloṣṭalakṣaṇa).

summary: The Saptalakṣaṇa is a set of seven mnemonic treatises for the Taittirīya Saṃhitā of the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda. They list the words that need special treatment when the padapāṭha is converted into saṃhitā, and the reverse. The parts cover the elision of visarjanīya after ā (śamāna), words that resist the usual sandhi (vilaṅghya), words followed by n- or t- (napara, tapara), groups of words with a- and ā- (avarṇi, āvarṇi), and words that are not divided by avagraha in the padapāṭha (aniṅgya). Recitation students use it as a reference aid.

summary: The Ṣaṭkāraka with its commentary Saṃbandhodyota is a concise Buddhist Sanskrit grammatical treatise on kāraka syntax and case relations by Rabhasanandin. Opening with homage to the Buddha, the treatise analyzes the six kārakas, syntactic relations (saṃbandha), and case inflection through the framework of whether an argument is expressed (ukta) or unexpressed (anukta) by verbal, kṛt, or taddhita affixes. The commentary illustrates syntactic principles with distinctively Buddhist examples alongside standard grammatical patterns.

summary: The Ṣoḍaśaślokīśikṣā is a concise Vedāṅga phonetic treatise in sixteen verses attributed to Rāmakṛṣṇa. It describes the traditional 63-sound inventory, classification and accents of vowels (svara), consonants, pratyāhāras, and places of articulation (sthāna). It concludes with guidelines for proper articulation, citing the classic simile of a tigress carrying her cubs without biting or dropping them.

summary: The Ahirbudhnyasaṃhitā is an important theological and ritual text of the Vaiṣṇava Pāñcarātra tradition, presented as a revelatory discourse taught by Ahirbudhnya (Śiva) to Nārada. This first volume (adhyāyas 1–36) details the cosmogony and metaphysics of the school, emphasizing the six divine attributes (ṣaḍguṇa), the emanations of Viṣṇu (vyūhas), and the cosmogenetic activity of his śakti embodied in the Sudarśana cakra. It also includes comprehensive treatises on mantravidyā, yoga, royal apotropaic rituals, and military/weapon sorcery (astramantra).

summary: The Akulavīratantra is an early Kaula / Yoginī Kaula scriptural text transmitted within the corpus ascribed to Matsyendranātha. It expounds an uncompromising non-dual realization of ultimate reality designated as the Akulavīra ('Hero of the Transcendent'), identified with innate bliss (sahajānanda) and the all-pervading divine nature within the practitioner's own body. Rejecting the doctrines of scholastic systems (Nyāya, Vaiśeṣika, Bauddha, Jaina, Somasiddhānta, Mīmāṃsā) as well as outward ritual and haṭhayogic technicalities, it teaches immediate liberation through effortless dwelling in the transcendent state.

summary: The Lakṣmītantra is a major canonical Pāñcarātra scripture (saṃhitā), notable for presenting the goddess Lakṣmī (Śrī) as the supreme creative and dynamic power (Śakti) of Nārāyaṇa. In 57 chapters, the text expounds Pāñcarātra cosmogony, the six divine gunas, the theory of vyūha emanations, mantraśāstra, ritual diagram construction (maṇḍala/yantra), and devotional surrender (nyāsa/prapatti). In this e-text, the root verses are accompanied by a Sanskrit commentary gloss by Pandit V. Krishnamacharya.

summary: The Puruṣottamasaṃhitā is a canonical Pāñcarātrāgama text framed as a discourse delivered by the sage Vasiṣṭha to inquiring ṛṣis, passing down instructions revealed by Puruṣottama (Viṣṇu) to Brahmā. summary: The Yajñādhikāra is a canonical ritual manual (saṃhitā) belonging to the Vaikhānasa Vaiṣṇava Āgama corpus, traditionally attributed to the sage Bhṛgu. It expounds temple architecture, vāstumaṇḍala preparations, installation of icons (pratiṣṭhā), daily and seasonal oblations, and expiatory rites (niṣkṛti) to counteract procedural blemishes. Alongside the Kriyādhikāra, Khilādhikāra, and Prakīrṇādhikāra, it constitutes one of the four major Ādhikāra treatises of the Bhṛgu division.

summary: The Āgamaprāmāṇya is a foundational philosophical and polemical treatise by the Śrīvaiṣṇava master Yāmunācārya. The text defends the scriptural authority (prāmāṇya) and orthodox Vedic status of the Pāñcarātra Āgamas against charges of heterodoxy, invalidity, or non-Vedic origin raised primarily by Mīmāṃsakas and Advaitins. Yāmunācārya argues for the intrinsic validity and divine authorship of the Āgamas by Nārāyaṇa and defends the orthodox caste status and temple-worship rituals of the Bhāgavatas, laying the foundation for Rāmānuja's Viśiṣṭādvaita Vedānta.
